#102236. Avalanche Fatality Warns About Early Ski Conditions In The Alps

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (802 w)
📖 Baca

Avalanche Fatality Warns About Early Ski Conditions In The Alps

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (802 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that little snow on the mountains doesn’t mean safe conditions.
  • Recent findings suggest that with the ski season barely underway, this is Europe’s first avalanche victim this season.
  • Most victims perished in the Alps: 40 in Italy, 35 in France, 33 in Austria, and 18 in Switzerland.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that little snow on the mountains doesn’t mean safe conditions. An American off-piste skier died in the Austrian Alps last weekend after he triggered a small slab avalanche. It was far too small to bury him, but it carried him into an open crevasse below.

Recent findings suggest that with the ski season barely underway, this is Europe’s first avalanche victim this season. Last year, 151 people died in avalanches in Europe between October 2025 and June 2026, according to the European Avalanche Warning Service (EAWS), a shockingly high number.

Most victims perished in the Alps: 40 in Italy, 35 in France, 33 in Austria, and 18 in Switzerland. It was the 13th most deadly year in the Alps since record-keeping began. It was also the highest tally ever since the “Winter of Terror” of 1951. Avalanche prevention standards have improved a lot since then, but the number of leisure skiers, climbers, and hikers in the mountains has multiplied as well. (Most of those 1951 victims lived in villages along avalanche paths.).

Last weekend’s accident took place at the Stubai Glacier ski resort. The glacier sections of the Alps typically open for skiing weeks earlier than other mountain resorts, thanks to their higher altitudes and glacial ice, which can provide good October skiing with just a thin layer of fresh snow on top. Stubai’s ski resort opened on October 9 this year.

A map of Stubai Glacier ski resort with the area where the accident happened circled in red. Photo: Stubaier Gletscher website.

It has been revealed that the skier was on his own, descending in an out-of-bounds area below East Daunkogel Peak at around 11:30am. His tracks on the snow show he eventually abandoned the snow-covered glacier and ventured onto a steeper, rocky area. At some point, he broke a small slab of crusty snow which dragged him some 50 meters into an open bergschrund, where he fatally fell 20 meters down, according to the Lawinen Report.

The accident site, with the skier’s tracks visible,  and the movement of the snow slab — 50m long and 25m wide — marked in pink. Photo: Lawinen Report.

It has been revealed that other skiers in the area saw the accident and raised the alarm, but the skier had died by the time they extracted him from the crevasse. The police said the slab was only 10cm to 30cm thick, and the slide was just 25 meters wide. The crevasse was 50 meters below the fracture point.

Sources indicate that avalanche risks are obvious on heavily loaded slopes, but the accident indicates that even a thin layer of unstable snow can cause a fatal fall. In this case, the snow had fallen recently on the verglass ice over glacier-polished smooth rocks, and had no time to settle. This is a typical early-season condition in mountain ranges around the world.

The accident occurred at nearly 3,000m of altitude on a shady northeast slope, where the snow hardly transforms and settles during the short days of late fall. To make things worse, the report notes that wind had picked up that morning, creating a weak crust on top of loose, cold, fresh snow, prone to breaking.

Sources indicate that the avalanche site on the following day, with most of the terrain covered by freshly drifted snow. Photo: LWD Tirol.

The second factor was exposure: the skier might have easily survived the fall if the terrain had been a clean snow slope, but he was on rocky terrain, where a simple fall can result in serious injuries. Most of all, the crevasse below created what the report described as a “terrain trap.”.

Sources indicate that fans of backcountry and ski touring are eager to hit the slopes with the first snowflakes, and the scarcely covered terrain may provide a false sense of safety from avalanches. But objective dangers go beyond the massive powder avalanches and also include falls on icy slopes. In addition, the glaciers are dry after the summer, and the crevasses are wide open.

After a mild fall, snow is falling heavily in the Alps this week, significantly improving conditions for the region’s ski resorts. Most of them plan to open this weekend. The snow will also offer backcountry opportunities, but conditions will remain highly unstable.

In a recent development, snowfall up to two meters is expected today in the Alps. Graphic by meteoexploration.com.

The avalanche report today by the Tiroler Avalanche Service (LWD Tirol) demonstrates low risk in the Austrian mountains, a remarkable risk (3 out of 5) in the Swiss Alps, and moderate risk (2 out of 5) in France.

According to recent reports, the avalanche forecast for today, November 19, in the Alps shows remarkable (level 3-orange) risk, especially in Switzerland. Graphic: LWD Tirol.

  • His father subsequently traveled to Japan and offered a reward of RMB500,000 ($75,000) for information leading to his recovery alive, or RMB100,000 ($15,000) for recovery of his body.

Today, November 19, the Yamanashi Prefectural Police announced that they had ended the search for Chinese climber Chen Jie, 25, according to the Japanese national newspaper Mainichi Shimbun. Chen disappeared November 8 on the main Yoshida Trail after continuing alone up 3,776m Mount Fuji during its closed season.

His two companions reportedly turned back because of deteriorating weather and inadequate equipment. Chen continued on his own without crampons or sufficient cold-weather clothing. His last video was sent that morning between 2,300 and 2,700m.

His father subsequently traveled to Japan and offered a reward of RMB500,000 ($75,000) for information leading to his recovery alive, or RMB100,000 ($15,000) for recovery of his body.

Ironically, Chen belonged to China’s Blue Sky Rescue Team, a volunteer search-and-rescue organization. His mother told local media that he had participated in rescues in China and had some mountaineering experience, including trekking and climbing in Nepal and Indonesia.

Breaking: Climbers Forge Upcoming Route on Mount Shiva Despite Limited Acclimatization

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (614 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Benjamin Bosshard and Philippo Sala will never forget their first experience above 6,000m and the newly introduced route they opened with Stefan Siegrist on India’s Bahai Jar, commonly known as Mount Shiva (6,142m).
  • Expeditions in the Indian Himalaya are usually quiet while they take place, because satellite phones and InReach devices are prohibited.
  • Siegrist had already visited the Chenab River Valley area in 2018 and climbed Shiva with Jonas Schild, but he still had designs on its unclimbed northwest ridge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Benjamin Bosshard and Philippo Sala will never forget their first experience above 6,000m and the newly introduced route they opened with Stefan Siegrist on India’s Bahai Jar, commonly known as Mount Shiva (6,142m).

Expeditions in the Indian Himalaya are usually quiet while they take place, because satellite phones and InReach devices are prohibited. After returning home, however, Stefan Siegrist reported the details, and the team’s cameraman, Christoph Detschmann, posted a video summary of the expedition:.

Siegrist had already visited the Chenab River Valley area in 2018 and climbed Shiva with Jonas Schild, but he still had designs on its unclimbed northwest ridge. At the end of September, he, Sala, and Bosshard reached base camp in the Kishtwar massif.

Industry observers note that the three Swiss climbers were prepared to endure a long period of bad weather while acclimatizing. To their surprise, a good weather window opened right away. It was too good to let go, despite not being properly acclimatized and Sala and Bosshard’s lack of altitude experience. The window was expected to last just three days. After many “discussions and doubts,” they left base camp on October 3.

Sala had a headache during the first night, but the following morning, they were all totally focused on the climb, and the tension disappeared. “We assumed that we were unlikely to reach the summit on this attempt, and that we would therefore be wasting our only chance before a major storm [brought] the season to an end,” Siegrist explained. “So from then on, the idea was simply to climb higher and acclimatize, without any pressure.”.

A moment of the climb, filmed from a drone by Christoph Detschmann.

Sources indicate that along the way, they discovered they had left their stove at base camp. No problem in 2026: The expedition photographer used his drone to carry the stove up to them. The use of drones was a hot topic during the recent Piolets d’Or: To what extent are they compatible with alpine-style criteria? While most accepted that drones could scout routes or sections out of view of base camp, many considered using them to carry equipment up a face to be a red line.

On Shiva, Siegrist states the delivery of the missing stove “proved essential to the success of the climb.”.

It has been revealed that the climbers spent their second night at 5,250m at the base of the northwest ridge. On the following morning, they had to decide whether to continue or retreat. They all felt well, but starting the highly technical ridge was a point of no return. At the same time, Siegrist recalls, they realized they really had a chance to summit. And so on they went.

Industry observers note that that night, they stopped at 5,700m in what Siegrist describes as a crucial moment. His partners had not been at that altitude before, and the latest forecast declared a storm the following day. They decided to wait and see what the morning looked like. No one slept at all that night.

In a recent development, the last meters before the summit. Drone image by Christoph Detschmann.

The sky was still clear when the team set off again at 4am, so they chose to keep going. “After a while, we finally reached the final slope, just 300m below the summit,” Siegrist wrote. By now, they knew they were going to make it. They reached the top at 7:44am, six days after arriving in Base Camp, and just in time to hurry down as the storm approached.

The climbers descended via the 1985 Japanese route (see topo below), and reached their base camp tents as it started to snow.

10 of the Hottest Hunting Suppressors on the Market in 2026

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2189 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • Industry observers note that it’s never been easier to get a suppressor for your hunting rifle.
  • I’ve been shooting every new suppressor I can get my hands on for years, and these are the best ones that I have used.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

Industry observers note that it’s never been easier to get a suppressor for your hunting rifle. But choosing one, for a first-time buyer, can be intimidating. There are thousands of options on the market and narrowing it down to the best can for your hunting rifle isn’t easy if you don’t know what to look for. So many new suppressors are hitting the market that what was a top-of-the-line can a couple years ago is just average today.

I’ve been shooting every new suppressor I can get my hands on for years, and these are the best ones that I have used.

Sources indicate that this is one of the best hunting rifle suppressors I have ever used. Like many others that are leading the pack, it’s 3D printed from titanium, making it both strong and economical. It measures 5 inches long and weighs just 5.75 ounces. Despite its lightweight profile, it’s very quiet. In fact, it’s substantially quieter than several other popular suppressors — something I noted on a recent antelope hunt.

This is one of my top picks because it’s simple, rugged, quiet, and you’ll hardly notice it on your muzzle. It is direct thread only and, because threads are cut into the suppressor itself, they cannot be changed like a HUB-compatible suppressor. For a hunting suppressor, that’s a feature, not a bug. At $900, this is a really good value. Many top-level hunting suppressors will cost you $1,000 or more.

In the year since its introduction, Airlock has released 30-cal and 7mm versions of the Zero Gravity, as well as a 3.7-ounce Zero Gravity Nano, which is designed for bolt-action centerfire .22 cals like the 22 ARC, 22 Creed, and .22-250 Rem. It’s slightly larger than a rimfire suppressor, but satisfyingly quiet.

The Nomad Ti XC is another excellent option for a hunting suppressor. Its 3D printed design allows for modern baffles and reduces weak spots. The front and rear of the can are threaded and it is compatible with HUB rear mounts. I prefer using a Silencerco Ti direct thread adapter on the rear, and the standard .308 front cap. Other companies like Salmon River Solutions are making accessories like a directional brake that threads into the front cap to further reduce recoil and tame down cartridges like the .300 PRC. As pictured, the suppressor weighs less than 10 ounces and works wonderfully for anything 30-caliber and under. A nice feature is the inclusion of deep tool notches which makes removing the HUB mounts easy without worry of damaging the suppressor.

Another great option, if you want a shorter overall length for your rifle, is the Nomad TiOTB, which has a chamber that extends back over the barrel. This suppressor has the same interchangeable endcaps, but works exclusively with a thread-over-brake mount.

Industry observers note that I’ve been shooting the TiTrex 300 Ti for several months now, and this is one of the best options for a general-purpose hunting suppressor out there. After all that shooting, it still only weighs 9.5 ounces, and it offers great mounting and front-cap modularity.

A couple years ago, the Silencerco Scythe Ti was one of few .30-cal silencers that light, but it’s been plagued by weld failure problems. The TiTrex 300 Ti is also made of titanium, is slightly lighter, and uses HUB mounts at the rear and an open-source front cap that works with the Silencerco Bravo front mounts. You can use a normal endcap or the short endcap brake, which helps reduce recoil, and both have great spanner wrench notches. It’s also compatible with some aftermarket Endcap brakes like the Salmon River Solutions Grim, which can help cut recoil even more.

Sources indicate that the TiTrex has a 3D-printed body and baffle system that is rugged, durable, and even full-auto rated. This is a great option to use with a front brake as a competition can, but that can also work well on your hunting rifle. It would also be a solid choice as your first suppressor. A unique feature is that the serialized portion of the suppressor is a stainless-steel band at the rear of the can, that can be moved to a different core if you manage to wear the original out or damage it somehow.

It has been revealed that there are three substantial trends in hunting suppressors in 2026, and the Buckskin 30 from Tenet tackles all of them. First, it’s 3D printed. Additive manufacturing has allowed companies to swiftly develop and prototype suppressor models while reducing weak points like welds on thin titanium.

Second, it incorporates a front brake. Suppressors reduce recoil by slowing gases as they exit the muzzle, and incorporating a brake on the front tames them even further. The Buckskin features a built-in brake that is non-adjustable and won’t come loose.

Third, it’s light. It’s printed with titanium and mine weighs 8.5 ounces — making it the lightest .30-cal suppressor I own. I’ve used this suppressor on my 20-inch 300 PRC, several 6.5 Creedmoors, and have been putting a lot of rounds through it on a 16-inch 7mm Backcountry. It does a great job at reducing recoil while adding minimal extra weight.

If you want more adjustability and increased recoil reduction, the Tenet Limited 30 is another suppressor to look at. These are more expensive, but feature a removable front brake that cuts your rifle movement dramatically. Mine has a two-port brake and, while the first generation of brakes tended to blast your face with gas, the recently-released gen 2 brake has small steps in the curved brake to disrupt that gas impulse. It’s much more pleasant. If spotting your impacts with larger cartridges is important to you, a can like this fits the bill.

In the days of year-long waiting periods, modularity was king for hunting suppressors. While modular cans have their place, a simple dedicated hunting silencer is hard to beat. This fully 3D-printed titanium can from Unknown Munitions weighs about 11 ounces and features a reflex design, meaning the rear portion of the suppressor goes back over the barrel. That reflex expansion chamber allows a shorter portion — about four inches — to stick out in front of your muzzle. This improves balance and gives you a more compact package than the average 8-inch suppressor. The reflex design also creates a noticeably duller sound signature, whereas some produce a very sharp, snappy sound.

Industry observers note that these are available in .30 caliber as well as 6.5mm and 6mm options, and models and fit over 0.75-inch diameter steel barrels and the OGL model fits larger carbon-fiber barrels. This suppressor isn’t modular, so you need to ensure compatibility before you order. Also check out their Reaper suppressor, which I haven’t had the chance to use, but should be another top contender.

In a recent development, I’ve used several of B&T’s Print-X series of titanium 3D-printed suppressors and have been impressed by all of them. Their modular VERS36 Ti model, however, deserves special recognition. To my knowledge, this is the lightest modular 36-caliber suppressor on the market, and it’s way cheaper than similar, more primitive cans were several years ago. If you’re wanting to get a suppressor to start out with, or to use on multiple hunting rifles, this is your jam.

In a recent development, it’s got 36-caliber baffles and comes with a .360 front cap. The rear is HUB-compatible and B&T makes nice titanium direct-thread adapters. You can get smaller front caps as well. If using on smaller cartridges or you just need a shorter overall package, the front section is removable. This is a flow-through design with spiral baffles that works well on bolt actions and gas-guns alike. It’s ideal for cartridges like the .350 Legend, but will work on anything with a .360-diameter bullet or smaller. I received mine through Silencer Central and it can be delivered to your door.

It has been revealed that the StingerWorx Evo Hunter is a lightweight suppressor that’s more affordable than the 3D printed titanium cans, and it’s also much more serviceable. A downside of most printed suppressors is that there isn’t a great way to remove large amounts of carbon buildup from the baffles. Soaking and ultrasonic cleaners help, but a lot of shooters want a suppressor that can be disassembled and manually cleaned.

Sources indicate that the Evo Hunter is just over 10 ounces, and it gets there by using multiple materials. It has a titanium blast baffle and chamber to provide a long service life, but uses an aluminum baffle stack downstream of that — where heat and abrasion isn’t as intense. If damaged, that front baffle stack is replaceable. Additionally, the Evo Hunter is compatible with StingerWorx’s front brake if you’re looking for additional recoil reduction. It’s got HUB threads at the rear and the blast chamber is deep enough to work with a variety of over-brake HUB mounts that you might already have. For the light weight, versatility, and serviceability, this can is a great value.

It has been revealed that there are lots of suppressors out there and, because many of them are so similar, lots of good ones can get lost in the mix. Because we cover a lot of leading-edge ultralight cans, don’t think that we don’t pay attention to budget options, too. There are bottom-tier suppressors that are very cheap — often made of mostly aluminum — that will work, but can also leave buyers dissatisfied. When it comes to bang for your buck, stainless steel is still one of the best materials for a more affordable can. The first suppressor I ever bought was a large .30-cal stainless can. It was durable and affordable and its weight was the only downside.

The Banish HNT 30 SS is a great example of a modern great value. It’s compact and, at 13.8 ounces, not excessively heavy. It’s suitable for virtually any hunting rifle .30-caliber and smaller, and similar in size and form to the lightweight Banish Backcountry titanium can. It’s got hub threads at the rear and comes with a direct-thread adapter. If you’re looking to try a suppressor for hunting and want a good-quality can, this is a great place to start.

If you’re looking for maximum suppression of your massive-bore cartridges, the Goliath Gen 2 from Liberty Suppressors is an excellent option. This beast of a silencer is 10.25 inches long by 2 inches in diameter and designed specifically for cartridges like the .458 Socom, .450 Bushmaster, and .45/70 Gov’t. While big, this can is relatively light. It’s got twice the volume of suppressors like the Silencerco Hybrid 46, but weighs only about 4 ounces more (22 ounces total). This is a perfect fit for anyone hunting with a short-barreled .458 or .450 Bushmaster, or a trapper-style .45/70.

The suppressor has a titanium sleeve and titanium baffle stack that’s removable and serviceable so you can shoot cast lead bullets and clean out lead fouling — unlike sealed suppressors. I’ve had a Liberty .22 rimfire can for many years, and this is essentially a much larger version of that. I’ve been shooting it on my .45/70 and it’s working wonderfully on my .338 ARC SBR with subsonic ammo.

It has been revealed that one of the best values in lightweight modular suppressors is the BDE from Primary Weapons Systems. I’ve been shooting the 5.56 model for the last several months, and it combines smart manufacturing with durability, value, and the kind of modularity a lot of hunters want. The BDE has hub threads at the rear, a blast chamber segment, and a 3D-printed main baffle segment. Forward of that, it has removable individual threaded baffle segments topped with an end cap.

This is a sealed suppressor, but baffles are designed to allow gasses to flow better and reduce backpressure, making a great option for both a bolt gun and AR-style semi-auto. Each segment of the can has wrench notches making disassembly easy, and you can customize to the platform you’ll be shooting. This has been living on my .223 practice bolt-action and the irregular surface contours do seem to help break up mirage. The BDE is also available in .30- and .36- caliber models, all with customizable baffle configurations.

According to recent reports, picking through the many different suppressor options can be daunting, and most good suppressors perform similarly. To find one that you’ll be happy with, consider details like construction and weight, but also the level of modularity you desire, or whether you’re just looking for a good value. If one of these isn’t quite what you’re looking for, I hope that seeing these options and features will help you home in on the model that you will be most satisfied with. The suppressor market is constantly evolving, and we will continue to use and test suppressors with the goal of helping you make the most informed decisions possible.

Latest Update: Two Inexperienced Teens Rescued After 20 Hours on Grossglockner

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (475 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two Germans, aged 15 and 18, spent almost 20 hours on Austria’s highest mountain before being evacuated by helicopter on November 15.
  • According to recent reports, initially, police reported that the pair had reached the 3,798m summit and become lost while descending.
  • Their ordeal began around 11pm on Saturday, November 14.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two Germans, aged 15 and 18, spent almost 20 hours on Austria’s highest mountain before being evacuated by helicopter on November 15.

According to recent reports, initially, police reported that the pair had reached the 3,798m summit and become lost while descending. The younger climber disputes this, saying they turned back near an alpine hut at 3,454m because his companion felt ill.

Their ordeal began around 11pm on Saturday, November 14. The pair had no previous experience with such a serious mountain but had prepared by reading websites, watching videos, training physically, and asking others for tips. They did carry crampons, an ice axe, a helmet, a rope, a belay device, and extra clothing.

It has been revealed that it took them a long time before they decided to turn around. The descent went well at first, but one spot seemed too dangerous to them. To get around it, they followed someone else’s tracks in the snow, but these suddenly disappeared. While looking for a way, they got stuck in deep snow. The older boy called for help at around 6:30pm on November 15, according to Austria’s public broadcaster, ORF.at.

It has been revealed that at first, rescuers tried to guide the pair down by phone. More than two hours later, the boys were still stuck, so a helicopter was dispatched. The rescuers found the pair, exhausted, disoriented, and hypothermic, at around 2,800m.

Sources indicate that A rescue helicopter brings the teens to safety. Photo: Mountain Rescue KALS.

Yesterday, rescue leader Peter Tembler criticized their lack of alpine experience and preparation. He told the German Press Agency that the pair lacked sufficient experience for the terrain and winter conditions. He also criticized their late-night departure.

Industry observers note that according to Tembler, a section that normally takes four to five hours took them almost 12. Other climbers reportedly advised them against continuing.

Tembler believes an increasing number of inexperienced people are attempting serious alpine routes, sometimes encouraged by social media accounts that downplay the difficulty. The disagreement has become a public debate about risk-taking, responsibility, and rescue operations.

As Austria’s highest peak, Grossglockner is a magnet for climbers of all stripes and has more than its share of controversy. In January 2025, a man abandoned his less experienced girlfriend high on the mountain. She froze to death, and an Austrian court later convicted him of manslaughter for leaving her behind. This summer, an altercation occurred on Grossglockner in which a guide insulted a passing climber and nearly pushed him off a cliff. At the same time, veteran alpinists are still setting bold newly introduced routes here.

In a recent development, according to Der Standard, Grossglockner gets 8,000 to 9,000 ascents each year, with an average of two dozen rescues annually. Between 2005 and 2025, 29 climbers have died on the mountain.

#102223. Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Stalking Cornfields During Deer Season

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3895 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Stalking Cornfields During Deer Season

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3895 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There are two things that my friend Harvey Wilcourt loves more than anything else.
  • In a recent development, harve and I had scheduled a day of winter fishing for walleyes, and the strategy was to meet at a well-known parking area near the lake and then decide upon a particular frozen-over bay that might offer the best results.
  • Sources indicate that at first, I shrugged my shoulders, not knowing in which direction he might have headed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are two things that my friend Harvey Wilcourt loves more than anything else. One is ice-fishing, and the other is eating peanuts. It might not sound as though that bears any relation to whitetail deer hunting, but one time it actually helped me to collect a very substantial buck.

In a recent development, harve and I had scheduled a day of winter fishing for walleyes, and the strategy was to meet at a well-known parking area near the lake and then decide upon a particular frozen-over bay that might offer the best results. As it happened, however, car trouble delayed my arrival by more than an hour, so naturally, when I finally reached our meeting place, Harve had already headed out onto the ice-shrouded lake.

Sources indicate that at first, I shrugged my shoulders, not knowing in which direction he might have headed. Then, I happened to look down at the ground near his parked vehicle, and guess what I spotted? Right, peanut shells! Right then, a wide smile came across my face because I instantly knew that tracking Harve would be easy.

It has been revealed that in most places, the trail was relatively thin, but occasionally I’d come to an abandoned hole in the ice where shells littered the entire area. Then, the trail would lead off into the distance to another hole, and then still another. Eventually, I spied my partner in a distant channel, and we spent the remainder of the day fishing together. Without the discarded peanut shells showing the way, I might have never located Harve and might have ended up fishing solo that day.

In a recent development, the irony is that several years later, I duplicated the same type of feat, but this time the trail eventually led me to an eight-point buck. To the best of my knowledge, whitetails don’t maintain any particular fetish for peanuts, but they do love corn. And after filling their paunches in a cornfield, it’s quite common for them to carry off a cob in their mouths and continue eating from it as they travel to a nearby bedding site. Sometimes, they’ll finish with the cob along the way and let it fall to the ground right there. Other times, they’ll carry the cob all the way back to the actual bedding location, perhaps to snack upon later.

In any event, I had been hiking along the edge of a large cornfield near my home in southern Ohio, and in coming upon a threadbare trail exiting from the corn, I had found a partially eaten cob. Recalling my amusing experience with Harvey, I decided to follow the trail, and just inside the leading edge of a nearby beech forest I discovered another cob on the ground, and then still another. All of the cobs were in various stages of deterioration, so I knew that they had been dropped at different times over a period of weeks. Large, fresh deer tracks of uniform size and large droppings provided additional clues, and eventually, more than 300 yards into the timber, I came upon a lone bed. That confirmed I was in a buck’s bailiwick, because had there been tracks of varied sizes and several beds, I could have inferred that the deer were only does.

Sources indicate that after resting the area for two days, I snuck back into the spot and quietly fabricated a makeshift blind behind a convenient blowdown overlooking the trail. Later, when there was just enough light to make a shot, a gray shadow materialized in the distance, traveling right along the trail. My arrow caught the eight-pointer at the base of the neck, and after sprinting 50 yards, the buck collapsed in a heap.

It’s no secret that bucks and corn go together like bacon and eggs, and we have plenty of all of those commodities, especially throughout the Midwestern agricultural belt. In fact, after talking recently with my local extension agent, I learned that in 1986, in the nine major farming states stretching from Ohio to Minnesota, more than 46 million acres of land were planted to corn.

Moreover, acquiring hunting permission in agricultural regions is invariably easier than it is on other privately owned lands because of the extensive damage often inflicted by wild animals. In Wisconsin alone, it was estimated that during 1986, deer destroyed more than $22 million worth of corn, and this cost each farmer an average of $490. Add to this the combined losses of alfalfa, soybeans, truck garden crops and other foods that whitetails regularly dine upon, and it should come as no surprise that though a majority of farmers certainly enjoy seeing deer on their land, they don’t take kindly to whitetail populations reaching such levels that they severely cut into the farmers’ annual incomes.

The exasperating problem that most hunters face is how to effectively hunt those often mammoth and intimidating cornfields.

The first task is to confirm that deer are indeed using the corn, and this is easily ascertained by merely hiking the perimeter of the field and looking for tracks entering and leaving the food plot. Obviously, the best time to do this is either after a rainy period, when the ground is soft, or after several days of light snowfall.

Industry observers note that if the region has been experiencing several weeks of dry weather, however, and the terrain is like hardpan, tracks are not easily detected. It is in this case that other types of insight must be applied to the hunting situation. For example, one time I discovered a cornfield where many stalks had been knocked down and countless partially eaten ears were on the ground. Initially, I thought that I had found a mother lode of deer activity, but I was dead wrong.

As I learned later, several raccoons had been at work. The telltale giveaway — pointed out to me by a friend who is a serious naturalist — should have been the fact that the ears were only partially eaten. Raccoons rarely eat an entire ear of corn; instead, they knock down a cornstalk and bite off just the tender tip of the ear, then move on to the next stalk.

Industry observers note that if the cornfield borders a climax forest, corn-hungry squirrels may also give the false impression that deer have been at work. But in this situation, the animals climb the stalks, nibble away at the ears, stuff their cheeks and then retreat to their dens, where the scavenged kernels are placed in storage. This leaves the ears still attached to the stalks but gives them a ragtag, moth-eaten appearance.

Sources indicate that if deer are working the corn, however, the clues to look for in the absence of tracks are scattered cobs on the ground that have been cleaned of almost every kernel of corn. Also keep on the lookout for droppings.

Once it has been determined that deer are hitting a particular cornfield on a regular basis, the best mode of hunting must be decided upon. And contrary to what you might expect, the best method of hunting is not necessarily the tactic you might like to use most, but rather the one that most appropriately falls in line with the agricultural cropping practices in your region.

It has been revealed that in many areas, conventional harvesting methods are engaged in sometime during October or November, when the corn is brown and cured. The picking operation leaves the cornfield in a stubble-like condition, yet there remains on the ground plenty of spillage residue to attract the interest of local deer. Under these conditions, with the previously standing cornstalks no longer present and the concealing cover therefore eliminated, midday hunting is virtually out of the question. The animals will predictably visit the corn only in the early morning hours or at dusk. If hunting pressure is intense in the region, the deer may even be strictly nocturnal in their feeding.

Conversely, in many other regions, it is becoming an increasingly popular agricultural practice to leave corn standing in the field for as long as possible. With grain-elevator storage costs escalating like never before, and future market prices always uncertain, many farmers nowadays are simply delaying their harvesting either until such time as they have a specific need for the corn for stock feed or until the price increases, which it often does in February or March. Consequently, the hunter now finds that he can effectively hunt the cornfields not only early and late in the day, but also during the midday hours.

Regardless of whether a solo hunter elects to use bowhunting equipment, a rifle, a slug-loaded shotgun, a muzzleloader or a handgun, there are four options to choose from when hunting standing corn: sneak-hunting in and around the corn; sneak-hunting in and around nearby heavy-cover regions; taking a stand designed to intercept the animals coming to the corn; or taking a stand designed to intercept the animals as they leave the corn.

Still again, the right method to use may not necessarily be the hunter’s favorite way to hunt, but it must be geared to existing conditions. The foremost determinant that I rely upon to make my decision is the presence or absence of wind — assuming there is standing corn, of course.

Sources indicate that on a windy day, I do not want to be in a tree stand. Wind is the result of downdrafts of cold air meeting warm air. Therefore, no matter which direction the wind is coming from, it will have a tendency to force scents down toward the ground, and this will readily give away a hunter’s location. Compounding the problem is the fact that deer do not like to move on windy days because the wind disallows the effective use of their sense of hearing. Calm days, on the other hand, or those during which the wind is only slightly and gently blowing from one specific direction are ideal for quietly waiting on stand for the deer to walk by.

Industry observers note that just the opposite is the case when hunting in and around the cornfield itself. Now is when a hunter wants the windiest conditions possible. This is because when whitetails bed during the midday hours, they feel most secure and safe by retreating into the heaviest, thickest cover they can find. In many agricultural regions, the terrain surrounding cornfields, such as gullies and forest lands, simply does not offer hiding cover that is as thick as that in the cornfields themselves. Consequently, the whitetails will commonly bed right in the cornfields in these areas.

Now it becomes obvious why the very time to hunt these cornfields is during periods of high winds. It is because under blowing conditions, a cornfield is a very noisy place. The leaves are dry and brittle later in the season, and the loud rustling and crackling noises that they make in the wind cover up so much human error in prowling around that a hunter can quite easily walk right up on deer without them suspecting his presence.

Moreover, a hunter doesn’t have to worry about his scent when hunting in a cornfield. Wind in a cornfield is a tricky thing. It hits the stalks and broad leaves and bounces every which way. As a result, deer in a cornfield may catch a hunter’s scent, but in most cases they will not be able to determine the direction from which it’s coming. As a result, they lock up, or freeze, in position because they know that if they attempt to run, they may blunder right into trouble. And if the hunter then happens to step into the right row of corn, he may have an easy shot at a stationary buck.

Sources indicate that in going back to calm days, during which patiently waiting in a tree stand or ground blind is the preferred method of hunting either standing corn or stubble fields, there are two tricks that I use to properly locate my stand. First, it’s necessary to engage in enough scouting to know in advance where trails are located. It must be remembered, however, that it’s quite common for deer to leave a cornfield via a different trail than the one they used to enter the field, assuming, of course, that the deer are bedding somewhere other than in the corn itself. Therefore, a morning stand to intercept the deer leaving the corn will undoubtedly be in a different place than an evening stand that has been set up to ambush deer coming from their bedding areas to the corn.

Industry observers note that thus, what a hunter initially wants to do after locating trails is to ascertain what time of day they’re being used. The direction in which tracks are pointing is a sure clue — if the tracks are pointing toward the corn, they were probably made in the evening; if they are directed away from the corn, they probably indicate an exit trail that the animals use in the morning. Also, the hunter should be on the lookout for corncobs. Because deer obviously do not carry cobs from their bedding region back to the cornfield, but do carry cobs from the field to their bedding sites, the presence of intermittent cobs along the trail indicates in no uncertain terms that the travel route is a morning trail.

It has been revealed that as a general rule, I do not like for either a morning stand or an evening stand to be too close to a cornfield where deer are feeding. If possible, depending upon his evaluation of the terrain, a hunter should try to situate his stands or blinds 100 to 200 yards from the cornfield so that he can overlook the exit and entrance trails that the deer are using to enter or leave the food plot.

There are several good reasons for this strategy. To begin with, the largest bucks in any given region do not like to expose themselves unnecessarily in broad daylight, especially in regions where hunting pressure is intense. They can pretty much be counted upon to leave the cornfield at the very hint of early morning’s first light. Because it may still be too dark to shoot accurately, the hunter wants to be farther back down the trail that the deer are using so that by the time they reach the stand location, it will be fully light enough to see.

Recent findings suggest that conversely, in the evening hours, the very largest bucks seldom enter a cornfield when the sky is still brightly illuminated. They like to linger back in the shaded, heavy cover of their bedding areas, sometimes not actually entering the cornfield until after full dark. Naturally, therefore, if a stand or blind is positioned close to the cornfield, by the time the deer reach the location, it will be too dark to see.

In all of this, it should be kept in mind that though the hunter doesn’t want to position his stand too close to the cornfield for either a morning or an evening watch, neither does he want his stand too close to the bedding area that the animals are using. This is simply too risky because the animals are very likely to detect the hunter as he tries to approach his stand site; and if they are spooked from the very region that they previously considered the safest place to be, they may not return for many days.

In fact, it’s worth mentioning that during the course of scouting, I always move slowly but make plenty of noise. Sometimes, I even whistle to myself as though I’m engaged in some type of routine outdoor work such as that of a surveyor or forester. Whitetails are accustomed to this type of minor disturbance, and they will simply circle around the intruder. And because the deer have the opportunity to hide or sneak away undetected, they’ll still have full confidence in the security of their chosen area, prompting them to return shortly after I’ve left.

Recent findings suggest that later, when I return to begin my hunting vigil, I stalk my stand. I actually sneak up on it just as though I were stillhunting through the woods. By doing this, the chances of any nearby deer recognizing my presence are much lower.

Pursuing whitetails when they’re actually in the corn is one of deer hunting’s most challenging and exciting endeavors. But the hunter should remember two things: If the terrain surrounding the cornfield is devoid of thick security cover, meaning that the corn itself is the very best place to hide and bed, the deer will probably cling to the corn all day and every day. This is especially the case if water is readily available in rain-filled puddles or tractor ruts. The second thing to remember — again — is that the windiest days are the best days to hunt.

Simply sneak-hunting around the perimeter of the cornfield can put venison on the meat pole, particularly during the early and late hours of the day, when the deer are feeding and have a tendency to work along “edges.” I’ve most often found this to be the case when the cornfield is bordered on one or more sides by lush hay meadows planted to some legume such as alfalfa, red or white clover or lespedeza. This is because it’s rather uncustomary for whitetails to gorge themselves on a single food type, as they are opportunists in their feeding habits and like variety in their diets. Therefore, if you know of a cornfield bordered by some other equally preferred food, you’ve hit paydirt!

In sneak-hunting around the perimeter of a cornfield, a hunter shouldn’t expose himself in the open by remaining along the outside edge. Instead, he should stay one or two rows inside the edge of the cornfield — just far enough in so that he’s concealed yet can still see along the outside edge and into the adjacent, secondary food plot. The only exception to this rule is when the cornfield butts up directly against a brushy thicket or other bordering cover. In this case, the hunter can remain along the outermost edge of the corn and move slowly along with minimal chance of detection.

If the entire outside perimeter of the cornfield has been worked and no deer have been seen, it’s now time to assume that the whitetails are deeper within the confines of the corn, where they are most probably either feeding or bedding.

According to recent reports, if the hunter is familiar with the terrain from previous scouting missions — before the corn was planted — he should try to recall the locations in the field where there were rock piles, soupy swales, sand pockets and the like. These exist in many fields, and farmers simply plow and plant around them. Once the surrounding corn has grown high, however, such places are hidden from view, and they are the very types of locations where deer commonly like to bed. The hunter should sneak up on these places during windy conditions, and he might very well shoot an unsuspecting deer right in its bed.

If firearms are being used and several hunting partners are working together, staging drives is an excellent way to push deer through the corn to the opposite end of the field, where standers are likely to have shots. But there are a few important points to bear in mind when using this method. If the cornfield is large, it is imperative that a large number of drivers — spaced no more than eight to 10 rows apart — be employed, because otherwise the deer, reluctant to leave the security of the cover, will tirelessly circle and sneak back between the drivers. Consequently, if there are only a few hunters participating in the drive, only smaller cornfields where the animals can be moved effectively in a predetermined direction should be hunted.

Also, in the interest of safety, drives in cornfields should ideally include stand hunters placed in tree stands, or at least on some other elevated vantage points such as hillsides or knolls. This way, they will be able to look down and through the rows of corn to see both the escaping deer and their approaching partners. Likewise, when they shoot from such higher locations, the angles of their shots will be acutely downward, rather than horizontal.

Bowhunters can also enact drives in cornfields, but instead of hunting parallel with the rows in an attempt to push deer to standers in the distance, they should hunt perpendicular to the rows. In this type of situation, no hunters need be placed on stand.

Recent findings suggest that along the edge of the cornfield, the bowhunters should be spaced about 100 yards apart. The team leader at one end of this drive line should then use his arm to signal the first hunter on the far end to enter the field. As this hunter enters the first row, he should look right and left, then move on to the second row, and so on. After about 30 seconds, the drive master should then motion the next hunter to enter the cornfield in the same manner. What results is that instead of a straight and even drive line moving through the field, there is a diagonal shift across the field. Therefore, if a hunter enters a row and sees a deer he wants to shoot at, he can do so to either his right or left with complete confidence in safety, knowing that his partners to either side are far ahead of or behind him. If he does not wish to shoot, the deer will usually run parallel to the rows and eventually offer a shot to one of the next hunters in the line.

Finally, one of the shrewdest ways I know to evaluate potential cornfield hunting situations, especially in unfamiliar regions, is to go to a local airport and hire a small plane to fly over the terrain. Most pilots charge an average of $30 per hour, and if two hunters split the expense, the cost per person is not prohibitive. But most important, in one hour of flying about 500 feet above the ground, a hunter can learn more about an area than he can in two weeks of driving back roads and scouting on foot. A topographic map should be brought along, and the location and configuration of every cornfield in the region should be marked. Adjacent terrain and cover should be carefully examined, and it then should be easy to determine with a high level of accuracy how deer are living, moving and feeding in each specific region.

Read Next: Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Deer Hunting When the Weather Finally Turns Cold.

Industry observers note that believe me, if there are cornfields in the region you plan to hunt, you can be sure that bucks are in the corn — if not continuously, then at least intermittently. In either case, you should make the effort to be on hand, too, and when you leave, the chances are excellent that you’ll be dragging your deer behind you.

This story, “Deer By The Ear,” appeared in the November 1988 matter of Outdoor Life.

This episode of the storm-chasing TV series Storm Rising is titled “High Plains Insanity.” Produced by National Geographic, it follows Reed Timmer and Mike Theiss as they attempt to navigate and document an increasingly unpredictable storm season.

The storm-chasing segments are filmed like an action movie but, as Timmer makes clear, thrills are not the primary objective. As the climate changes and disrupts weather patterns, tornadoes are no longer limited to traditional seasons and ranges.

“That’s why we need to be on the ground directly in the path of these tornadoes,” Timmer explains, “to record data that no one else is getting.”.

In a recent development, driving into a potential tornado in Montana. Photo: Screenshot.

It has been revealed that with hurricane and tornado seasons now overlapping, the duo is forced to split up to cover the widest possible area and collect the most data. For the tornadoes, this means deploying a probe into the funnel.

Up north in the High Plains of the U.S. West and Midwest, Timmer and his dog Gizmo narrowly miss storm after storm. Gizmo is better tech giant but is a very poor navigator, while Timmer isn’t much better. He constantly makes wrong turns as he tries to navigate, drive, and prepare equipment. He does take the time to explain the basic weather science behind what he is failing to catch, such as the conditions that created the baseball-sized hail pummeling his windshield.

Timmer and Gizmo drive through the aftermath of a powerful tornado in the Black Hills of North Dakota. Photo: Screenshot.

In a recent development, in Florida, Theiss sleeps in his car to maintain a constant vigil along the coast. Our current scientific abilities, he explains, allow us to track the movement of hurricane systems with decent accuracy. But predicting their strength is much more difficult. Systems can suddenly turn deadly or fizzle out with equally short notice. In this case, the terrible-looking storm comes to nothing. He heads back up north to rejoin Timmer and Gizmo.

Sources indicate that gizmo buffeted by fierce winds. Photo: Screenshot.

In a recent development, the reunited trio prepares for a final effort, complete with a windshield-replacement sequence. They immediately drive into the gathering storm, passing through a hail core which, of course, destroys the fresh windshield. The Lord giveth and taketh away, et cetera. Soon they’re racing on a near-empty tank, as the powerful storm threatens to touch down at any moment.

In a recent development, it’s their last chance this season to deploy the probe. When, after a long, tense chase, they actually manage to do it, both erupt into cheers. Gizmo appears unmoved, despite the fact that this ground probe, deployed in a storm of this type, in this area, has never been deployed before and is sure to yield valuable scientific data.

A Routine Invasive-Species Survey in Lake Ontario Turned Up Something Much Stranger

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (439 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Routine research in the Great Lakes system morphed into an unusual catch this fall.
  • Fish and Wildlife Service survey crew caught a rare yellow burbot in October, according to a statement last week.
  • “The finding is notable because burbot populations in the lake are extremely low,” the agency wrote on Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Routine research in the Great Lakes system morphed into an unusual catch this fall.

A U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service survey crew caught a rare yellow burbot in October, according to a statement last week. The fish came from Oswego Harbor, New York, which is on the southeastern side of Lake Ontario. It’s a significant find for more than just its color variation.

“The finding is notable because burbot populations in the lake are extremely low,” the agency wrote on Nov. 10. “The species typically inhabit deeper, cooler waters than those found within the harbor.”.

It has been revealed that running the full length of an arm, the off-colored native burbot had xanthochromism, a genetic mutation that causes an animal’s pigment to be excessively yellow or orange. In fish, it displays on their scales and fins, but it can also show up on furred animals. It’s less common than albinism in the wild, but it’s also not unheard of.

A 6.6-foot orange-Creamsicle nurse shark turned up with the same condition, plus albinism, in 2024 in Costa Rica, and the first case of xanthochromism in a sunset-colored snook in the Gulf was documented in 2024.

According to recent reports, the variation might be appealing to fishermen, but it’s less fun for the fish themselves. Their bold coloring reduces their ability to hide within their habitat, which means they’re easy prey and often have shorter lifespans.

The deadly-bright hues look similar to banana trout, but that’s a different scenario.

According to recent reports, palomino trout, or bananas, are popular stockers for pond practice. They’re also covered in shades ranging from yellow to orange, but they’re bred that way on purpose. Hatcheries breed them from a mutant rainbow trout strain that lacks the dot pattern but keeps the bow’s notorious red lateral stripe. Despite the golden color, they aren’t related to California golden trout. The strain traces to a single yellow-mottled rainbow fingerling found at a West Virginia hatchery in 1955 and was introduced to anglers in 1963.

Read Next: These Are the Biggest North American Catfish of All Time.

According to recent reports, as for the yellow burbot in Oswego, it wasn’t released. Its body condition was in decline, so the fish was sent to Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine to be studied. It’s one of many fish analyzed during the region’s Aquatic Invasive Species Survey. The goal of the survey is early detection of a problem throughout the many bodies of water in the Great Lakes system, including harbors and rivers. Researchers use electrofishing, fyke nets, and gill nets to collect specimens for the survey.

#102212. The Burris Buck: How I Tagged the Biggest Mule Deer of All Time

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 20m • 📚 Deep Dive (4086 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

The Burris Buck: How I Tagged the Biggest Mule Deer of All Time

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (4086 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story, “Greatest Mule Deer of Them All,” appeared in the December 1975 issue of Outdoor Life.
  • I was walking the edge of a small canyon in Colorado’s San Juan National Forest when a rifle roared half a mile or so ahead of me.
  • Sources indicate that when I heard the shot I decided to get to a vantage point on the plateau as fast as I could, so I took off at a dead run.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story, “Greatest Mule Deer of Them All,” appeared in the December 1975 issue of Outdoor Life. Burris’ buck remains, all these years later, the No. 1 typical mule deer buck ever taken by a hunter, according to the Boone and Crockett Club. The antlers are now owned by Cabela’s. Burris tagged the buck on Oct. 19, 1972 in Dolores County, Colorado.

I was walking the edge of a small canyon in Colorado’s San Juan National Forest when a rifle roared half a mile or so ahead of me. Till then I’d figured on stillhunting to a plateau covered with scattered oak brush 400 yards north of me. A clump of brush there would have been a fine place to take a stand.

Sources indicate that when I heard the shot I decided to get to a vantage point on the plateau as fast as I could, so I took off at a dead run. I was almost on the plateau when I noticed movement in the oak brush and aspens on the other side of the canyon. I slammed to a stop and stared at the biggest deer I had ever seen. His body was enormous, and his rack seemed large enough for an elk.

Sources indicate that he wasn’t running flat out, but I knew I had to shoot in a hurry. The range was about 250 yards. The buck was moving up the canyon and away from me when I found him in my Leupold 3X-to-9X scope, I put the crosshairs on his back and touched off my Sako .264. He went down in his tracks. My big-game handloads consist of 125-grain Nosler bullets backed with 66.5 grains of No. 4831 powder. It’s a very potent load.

Sources indicate that related: My First Buck Was the Biggest Typical Mule Deer Ever Taken with a Bow. I Almost Discarded the Antlers.

In a recent development, I watched him for a while to make sure he wasn’t going to get up, and then I ran down a side canyon and up the other side of the big one to the fallen buck. When I ran my hands over the huge 18-point rack, I knew the antlers were very good. I was sure the deer would score high in the Boone and Crockett Club’s record book.

Recent findings suggest that if someone could have told me that my 1969 Colorado buck wasn’t even good enough to make the minimum score for listing in the record book, I wouldn’t have believed him. That’s the way it turned out, but a still bigger deer was ranging the same stretch of country.

Industry observers note that I’m 37. My wife and I live in Seguin, Texas, with our 17-year-old son and two daughters, aged 15 and eight. I’m a construction superintendent with an outfit that builds shopping centers, high-rise office buildings, and similar units.

Recent findings suggest that except for 3½ years spent in the U.S. Air Force, I’ve lived in Texas all my life. I began hunting when I was seven. My dad got me started and taught me to be a good hunter. I killed my first Texas whitetail when I was 13, and I’ve been nuts about deer hunting ever since. Though many of our Texas deer are so small we call them jackrabbits, we do have some large whitetails in the southern brush country. Some of those bucks field-dress at 200 pounds or a bit more, and some have exceptional antlers. Many years of hunting brush-country deer gave me trophy-hunting fever.

Recent findings suggest that I have always wanted to hunt Dall or Stone sheep in Alaska or British Columbia, but I’ve never had the money or the time. I finally decided that the next-best thing was to stay with deer and hunt trophy antlers.

In a recent development, my interest in camping had a lot to do with that first mule-deer hunt in Colorado in 1969. My friends and I have several four-wheel-drive vehicles and an assortment of camping gear. Charlie Fuller of Floresville, and Jack Smith of San Antonio, do a lot of hunting with me. Jack is my age. He’s a carpenter. Charlie, a few years younger, has a fertilizer-application operation. Both like to hunt deer the way I do, and they like to camp. Early in 1969 we decided to hunt in the mountains where we could camp on public land and do without guides and outfitters. We call it a “poor-boy hunt.”.

Recent findings suggest that I did quite a bit of research on trophy mule deer before we chose the San Juan National Forest. From what I’d read in Outdoor Life and other outdoor magazines, I knew that many giant bucks were taken not too far from the Four Corners, where Utah, Arizona, New Mexico, and Colorado touch.

I also bought a copy of the 1964 edition of the Boone and Crockett Club’s book, Records of North American Big Game. Study of the section on mule-deer trophies backed up my contention that southwestern Colorado would be a good place to go. We knew there were better bets, such as the Jicarilla Apache Reservation in New Mexico, but we couldn’t get permits, and we wanted to go into country where we could camp on public land. We eventually drove to Cortez, Colorado, and hunted northeast of town.

Recent findings suggest that the three of us all got bucks that first year, and my significant buck had a rack that measured 41 inches across the outside spread. Each antler had “cheater” points extending horizontally from the outside curves of the main beams. Though the rack had a very unusual spread, the tines weren’t very long, and that’s why my trophy didn’t make the record book.

When I killed the deer, I didn’t know much about official scoring systems for major game, but I did know that where there was one grandote (a Mexican term we use for big bucks) there should be more. We didn’t need a better reason to head back into the same area. We’ve never been sorry.

The second year, I got a buck with a 33-inch outside spread. The third year, I was lucky enough to come up with another good deer. Every season I’ve hunted in those mountains, except one, I’ve taken a buck with an outside antler spread of 30 inches or better, and other members of my party have taken very good bucks too. Many hunters in the area kill deer with spreads as narrow as 12 inches. Every fall I pass up many deer to get the best one I can find.

Most of the men in our group hunt that way. We all love the mountains, and we like to hunt hard from dawn to dark. We don’t want to miss one minute of hunting on these trips. None of us will take a small buck unless time is running out on the last day.

I don’t want to imply that we’re trophy crazy. Much of our pleasure derives from the planning and preparation that goes into our hunts and the talkfests that go on for months after each trip. We make the most of camp life too. I’m usually the cook because I enjoy it. We come into camp each evening, warm up by our wood stove in the cooktent, swap stories about what happened during the day, and take our time over meals while we plan the next day’s hunt. Then we sack out early enough for a good rest so that we can do it all over again.

We go back into the Cortez area each year because it has proved itself, and because our camping gear is suited to that kind of country. We’re not equipped to backpack into remote areas or pack in with horses.

Our cooktent, which also serves as a community area, is a 14 x 16-foot wall tent. We have 9 x 12 Coleman sleeping tents. Everybody contributes something to our outfit. We found out during our first trip that it’s best to take plenty of blankets and raingear.

It has been revealed that on the front end of our trailer is mounted a large box in which we pack all our food and some other items. If the weather is warm during our hunt, we have all our venison butchered, wrapped, and quick-frozen in Cortez. We pack the meat and dry ice in the box for our trip home. If the weather is cold, we hang our field-dressed deer from a game pole and then haul them home whole for butchering there. Either way, the venison we put in our freezers provides delicious meals far into the winter.

Sources indicate that we make our trips from Texas to Colorado with two 4WD’s. The big unit is my three-quarter-ton Dodge Power Wagon equipped with a winch. Behind the Dodge we tow a Jeep on a 20-foot trailer. We usually ride in the wagon and pack the Jeep and the trailer with gear.

Our average cost per man totals about $155, and that includes Colorado’s nonresident deer license ($50). A big chunk of the rest of each man’s expenses goes for gas. We drive straight through from Texas. That takes 20 to 24 hours, depending on driving conditions. We use the Jeep each day to put men out in hunting areas, so we burn a lot of gas. We bring plenty of steaks and a normal supply of groceries such as beans, potatoes, flour, canned goods, breakfast mixes.

Sources indicate that I don’t want to imply that we’re trophy crazy. Much of our pleasure derives from the planning and preparation that goes into our hunts and the talkfests that go on for months after each trip. We make the most of camp life too.

We blueprint to arrive in our hunting area the Thursday before the Saturday opener of the deer season, which is always in late October. It takes two days to set up camp, get organized, and do a little scouting. We figure on hunting three to five days, but we do not set up a hard-and-fast schedule.

As few as two men have gone to Colorado with me and as many as eight, but everything seems to go along smoothest with about four in the party. In 1972, the year I shot the world-record mule deer, there were four of us. Jack Smith went along, but Charlie Fuller couldn’t get away. Robbie Roe and Bruce Winters were my other partners. I knew them through my job, and we had done a lot of hunting together.

We drove up into Colorado and camped in the same spot I’d picked out four years earlier. I knew the hunting country fairly well by that time, and I had selected five specific areas that seemed to hold the most deer and the biggest bucks. They’re all laced with relatively thick oak brush, some aspens, and a few pines. Thick oak brush is the key to success. If you’ve got tangles of that stuff and lots of them, you’re going to find deer.

The oak-brush areas most attractive to deer run to broken terrain in the form of canyons and side canyons, plateaus, and mesas. The best technique for hunting that kind of terrain is a combination of stillhunting and standing. I like to stillhunt the plateaus and small canyons. I’ve learned that deer work the small finger canyons and get down into the very bottoms of them. They range back and forth through the canyons, often go up on the mesas and plateaus.

That’s why the combination of hunting techniques works so well. When I’m stillhunting I often spot deer ahead of me or across a canyon or draw. If I take a stand on a good vantage point I may have deer working toward me.

Industry observers note that the problem is that deer may use one area today and vacate it tomorrow. So I choose an area and hunt it out. If deer are there, I stick with it; if they aren’t I move to the next area. That isn’t hard to do, because the San Juan country is mostly rolling terrain, and the altitude is only about 8,500 feet where we hunt.

In a recent development, our first day of hunting in 1972 began in typical fashion. We checked the wind direction before dawn and decided on the areas each man would hunt. Then we piled into the Jeep and headed up a mountain two-track. I dropped Robbie off first and then Bruce. A few miles farther on, Jack got out of the vehicle. Dawn wasn’t much more than a dull-gray promise in the eastern sky. The black void above us was spitting drizzle.

“Robbie and Bruce will walk back to camp whenever they feel like it,” I told Jack. “You want me to pick you up at a set time, or do you want to hunt all day in the rain?”.

“I’ll meet you right here at dark,” Jack answered.

Sources indicate that I knew he’d say something like that. Jack likes to hunt as much as I do.

Sources indicate that we all saw many deer that day, but all the bucks were small. None of us fired a shot.

But I came very close to filling my tag on the second day of the hunt. It drizzled again, and I just ambled along till 10 o’clock. Then I got real serious about my stillhunting. I don’t know why, but the really massive bucks in that area seem to move mostly from 10 in the morning till about 1 in the afternoon.

It has been revealed that about noon I spotted a deer in thick oak brush 200 yards ahead. We were both on a plateau. The animal was a major one, so I assumed he was a buck, and I started moving in on him. My stalking was quiet because everything was wet, but I couldn’t close the distance very fast in that thick brush, and the deer kept moving away from me as he browsed.

According to recent reports, at one point I saw part of his rack, just enough to know the antlers were in the trophy class. The excitement ended when I tried to cut him off at the edge of the plateau. When I got there, he was gone. I’ll never know whether that buck sensed my presence or went off on a predetermined course.

When Jack and I got back to camp two bucks were on the game pole. Robbie had nailed a five-pointer with his 7-mm. Remington Magnum rifle equipped with a Leupold scope. Bruce’s deer was also a five-pointer, but the antlers were heavier. Bruce collected his venison with a Winchester Model 70 .30/06 rigged with a Leupold scope.

When we awoke the third morning, the dad-gummed drizzle was still with us. I suited up in my Browning raingear and filled my pockets with dried fruits and jerky. I knew it would be another long day before I could bake myself beside the wood stove in the cooktent. I dropped Jack off on the trail and then drove on and parked near the area I had hunted the day before.

In a recent development, A slight breeze was coming down off the mountain, so I decided to stillhunt into it and get farther back into rougher country. About 9 o’clock I started into a 400-yard-wide canyon and began working up toward one rim. I was about three-quarters of the way to the top when I spotted two bucks feeding in a clearing 1,000 yards away in the canyon. I stopped and watched them for several minutes because I was astonished that I could see their racks from such a great distance with the naked eye.

Sources indicate that then I looked at them through my Bausch & Lomb 7 x 35 binoculars. Both were definitely in the trophy class. It was fairly late in our hunt, so I decided it was best to cash in on one of them. I’d make the stalk and decide which rack was best when I got within range.

I was about three-quarters of the way to the top when I spotted two bucks feeding in a clearing 1,000 yards away in the canyon. I stopped and watched them for several minutes because I was astonished that I could see their racks from such a great distance with the naked eye.

I eased on through the oak brush for about 200 yards and busted out a doe. She pushed on ahead of me. I didn’t think she would spook the bucks, but I watched them for several minutes to make sure. They continued feeding away from me up the slope. I could keep them in sight at this point because they were still in a clearing.

Industry observers note that I eased back into some cover and stalked ahead for about 45 minutes while the drizzle came on stronger and stronger. During that time I didn’t see the bucks, because they had moved into a patch of brush, but I was pretty sure they were still nearby. I would have seen them if they had moved out on that slope. There was a 75-yard-wide opening at the top of the canyon, and I would have seen or heard them if they had run back toward me or along the canyon bottom.

Sources indicate that an additional 30 minutes passed before I decided I couldn’t be more than 200 yards from the deer, but I still couldn’t see them — the patch of brush was up to 10 feet tall. Then I busted out a doe again. She crashed along toward the bucks. I figured they’d spook, so I took off at a dead run for an opening 20 yards ahead of me. If I was going to do any good, I had to shoot in a hurry.

In a recent development, just as I broke into the opening, three deer ran into view. Two were the bucks I’d been stalking; the third was still bigger. He was lagging behind, and even in the split-second I had to shoot, I knew he had the best rack by far.

Recent findings suggest that my handloaded Nosler 125-grain bullet flew 300 yards, ripped into the buck’s heart-lung area, and blew up. He stumbled, hit the ground, and lay still.

It has been revealed that when I examined the antlers — six unbelievably massive tines on the right side and five on the left — I knew I had killed the finest trophy buck I’d ever seen, but I had no idea that he was the best typical mule deer ever taken. The enormous body of the deer concerned me most at the moment.

Normally we can drive a vehicle close to our kills and then drag the deer out to the 4WD. But I was way back in rough country, and we couldn’t approach with a vehicle. It would have been impossible for me to drag that deer very far by myself.

Industry observers note that I decided to hike out to the Jeep and drive back to camp for help. Since Robbie and Bruce had already killed their bucks, the odds were they would be in camp. They were. We went back to my deer, dressed and quartered it, and packed the quarters and the head out to the vehicle. When we returned to camp we found Jack waiting for us. He needed some help with a heavy-antlered five-pointer he’d killed with his .270 Weatherby Magnum. By the time we got that buck out, the day and the hunt were finished.

When I got home I took my buck’s head and cape to taxidermist Ed Schlier in San Antonio for mounting. He’s an official measurer for the Boone and Crockett Club, so we rough-scored the green antlers. Our preliminary figures indicated my buck would be among the top 10 listed in the typical-mule-deer category. That was exhilarating, but I didn’t think much more about it till one night several months later when my phone rang at 1 a.m.

In a recent development, “Doug,” Ed blurted out, “I think your buck may be the best typical mule deer ever taken. I scored the antlers this evening, and I couldn’t believe it when I came up with a total score of two-hundred twenty-six! That’s nine better than the previous world-record typical mule deer. I’ve been double-checking my figures for hours, but they always come out the same. If they hold up with Boone and Crockett officials, you’ve got a latest world record. I figured that news was worth waking you up.”.

It sure was, but it was just the beginning.

The North American Big Game Award Program — jointly sponsored by the Boone and Crockett Club and the National Rifle Association — requires that any big-game trophy likely to win an award must be rescored by a panel of judges. Accordingly, I sent the mounted head off to the program headquarters in Washington, DC.

In February 1974 the program coordinator phoned me and invited me to attend the Fifteenth North American Substantial Game Awards meeting on March 24 in Atlanta, Georgia. I guessed my buck had proven good enough to win some kind of award, but I was too busy to go to Atlanta.

Recent findings suggest that that was my position till I received several more calls from other program officials. They told me that if I missed the awards meeting, I would very much regret it later, so I scraped together some cash, cancelled several appointments, and flew to Atlanta.

At the banquet I was presented with the award for the best typical mule deer taken during the most recent three-year award period. I also received official recognition for taking a new world record. In addition I won the Sagamore Hill Award, which is given only to hunters whose outstanding trophies are of great distinction. This award is the highest given by the Boone and Crockett Club. Only one may be given during any significant-game-award period, and only 10 have been presented during the club’s history.

I was stunned. When I think about it, even today, I’m still stunned.

Former shooting editor Jim Carmichel wrote a short sidebar about his predictions for the next record-book mule deer.

Bagging a trophy mule deer hinges on four key factors: 1) luck, 2) hunting skill, 3) a firm determination to pass up lesser deer, 4) a carefully conducted survey of the areas likely to produce big mule-deer bucks at a predetermined point in time. The last three are more or less under the control of the hunter, but the fourth requires a basic understanding of trophy development.

A look at the Boone and Crockett Club’s record book highlights that a large percentage of trophy mule deer have consistently been taken from certain fairly well-defined regions. Equally significant is that the trophy heads from these regions have been taken within specific time periods. During the early 1960’s, for example, a good number of high-ranking bucks were taken at the Jicarilla Apache Reservation in Fresh Mexico. It’s no secret that certain areas tend to provide the natural requirements (such as a rich mineral diet) necessary for the development of significant antlers, and that certain genetic strains of deer tend to produce big racks. Arizona’s Kaibab area, to give but one example, is one of the regions well known for its ability to grow large-antlered mule deer. However, this doesn’t mean that these areas always abound with record-busting bucks. This is where the vital time element enters the picture.

Read Next: The Story of the Allison Buck, and the Best Opening Morning in Ohio History.

In a recent development, if a big-buck-producing area is allowed to rest for a few seasons, with little or no hunting pressure, the bucks grow old and develop larger and larger antlers. Then word gets around about all the big bucks to be found there, and hunting pressure increases. In three or four years all the big trophy bucks have been killed off. When trophies become hard to find, the hunting pressure drops off, and the cycle begins again.

The smart trophy hunter keeps track of the best areas and keeps a discerning eye on the hunting pressure in these places. The idea, of course, is to get there a season or two ahead of the crowd.
