In a recent development, the holiday season is meant to be a time to relax, be with friends and family, and, ideally, get some climbing in. Don’t let the obligation of holiday shopping take up too much of your time—the editors at Climbing have determined what we believe are the best gifts for the climber in your life, whether a gym, sport, trad, or ice climber, a burgeoning mountaineer, an all-arounder, or someone who hasn’t tried climbing yet, but is eager to get started.

Recent findings suggest that whether you’re crimping sharp Smith Rock incuts, jamming perfect Indian Creek splitters, or bearing down on your gym’s fresh new set, you are, at some point, going to tear up your skin. Fear not! Rhino Skin Solutions makes a purpose-built skin balm to restore your digits as efficiently as possible. Split+ is a roll-on cream that comes in two sizes (5oz and 3.4oz) and uses beeswax, vitamin E, arnica, dragon’s blood, and tea tree oil, offering a blend of occlusive (sealing) and antibacterial properties.

Ocun’s new Jett S climbing shoes are as comfortable as they are affordable, and best suited for the gym. They excel at precision placements and perform well on steep terrain, hooking, and scumming, on everything from 5.13 tech to the Tension Board 2 at 40° overhanging.

Sources indicate that last year, Petzl updated the Connect Adjust to make a good item great: they slimmed down the dynamic tether from 9.5mm to 9.0mm, making it noticeable lighter and easier to extend/contract. The belay-loop attachment point is now a sewn Dyneema webbing, rather than the thick rope itself, and as a result feels lower profile on the harness. The Connect Adjust also now features a pinhole to attach accessory cord to; if weighting the Connect, clip a carabiner into the accessory-cord loop and it will easily disengage.

In a recent development, edelrid’s Ohmega brake assistant is a crucial belay tool for partnerships where the climber weighs significantly more than the belayer. By adding friction, the device makes the belayer “heavier,” reducing the size of whips and keeping the belayer on the ground during a fall. We recommend any climbing duo with a notable weight difference to invest in one.

According to recent reports, the Friend Camming Device is one of the most legendary and trusted pieces of climbing equipment. Newly updated for 2026, the Friends are a tiny bit lighter than the previous model, but, most importantly, they come with a fresh, seamless “Magic Cord” sling. The bartack-free sling enables smooth extension so you can enjoy your leads without rope drag.

Industry observers note that the Free Wall is the ultimate quiver-of-one backpack for rock climbers, made from a super-tough recycled nylon that our testers hauled for thousands of feet this summer. Unlike a traditional major-wall haulbag, with its simple, monolithic compartment, the Free Wall Pack is designed with on-the-wall access in mind: two internal pockets, two gear loops, and a large external pocket on top of the lid.

According to recent reports, apparently Scarpa’s Veloce is designed for beginner and intermediate climbers who spend all of their time at the gym—but our experienced field tester didn’t get the memo. After a quick break-in period, they became his go-to shoes inside and out, where he clipped the chains on the two hardest sport routes he’s sent in the last decade.

According to recent reports, black Diamond’s Magnetron has the smoothest operation of any triple-action carabiner we’ve ever encountered; a true one-handed operation that provides immediate security upon letting go of the gate. Its pear shape is ideal for belaying and rappelling, and it has a surprisingly narrow nose, making it easy to clip into chain anchors and busy masterpoints.

Recent findings suggest that these insulated rubber gloves were originally designed for fishers, but nowadays you’re equally likely to see them on ice climbers, especially on steep water ice in the Pacific Northwest. The Temres 282-02 is the only fully waterproof glove we’ve ever worn, and they climb decently well thanks to a supple, dexterous rubber, and a wool liner that doesn’t migrate much within.

Climbing tape isn’t just for hardcore climbers nursing a busted pulley or gobie—it’s a needed part of any decent first aid kit, repair kit, and can help you fashion a makeshift stickclip in a pinch. (BYOStick). Tension’s climbing tape is some of the stickiest we’ve used, performing well in both sweaty and freezing environments. The Tri-Pack includes a one-inch roll ideal for larger body parts like wrists and ankles and for making tape gloves should you forget yours at home, the half-inch roll works well for large blisters and flappers, and the 0.3-inch roll is preordained to fit individual digits.

What gift could be better than continued access to America’s best rock climbing? Gift your climbing partner a membership to Access Fund, the largest climbing advocacy movement in the country, which tirelessly protects and conserves historic areas—and opens upcoming ones. They’ll even get a free t-shirt.

According to recent reports, the daughter of Climbing’s editor in chief, Maya Silver, has worn the Black Diamond Momentum kids’ climbing shoe for the past four years. Once she finally outgrew it this last summer, the decision was easy to order her another pair. Like the adult Momentum shoe, the Momentum kids is super comfortable thanks to its neutral last, easy to get on/off with a simple Velcro closure, and offers sufficient performance for most little crushers.

#102149. 7 Ultrarunning Lessons Des Linden Learned from Her 100-Mile Debut

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1527 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Trailrunnermag ↗ Open Full Page

7 Ultrarunning Lessons Des Linden Learned from Her 100-Mile Debut

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1527 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Andy Cochrane and Nick Danielson were on the ground outside of Fountain Hills, Arizona, on October 31 to document Des Linden’s 100-mile debut at the Javelina Jundred.
  • Despite Des Linden returning to Javelina Jundred “jeadquarters” five minutes ahead of schedule and in first place, I was worried.
  • It has been revealed that being a freelance filmmaker feels a bit like being a mercenary: One moment you have no aims for the rest of the year, and the next, you’re hopping in a rental van and rallying across the Southwest during a historic October storm to get to the next job.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Andy Cochrane and Nick Danielson were on the ground outside of Fountain Hills, Arizona, on October 31 to document Des Linden’s 100-mile debut at the Javelina Jundred. They bore witness to her exceptional first 60 miles, during which she took the lead in under-course-record pace, all the way through to her gritting out the remaining 40 miles to a ninth-place finish. They spoke with Linden after the race to find out what she learned—and why she’s already angling to come back.

Despite Des Linden returning to Javelina Jundred “jeadquarters” five minutes ahead of schedule and in first place, I was worried. I had followed her for the final half mile, camera rolling as her leg visibly seized up, likely from cramping. She had run 60 miles at course record pace, but still had forty to go—a long way without a fully functioning lower half. Linden sat on a chair and talked through the situation with her crew. A shoe switch, a lot more electrolytes, and roll the dice. Before I get into how the rest of her race played out, let me back up.

It has been revealed that being a freelance filmmaker feels a bit like being a mercenary: One moment you have no aims for the rest of the year, and the next, you’re hopping in a rental van and rallying across the Southwest during a historic October storm to get to the next job. This is exactly what my business partner Nick and I did after getting the call to document Des Linden’s first 100-mile race at the Javelina Jundred on October 31.

After landing in Salt Lake City, we picked up a camper van from Roadsurfer, threw our bags in the back, and headed south on I-15. A quick stop in Moab for a 50K race of our own was followed by four days evading floods and trying to figure out which desert roads were impassable after the recent downpours—which turned out to be pretty good foretelling for the race itself.

On the three previous occasions we’ve attended this event, it has been a delightful closing chapter to the season; Javelina has served as a sort of reward for making it to the end of our race coverage for the year, where the burden of logistics is removed from the job of filming. Instead of chasing athletes across the dirt roads of the Sierra Nevada at the Western States 100 or around a heavily glaciated massif at UTMB, the athletes at Javelina run in circles back to you. Five circles, to be exact. Adding to the enjoyment factor, Javelina is typically a giant Halloween party with racers and spectators dressed in costume under the warm desert sun.

Industry observers note that however, this year was a little different. Deluge after deluge in the 24 hours leading up to the race saturated the race course. The sky relented just before the gun went off, but by the time the race had ended, over two more inches of precipitation had fallen. Not exactly what you expect for an event in the arid Sonoran Desert outside Phoenix, Arizona, but that’s why we love ultrarunning.

It has been revealed that we did our best to keep the cameras dry and our bodies warm as we followed Linden on her third ultra—well, fourth, if you count the road 50K world record. Despite a stunning road running resume, Linden was quick to point out that she’s still a newbie at trails and ultras but is excited to keep learning. Javelina’s first three laps were nearly perfect. But soon after her body shut down it was a struggle to make it to the finish line. At one point she had to stop for almost an hour, sitting and stretching until her legs finally relaxed and let her move again. And move again she did: Linden finished her first 100-miler as the ninth woman in 16:58:01, about three hours off winner Heather Jackson. We sat down with her the day after the race to learn her biggest lessons from the process.

Linden’s biggest takeaway from Javelina is to treat 100-milers, no matter the course, weather, or circumstances, with a ton of humility. Because they ask so much of your mind and body and are a completely unique style of racing, you can’t race a 100-miler like any other distance. “Just like when I started marathons,” Linden stated, “I learned that if you’re cavalier with how you race it, you’ll pay the price at some point.”.

In a recent development, linden was patient on her first 20-mile lap, sitting a few minutes back from the leaders. Feeling good, she picked up the pace on the next two laps, picking off all of the ladies in front of her to take the lead around the halfway mark. By the time she made it to the end of the third loop at mile 60, she had a six-minute gap on second—but her legs were starting to cramp.

Survival quickly became the goal of lap four and the best way to do that was by listening to her pacer, Magda Boulet. Thankfully, there is no one on planet Earth better suited for the job. Boulet, a fellow U.S. Olympian in the marathon, is also a Western States winner and president of GU Energy Labs. She helped coax Linden forward, made sure she kept fueling, and stuck with her through all the ups and downs.

One of Linden’s biggest challenges in the transition from road to trails and marathons to ultras is how much she needs to consume during a race—and how hard it is to catch up if she falls behind. At Javelina, Linden took most of her calories and carbs with fluids, drinking three half-liter (500 mL) bottles each lap. This fueling plan was developed for the typical heat of Javelina, but still worked well, as daytime temps almost hit 80 degrees Fahrenheit with 100% humidity.

Unfortunately, it wasn’t enough to keep her lower body from cramping around mile 60, which forced her to stop and stretch many times on the fourth lap. That setback resulted in her giving up the lead and ultimately the chance to win the race. “The fueling game has changed the sport,” Linden noted. “You see it on the roads, but especially here. It’s something I will keep working on, probably forever.”.

Industry observers note that assuming Javelina would be hot and dry like just about every other year, Linden packed for those conditions, putting her focus on cooling strategies and nutrition for the heat. She expected hardpack trails and excruciatingly hot sun, but the weather gods had other intends. Heavy rain required Linden and her crew to scramble to find key pieces of gear, including a raincoat. And because lap four took much longer than expected, Linden ran the last couple miles of it after the sun set, sans headlamp.

According to recent reports, next time she’ll prepare for worst-case scenarios, but will also understand when to pull the plug. “You need to know when to be tough and when it’s enough,” Linden said. “If I had to do another lap, I would have been on the edge of hypothermia and the trails were so, so slippery. There is nothing wrong with saving it for another day, but also great value in staying tough.”.

Sources indicate that pacing strategy is different at every ultra, but there are some broad themes that apply to the majority of runners and racers, especially for someone with Linden’s ability to close in the back half if she’s feeling good. Surprisingly, this is similar to how she used to strategize for marathons. The first third should feel easy, the middle third is about keeping the pace steady, and the final third is when the racing begins. “The first three or even three-and-a-half laps are transportation,”  Linden stated, “the final lap or two is about racing.”.

Industry observers note that when things got hard for Linden on the final two laps, she leaned into her crew to get to the finish. After a lap with Boulet, Linden picked up her husband Ryan as a pacer. He’s one of the most positive and energetic people you’ll ever meet, and his positivity and drive—paired with a little patience—helped get her through heavy rain and strong winds in the last 20 miles.

It has been revealed that her main support at Javelina HQ was Charlie Lawrence, the 100K world record holder and good friend. “A crew that knows you well, knows the sport well, and knows the emotional ups and downs of 100 miles is a real difference maker,” Linden noted. “I was excited to be around everyone all week, so it was good energy going into the race, which is key.”.

While Linden isn’t sure what the future holds or what her race calendar will look like next year, she walked away from the race with a surprising feeling. “I 100% want to come back to Javelina, it feels like unfinished business,” Linden stated. “I didn’t think it would be this clear, but I know I can do so much better here.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more.

The development of heated gloves—like with heated vests—is one of the better innovations in outdoor wear. As much as we enjoy spending time in nature during the winter months, we hate cold hands. It’s hard to concentrate on your hunt or effectively work if your fingers are so cold you can no longer feel them. For anyone with arthritis or other hand pain, it can be downright painful to venture out in winter. Luckily, battery-operated heating elements are here to change the game.

Wading through the hundreds of different options to find the ideal gloves can be a chore. That’s why we’ve done the homework for you. It doesn’t matter if you need something for work or for ice fishing, we’ve got you covered with the best heated gloves available for cold weather.

When it comes to battery life, the Ororo heated gloves—which feature three heat settings—performed better than I expected. I was able to run the gloves on the maximum temperature setting for approximately three to four hours and on the medium setting for at least five. However, the low setting was where they really shined. These gloves ran for a solid eight hours on that setting. Because they were so warm even without turning on the electricity, I highly doubt I’ll ever use the medium and high settings.

Sources indicate that my only real complaint is that I feel the dexterity could be better. The insulation makes the fingers a bit too fat for shooting a rifle or shotgun. But the grip on the palms and fingers has a tacky feel to it that’s perfectly suited for working with shovels or other hand tools where super fine control isn’t needed. I’ll be using these to clear the driveway of snow once winter returns to Michigan. These gloves would also be excellent for operating a tractor, ATV, or snowmobile in cold temperatures.

Sources indicate that the Savior gloves are plenty warm without an electric feature. But they also feature larger 2200 mAh batteries that help keep your fingers toasty through longer days outdoors. Because they are waterproof and thick, you can wear these gloves whenever there is snow or slush on the ground. The windproof quality makes them an excellent choice for work or riding a motorcycle, too. They are thick, so there is some dexterity loss. But Savior Heat made the button for heat control quite large, so you can easily operate it without removing the gloves.

In a recent development, these gloves are a hair on the expensive side. But that’s to be expected for this battery size and durability. While we like these gloves best for work—like construction or ranch work—they are versatile enough to be used in a variety of outdoor scenarios.

Surprisingly, there are not a lot of dedicated hunting gloves featuring electronic heating. This pair is both windproof and waterproof—perfect for hunters who don’t like to head in once the weather takes a turn for the worst. The 7.4V battery packs will help the warming functions last through a full day in frigid temperatures, and the buttons are large enough that you can operate them while wearing the gloves. Plus, they have fingertips that can operate a touchscreen.

The three heat settings allow you to customize just how warm your hands are (and the soft cotton material is extra cozy). However, we wish there were more camo patterns other than Realtree Edge. Not that the deer will notice or care, but some of us like our camo outfits to match.

The Snow Deer gloves offer surprising dexterity for thicker gloves. They are suitable for everything from hunting to motorcycling thanks to the sheep leather palms that help provide additional grip. The heated wires in this pair of gloves extends completely to each of the fingers, making them a great option for anyone with arthritis or circulation complications in the hands. There is also fleece in the glove liners to help retain heat and repel moisture.

These gloves have a shorter battery life than some of the other options on this list. But they’re very well constructed. Features like the sheepskin palm and fleece lining add a lot of additional value for the money here. If you need gloves that are versatile for more than one outdoor activity, these are the ones to consider.

These featherweight gloves offer a great deal of dexterity that’s ideal for work or recreational activities in bitter cold conditions. The extra reinforcement of the palm and inside of the fingers further emphasizes the fact that these gloves are made with cold weather activities in mind. You can also cinch the cuff tight to prevent extra snow and wind from getting in at the wrists and dropping your core body temperature.

Recent findings suggest that these heated gloves have a slightly shorter run time than we’d expect for a battery of this size. It runs for about two hours on high, three hours on medium, and five hours on low. Extra batteries are a necessity if you need them super toasty for long periods. That stated, we think the shortened runtime is a decent tradeoff for the extra dexterity offered by these gloves.

For the gloves I tested, I first made sure the batteries were fully charged. I then ran each pair on the highest warmth settings to assess the battery life of each glove. I also wore the gloves while performing a variety of activities both recreational and for work. This allowed me to evaluate the comfort and dexterity of each pair. Additionally, I considered the following factors when making my decisions:.

There are a few different types of heated gloves. The most popular style utilizes an electronic battery system and heated wires in the fabric, which is extremely effective for staying warm. The downside is that gloves like this are often expensive and require frequent recharging. Most have a battery life of six to eight hours depending on the set intensity level.

It has been revealed that there are also gloves and mittens with small pockets for chemical hand warmers. One pro to this style is the reduced cost. Of course, you can only use the disposable hand warmers once before tossing them in the trash. There’s also waste from the airtight wrappers this style of warmer is sealed inside, so it’s not exactly the greenest solution out there. But you don’t have to worry about charging any batteries and you can swiftly replace the warmers in the field once they lose heat.

Recent findings suggest that when picking a glove, think about how you blueprint to use it. Thicker gloves are great if all you plan to do is ride a snowmobile or ATV. However, they can quickly become useless if you need to do more delicate tasks. Thick gloves can make it difficult to squeeze the trigger on a rifle or work on an engine. Think about dexterity and how much you’ll need. At the same time, be careful not to buy gloves that are too small or too tight.

According to recent reports, for gloves that will be used primarily for working, it pays to go with thicker materials like leather that are built to take abuse. Ideally, the palms will be reinforced for heavier tasks like ranch work. It’s not a bad idea to go for work gloves that are waterproof—or at least water-resistant—either.

Many clothing manufacturers are now making their gloves with at least one specialized fingertip designed for operating a screen. The quality of these fingertips varies depending on the glove. Some gloves just don’t have the dexterity for typing or sending emails effectively. But quality ones make for great hunting gloves when you want to stay in touch with your buddies without losing any warmth.

In a recent development, mittens are almost always warmer than gloves, and that includes heated mittens. This is simply because mittens allow your fingers to share warmth and slow heat loss. Of course, this comes at the cost of dexterity for more precise tasks.

According to recent reports, it can be a bit of a balancing act to find the right fit for warm gloves. Go with gloves that are too loose and you lose dexterity and warmth. If the gloves are too tight, they might cut off circulation. The ideal solution is to find gloves that fall somewhere in between. The gloves shouldn’t be so tight they feel restricting, but they also shouldn’t fall off your hands.

Waterproof capabilities vary from glove to glove. Some have that feature built in standard while others may need to be kept out of the snow and ice to function properly. Be sure to read the fine print on any pair you buy first. Most work gloves are built rather ruggedly and will handle a little water.

Recent findings suggest that while the technology for heated gloves continues to improve, the Ororo gloves were a standout for us in terms of battery life. These large versatile gloves will get you through the worst sub-zero temperatures that nature can dish out, and the competitive price makes them a solid option for gearing up for another long winter. Even if you choose another pair on this list, the best heated gloves will keep your digits nice and warm all season long.

The Most Unexpected Ski Adventure in North America Might Be in Michigan

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (954 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Skimag

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that it’s breakfast in the main yurt, so the girl from the kitchen is again standing on a chair and rubbing the dome of a snow globe.
  • According to recent reports, “Grant us snow, almighty spirits of winter,” she begins, raising the globe above her head.
  • It has been revealed that the Midwest is a peculiar place for a ski pilgrimage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Marcus Caston, Mt. Bohemia, Mich. (Photo: Keri Bascetta).

Recent findings suggest that it’s breakfast in the main yurt, so the girl from the kitchen is again standing on a chair and rubbing the dome of a snow globe. Eyes shut tight, she shouts over the gathered skiers.

According to recent reports, “Grant us snow, almighty spirits of winter,” she begins, raising the globe above her head. “By your power, give us powder. Amen.” She is our shaman.

“Amen,” we all murmur along and mean it.

It has been revealed that the Midwest is a peculiar place for a ski pilgrimage. But on Michigan’s isolated Keweenaw Peninsula, known as “the fin,” Mount Bohemia has no shortage of true believers. And they’re not coming for the corduroy. This expert-only backcountry resort is ungroomed, technical, and seriously steep. Signs across the mountain are clear: NO BEGINNERS ALLOWED.

It has been revealed that while skiers scour the globe for powder, Michigan has been sitting on one of the country’s most unlikely stashes. Bohemia sees almost 300 inches annually, with no snowmaking. Here, bad weather is usually good news. Arctic air sweeping over Lake Superior’s warmer water produces storms that bury the Keweenaw. This lake-effect snow is remarkably light and dry—the kind you’d travel to Utah or Japan to find.

In a recent development, on paper, Bohemia’s numbers seem modest: 900 vertical feet, 585 acres, and just two lifts. Yet over 90 percent of its runs are black diamond or better, including the region’s only triple-blacks. Boho has the untamed feel of backcountry skiing, minus the skinning. Its dozen or so named territories—mostly sprawling glade districts—each have distinct temperaments.

“It can take two or three visits before guests get a feel for the mountain,” notes Vern Barber, Bohemia’s general manager.

Industry observers note that I spend one morning adrift in one of the territories, Extreme Backcountry, a half-mile-wide expanse of Bohemia’s toughest terrain. Its high-angle tree runs, cliff drops, and narrow chutes kept funneling me onto unexpected lines. Supposedly, somewhere out there is a frozen waterfall drop I never managed to find. I wasn’t going to hit it. I just wanted to look.

According to recent reports, now I’m farther out in Middle Earth, another territory, surfing Boho’s longest runs through twisting hardwoods. Less steep, but somehow more exhausting. This is where skiers come to explore, hunting for pockets of untouched powder.

Recent findings suggest that I stop at a trail marked “Helm’s Deep.” It took several attempts to find this place. Even then, it felt like an accident. The entrance is just a gap interrupting the tangle of trees—my only way down. Two clicks of my poles, and I drop in.

Dry powder explodes on my first turn. Branches rake both sleeves as I weave between trunks. Each bank hides what lies ahead. I barrel over a blind rise straight toward a stand of maples. I slash hard right and spray snow against the bark. Off balance, I slip through a drift and down a steep-sided gully.

“You’re rowdy,” I grunt as the trees finally open. With room to breathe, I find my rhythm. Ahead lie 30 yards of untracked pillows. I point my tips and charge.

By the time I pop out at the bottom, a throng of skiers is already waiting. Not for a chairlift, but for a bus. Bohemia’s farthest backcountry runs spill onto Lac La Belle Road, where a fleet of buses collects those who make it out of the woods. Over four days, I’ve shuffled through far more bus lines than lift lines. With luck, the next shuttle will be the elusive ABBA bus, plastered with Swedish memorabilia and bumping “Dancing Queen.” Today, I’m not so lucky. I climb into a regular bus for the day’s last ride, legs shot.

In a recent development, as we pull into base, the parking lot is just getting started. Around a fire barrel, a haggard congregation passes bottles and joints. Skiers still in bibs boil noodles on camp stoves between RVs and Sprinter vans. This crowd feels familiar—as if every little ski hill I grew up on in Michigan sent its most adventurous regulars.

The village itself is a jumble of yurts, stitched together by gangways. It houses bars, a hostel, and a surprisingly elaborate Nordic spa. Its 30-person hot tub was dubbed “dude stew.” But Vern claims they don’t call it that anymore.

It has been revealed that for a place that wears you out by noon, Boho has a strange amount of energy after dark. Inside the North Pole Bar, skiers running on beer and pasties belt out “Country Roads” with the band. The party stumbles outside to packed pools and saunas. Much later, some hooligans will hike halfway up the frontside and sled down on stolen cafeteria trays. I am one of them.

According to recent reports, on my last morning at Mount Bohemia, a particularly nasty blizzard has blown in off Lake Superior. Word is spreading through the yurts: high winds and whiteout have shut down the lifts. The buses aren’t running.

Skiers gather at the back of the village, their helmets and jackets already covered in powder. Out of the blowing snow, a single snowcat materializes. Vern himself is behind the wheel. The wind forces him to park at an angle to wrestle the door open. Skiers cram aboard, a handful at a time, bound for the summit.

I join the others in line. We laugh and curse as the snowcat is swallowed again by the whiteout. Powder is piling up around our shins. Above us, the glades are already buried. I can’t feel my toes. It’s a perfect day.

Not a bad place for a pilgrimage.

  • It can build until you’ve got flocks working at two or three levels, and there’s less need for calling than there is for air traffic control.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the best thing about timber hunting is the way ducks multiply. A pair starts to circle, and that pair becomes four, then eight. Eight turn into 20. Somehow, the sight of ducks working over a timber hole draws more ducks from everywhere. It’s almost like squirrels running out onto branches to see what the others are chattering about.

It can build until you’ve got flocks working at two or three levels, and there’s less need for calling than there is for air traffic control. I’ve seen that in Arkansas, but we won’t see it here—in a duck-poor state a couple hundred miles north. The two dozen mallards wheeling over our heads are as good as it’s going to get. But from where we stand, pressed tight to the trees, two dozen is more than good enough. ­Editor-​in-​chief Colin Kearns and I are doing that thing where you look down but roll your eyes up, trying to peek at ducks without flaring them, and our hearts are beating fast.

Two drakes peel off the bunch and backpedal into the hole. Travis Mueller, a Banded pro staffer, tells us not to shoot. He’s hoping the rest will follow. Kearns and I nod our heads—imperceptibly, we hope—and hold our guns ready. The rest of the ducks make one more circle, but higher and looser. Then they slide away. With the birds in the sky gone, we settle for the two in the bush. Jumping the two drakes, ­Kearns and I each shoot one. While we wish the rest had come in, the sight of these two in the trees, hanging over the decoys and lit by the morning sun, makes Kearns an instant convert to woods hunting.

Mueller, who scouts as hard as anyone, found this spot in spring by looking for beavers. Beavers plus woods equals flooded timber anywhere, and we’re standing in knee-deep water in the soft maples and willows growing between a couple of oxbow ponds. Mueller hunts here to get away from the crowds on the big water, but crowds have a habit of following successful hunters.

According to recent reports, the first rule of timber hunting: No one talks about timber hunting. Good hunters are secretive. Mueller is a great hunter, so it’s no surprise he’s long since crossed the line from secretive to completely paranoid. We left the ramp extra early this morning to avoid detection. Even so, Mueller fretted the whole way that a couple of kids he thinks are watching him might have found his spot.

Sources indicate that when we got to the hole, Mueller was sure his enemies were onto him. Three hundred mallards that had been sitting here yesterday weren’t here; someone must have run them out. And the decoys were missing—no doubt, in Mueller’s mind, stolen by the competition. As Kearns and I found fallen trunks for our gear, Mueller was looking for the bag of decoys he had stashed. We could hear him sloshing and cursing in the darkness.

In a recent development, in traditional flooded green timber, a lack of decoys wouldn’t be a problem. Old-school hunters in Arkansas relied on calling and ripples kicked in the water to attract ducks and went without decoys. Here, though, decoys and spinners are an advantage. There are no acorns to attract ducks. Birds don’t come to flooded soft woods to eat. They want a place to hide out and loaf. The ducks we’re after are trading back and forth between a couple of refuges, or coming back to the woods after feeding in the cornfields. They need enticement. In the words of a famous timber hunter: “There are two places you can kill a duck. Where he wants to be, and where he don’t mind goin’.” This is a don’t-mind-goin’ spot, hence, the need for decoys and spinners.

When Mueller finally shines his flashlight in the right place, he finds the decoy bag. The hole is still secret. In fact, we’ll see no other hunters nor hear any shots but our own this morning. Those 300 mallards? Who knows. They were probably fresh arrivals that dropped in, then found other ducks and relocated.

It has been revealed that with two dozen decoys in the hole and four spinners going, we’re looking good. Spinners work well in the woods, Mueller believes, because ducks lose sight of them, then see them again, as they pass over the latticework of branches. And the sun is shining. “Sun’s out, guns out” is a truism of timber hunting. Decoys show up, spinners flash, and the sun creates shadows that make it easy to hide beside a tree.

Mueller blind-calls, quacking at random intervals to whom it may concern. Often in timber hunting, you don’t see the ducks you’re calling or decoying until after they have seen you. We’re not aware of the flock until we hear the whoosh of wings overhead. When the birds drop in I miss, Kearns kills a greenhead, and Mueller shoots a bluewing drake, fully plumed, unheard of at this latitude with 10 days left in the season. It’s been a strange migration year.

We peck away at a few more, and call it a morning, being careful to pick up our hulls both because it’s what you do, and to hide any sign of our presence. For good measure, we pack the decoys out, too. A flooded hole in the woods is worth keeping secret.

Audrie Pelosi’s Couch Was “Always Open to Crash On”

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (457 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Climbing

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Audrie Pelosi found climbing after moving to Baraboo, Wisconsin.
  • In a recent development, “She was an exceptional climbing guide and human being,” Apex Adventure Alliance wrote in a statement to Outside.
  • Sources indicate that originally from Duluth, Minnesota, Pelosi had long structured her life around her various passions: snowboarding, cycling, and, eventually, an all-encompassing love of climbing and the community around it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Courtesy of Michael Hall).

Audrie Pelosi found climbing after moving to Baraboo, Wisconsin. It wasn’t long before the quartzite cliffs of Devil’s Lake became a cornerstone of her life. She climbed there, worked there, and eventually became its steward as a guide with Apex Adventure Alliance (AAA), bringing new climbers to the same arena in which she’d begun.

In a recent development, “She was an exceptional climbing guide and human being,” Apex Adventure Alliance wrote in a statement to Outside. “She was a force in our community and at our guide service. We all will miss her dearly.”.

Sources indicate that originally from Duluth, Minnesota, Pelosi had long structured her life around her various passions: snowboarding, cycling, and, eventually, an all-encompassing love of climbing and the community around it. Her passion radiated outwards: she volunteered locally and, in 2026, ran for a Wisconsin Climbers Association board seat, hoping to become more involved in stewardship and community building. “I believe in showing up, doing the work, and listening to the community,” Pelosi wrote in her candidate statement.

Recent findings suggest that “With her friends and community, Audrie was so generous,” mentioned Garrett Hopkins, AAA’s owner. “That generosity flowed into her climbing, biking, and snowboarding too. When I was living on the road, I knew her couch was always open for a spot to crash if my van was being repaired. She spent countless hours with young climbers in an effort to elevate the safety of the next generation coming up.”.

Sources indicate that pelosi met her husband, Jimmy “The Fox” Robinson, at a snowboard event at Welch Village, Minnesota, and in 2023 the two married atop Mount Bohemia (1,465ft) on Lake Superior. From then on, Pelosi had the nickname “Mrs. The Fox.” One of her friends, Anastasia Exterovich, set up a GoFundMe to raise money for Pelosi’s family in the wake of her passing. She called the pair the “raddest couple.”.

In a recent development, “In my last conversation with Audrie, she joked about selling her handmade bike chain link earrings to anyone who wanted them for ‘free.99,’” Exterovich wrote. “It was such a simple statement made in passing, but it perfectly encapsulated who she was as a person. Even when she didn’t have much, she would give things away freely without hesitation, whether that was earrings, a smile, a laugh, a quick bike tune-up, or a belay.”.

According to recent reports, pelosi passed on May 30, 2026 working as a guide at  Devil’s Lake State Park, teaching a climbing course near the park’s East Bluff. During the course, Pelosi fell from the bluff and suffered fatal injuries. She is survived by her husband, her family, and the broader climbing community in Wisconsin.

The 9 Best Snowshoes of 2027

  • After a season of snowshoe-testing in blizzards, sub-zero temps, and alpine ice, our top pick is the MSR Revo Explore ($290) for its light weight, flexibility, and impressive grip.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

According to recent reports, L.L. Bean Pathfinder BOA Rec Snowshoe Package.

Retrospec Drifter Lightweight Snowshoes.

After a season of snowshoe-testing in blizzards, sub-zero temps, and alpine ice, our top pick is the MSR Revo Explore ($290) for its light weight, flexibility, and impressive grip. Looking for a crazy-affordable pair that will last for years? The Retrospec Drifter Lightweight Snowshoes ($50-70) are nearly bulletproof, easy to manipulate with gloves on, and provide a full feature set. This year we added the L.L. Bean Pathfinder Snowshoe Package (Best Snowshoe Package) and Atlas Montane ($250) (Best for Deep Snow.).

Industry observers note that snowshoes are some of the oldest winter gear known to humankind—the tech literally has prehistoric origins, with rudimentary versions dating back nearly 6,000 years ago. Today, the top ‘shoes boost flotation, grip, and ease of use, all while shaving weight. Over the years, our testers have tried hundreds of models in waist-deep drifts, through wet, cement-like snow, and on steep, icy slopes, all in the name of narrowing down the top of the class. Here are the best snowshoes of 2027.

Sizes: 22, 25 in Weight: Men’s: 3.8 lbs (22 in), 4.1 lbs (25 in); Women’s: 3.6 lbs (22 in), 3.9 lbs (25 in) Maximum Load: Men’s: 180 lbs (22 in), 220 lbs (25 in); Women’s: 180 lbs (22 in), 210 lbs (25 in).

Pros and Cons + Excellent traction + Easy-to-engage heel lift + Very secure binding – Pricey.

The Revo Explore snowshoes from MSR have been a tester favorite for over a decade: They’re lighter, more flexible, and grippier than most snowshoes on the market today. Credit a hybrid construction, which combines a tough, injection-molded plastic decking with a jagged-edged steel frame and pivoting toe crampon. The 2026 model keeps last year’s newly introduced binding—the TPU rubber stretch mesh Paradigm—which continues to impress testers with its security and comfort. The ridged, steel frame boosts side traction, while the two front toe crampons and a small, tooth-lined crossbar provide enough bite to stick to icy hills and steep ravines. Our Oregon tester reached for them in everything from deep powder to spring crust in Eastern Oregon’s Wallowa and Blue Mountains—when other people weren’t using them. “My husband makes fun of snowshoeing (he’s a skier) and claims to hate it, but I caught him happily using this pair,” she mentioned.

Sizes: 20.5, 22.5, 26.5 in Weight: 3.6 lbs (20.5), 3.8 lbs (22.5), 4lbs (26.5) Maximum Load: 180 lbs (20.5 in), 260 lbs (22.5 in), 300 lbs (26.5 in).

Pros and Cons + Excellent grip + Comfortable stride + Tall heel lift – Expensive.

The Highlander Instinct takes the snowshoe crampon and dials it up to 11. Most snowshoes have a basic underfoot crampon for some traction on slopes, and a few brands add teeth around the edges. The Highlander Instinct uses a stainless steel crampon under the toe that’s as long and sharp as some mountaineering crampons we’ve used, plus lateral grips around the edge of the chassis and mini serrated grip bars at strategic grip points across the platform. Over three days of steep, icy hills in Rocky Mountain National Park, our tester didn’t slip once, aided, in part, by the easy-to-use heel lifts. The rockered profile and wasp-waist shape allow a natural stride and help the crampons bite, no matter the incline. That narrow waist and tapered tail kept these easy to walk in, too, without the waddling common in most wider snowshoes. They floated well in a few inches of new snow, but drifts of more than a foot proved challenging. The BOA bindings were easy to adjust even with bulky gloves, and once dialed in proved extremely comfortable and secure.

Sizes: 25, 30, 36 in. (men’s) 21, 25 (women’s) Weight: 4.9 lbs (25 in), 5.6 lbs (30 in), 6.5 lbs (36 in) Maximum Load: 200 lbs (25 in), 250 lbs (30 in), 280 lbs (36 in).

Pros and Cons + Great traction on hills + Easy to adjust, glove-friendly binding + Wide range of sizes – Wider decks can be cumbersome.

L.L. Bean’s Pathfinder snowshoe package impressed beginners and experts alike among this year’s Rocky Mountain test team. The BOA bindings—not often found in beginner-friendly packages—were a fan favorite, snugging promptly over mountaineering boots and casual snowboots and never needing another adjustment. The bindings were easy to use while wearing gloves and mittens, a big plus on a trip to Rocky Mountain National Park’s Emerald Lake where the windchill dropped to -20 degrees.

In a recent development, on a windy, late-season day in the Indian Peaks, the crampons easily bit into steep ice crust in the morning, and the decks—made of high-density polyethylene—floated over thick corn snow in the afternoon. The poles are sturdy aluminum and adjust with an external lever lock that never failed or stuck. The only con was the width of the frame, which occasionally snagged on willow tips and low-hanging branches. But once in the open powder above treeline, the wider area underfoot became a plus. If you want a sturdy set of snowshoes and poles that holds up in most winter conditions, the Pathfinder Package delivers.

Sizes: 22, 25 in. Weight: 3.8 lbs (22 in), 4 lbs (25 in) Maximum Load: 180 lbs (22 in), 210 (25 in).

Pros and Cons + Good traction on slopes + Easy-to-use binding + Heel lift – Expensive.

Sources indicate that many snowshoes are unisex, which means they tend to be too major for lighter folks who don’t need the oversized frame. The women’s-specific Lightning Ascents are nearly an inch narrower and five ounces lighter than the men’s version, making them perfect for smaller people with narrow gaits. The Ascent’s binding, a comfortable rubber mesh toe cup that secures via two rubber side straps that buckle into place, is simple to use with just a quick two-handed pull. The tooth-lined stainless steel frame and pivoting, two-pronged toe crampons impressed on outings in Rocky Mountain National Park’s Glacier Gorge, where our 5’4”, 115-pound tester tackled icy sidehills and slippery windcrust. But the Lightning Ascent isn’t just ideal for smaller snowshoers: Our 5’10”, 155-pound tester also found the precise, narrow ‘shoe design useful while climbing the gullied slopes of northern Vermont.

Sizes: 20.5, 23.5, 27 in. Weight: 3.6 lbs (20.5 in), 3.8 lbs (23.5 in), 4 lbs (27 in) Maximum Load: 180 lbs (20.5 in), 260 lbs (23.5 in), 300 lbs (27 in).

Pros and Cons + Intuitive BOA system + Multi-direction crampons + Flexible + Heel lift – Expensive – No tail extensions – Not great in powder.

Industry observers note that for those who loathe fiddly snowshoe bindings, the Symbioz Hyperflex Instinct is a godsend. While several snowshoes incorporate BOA closures into their design, few are quite as simple as the Instinct’s. The design: a single knob that tightens the toe, sides, and heel using interlinked cables that run through the perimeter of the binding, eliminating any and all trailhead exasperation. It takes fewer than 10 seconds to step into and secure the snowshoe, but the Instinct stayed glued to our boots all day long, even while walking on bumpy, uneven terrain in Colorado’s Indian Peaks Wilderness. Another characteristic we loved: flexible decking made of injection-molded polypropylene. The pliable material gave us just enough torsional flexibility to enhance comfort and reduce ankle-twisting on uneven surfaces. While sidehilling through a labyrinth of postholes in Rocky Mountain National Park, eight lateral stainless steel teeth kept our Colorado tester upright and stable.

Size: 25 in Weight: 2.2 lbs (Tru Trak bindings), 2.4 lbs (Spin Bindings) Maximum Load: 215 lbs.

Pros and Cons + Lightweight + Easy-to-use BOA-style bindings – Below-average traction – No heel lift.

Industry observers note that over a pound lighter than the next-lightest snowshoes in our test, the Elite Race Ultralights, designed for endurance and adventure races, delivered on their name. Even with ultralight bindings and minimalist crampons, these snowshoes impressed testers with their durability. The PU-coated nylon mesh decking and aluminum alloy frame stood up to rock-studded snow slopes and scraped across ice with barely any sign of wear. Our testers loved them for their comfort and ease of use; thick foam padding around the binding straps eliminated hot spots, and once set, they stayed on without further adjustment. The narrow tails let you walk—or run—with your normal stride. One tester taught several Avalanche Terrain Avoidance classes for the Colorado Mountain Club in these snowshoes, where their ease of use and float in five inches of new snow was the envy of all her students. There is a cost to mild crampons and the simple plastic ridges on the perimeter frame: The Ultralights gripped well on moderate slopes, but skidded a bit on steep ice.

Recent findings suggest that sizes: 21, 25, and 30 in. Weight: 4 lbs (21 in), 4.2 lbs (25 in), 4.8 lbs (30 in) Maximum Load: 120-250 lbs.

Pros and Cons + Very affordable + Convenient, effective heel lift + Glove-friendly bindings – Heavy.

The updated version of our perennial budget pick, the Retrospec Drifter, impressed with good flotation, comfortable heel lifts for hills, and glove-friendly bindings.

The double ratchet strap bindings proved secure, intuitive, and easy to adjust, with buckles that were large enough to be manipulated without removing our gloves. The heel lift was ideal for 30-degree slopes in Rocky Mountain National Park, and was much easier to flip up or down—even with gloves on—than last year’s model. For a shoe that costs less than a quarter of some of our other winners, that’s an impressive feature set.

Plus, the Drifter is just about as bulletproof as a snowshoe gets: The one-piece polypropylene deck and aluminum alloy frame didn’t show a scratch from early-season rocks, surprise tree roots, and a long rattly drive in a roof box full of pointy gear.

Recent findings suggest that our Colorado testers found the underfoot crampons perfect for hard snow in the Indian Peaks, but with only six main crampons beneath the toes and no teeth around the perimeter, anything steeper than a 20-degree slope felt pretty sketchy when iced over. The Drifters also aren’t particularly strong in the flotation department: Our five-foot-four tester, who used the shorter 21-inch version, struggled to stay afloat the most.

But for $50, these snowshoes pack plenty of great features into an adventure-ready, accessible package.

Size: 22 in Weight: 3.6 lbs Maximum Load: 180 lbs.

Pros and Cons + One size fits all + Affordable + Impressive traction + Float tail-compatible – No heel lift.

It has been revealed that described by testers as “aggressively sturdy,” these near-unbreakable injection-molded snowshoes will get you where you want to go with minimal fuss and fear of equipment failure. The stiff plastic body doesn’t have a lot of flex to match a hiker’s gait, but was ideal for packing down the trail for our Oregon-based tester’s three adventuring huskies.

Recent findings suggest that the Evo Trail’s serrated steel traction rails, four-toothed toe crampons, and plastic, anti-slide ridges kept our testers upright, even on crusty sidehills. Flotation is great, too, for such a small snowshoe. One of our Pacific Northwest-based testers took the Evo Trails through 20 miles of deep, unconsolidated snow in Oregon’s Blue Mountains and stayed on top of the powder the entire time—no easy feat in the chilly, snowbound region.

This year’s model uses the brand’s Paraglide binding, which combines a wide piece of stretch mesh over the toe with a simple heel strap. They climb decently well without a heel lift, though we think it should be a standard feature, even on this entry-level ‘shoe.

Sizes: 23, 27 in (women’s), 25, 30, 35 in (men’s) Weight: 4.3 lbs (25 in), 4.7 lbs (30 in), 5 lbs (35 in) Maximum Load: 160 lbs (23 in), 200 lbs (27 in), 200 lbs (25 in), 250 lbs (30 in), 300+ lbs (35 in).

Pros and Cons + Great float + Heel lift + Good traction on hills – Bindings can be fiddly.

In a recent development, the Atlas Montane’s lightweight PVC decking and an aluminum tube frame combine for a classic deep-powder snowshoe. Our six-foot-two, 200-pound Colorado tester took the 30-inch version for a winter ascent of Longs Peak and floated easily over two to three feet of fresh snow, even with a pack full of heavy climbing gear. Even the smaller decks (down to 23 inches) wowed our testers with easy traverses of powdery alpine meadows and serious forest drifts. Underfoot crampons and carbon steel lateral grips at the snowshoe’s midpoint kept footing sure and steady even on icy sidehills.

According to recent reports, the Montane is wider than most of the other snowshoes we tested in both the men’s and women’s models, which gives this ‘shoe its superior flotation, but it does take a moment to adapt your gait and stop banging the snowshoes together. Our testers found the strap bindings fiddly with thick ski gloves on, but once the two straps were latched in place, they stayed there for the whole trip. On powder days, the flotation more than makes up for the simple, slightly inconvenient binding. If you’re planning off-trail travel in deep snow, especially if you’ll be carrying heavy overnight packs, these are the snowshoes for you.

Industry observers note that flat, uncomplicated terrain doesn’t require too much from a pair of snowshoes. Simple, comfortable bindings and a deck that provides adequate flotation are all you need. If icy slopes or deep snow aren’t in your future, save money with a budget pair made from heavier molded plastic and less aggressive traction.

Sources indicate that on the other end of the spectrum are snowshoes built for challenging terrain—slushy hills, narrow singletrack, or mixed rock and ice. A secure wrap around the heel and/or multiple straps along the foot are vital for stability. Quick binding systems, like those that utilize a BOA twist lock, are helpful when taking snowshoes on and off in precarious terrain and a huge time-saver compared with fiddly three-strap setups. Snowshoes geared towards mountainous ascents will have a wider variety of spikes and crampons underfoot—and in more abundance—to offer grip both horizontally and laterally, and to bite through different types of ice. A heel lift that provides about 2 inches of lift (that’s easy to flick open and closed with either gloved hands or a trekking pole) is a must for giving your feet and calves an assist on the steeps.

In deep, fresh powder, you’ll want wider, longer snowshoes (or those that come with extensions) for superior flotation. On the flipside, if you’re headed out on a weight-conscious backpacking trip and/or plan to strap the snowshoes to your pack for much of the trip, prioritize lightweight construction, like a pair made from aluminum and TPU-coated nylon, for reducing fatigue on-foot and outside your pack.

Over the past several years, our veteran testers braved blizzards, sub-zero temps, and icy alpine climbs to find out which snowshoes are really the best. Only nine models stood up to the rigors of our testing to earn a spot on this list.

Sources indicate that we looked at design, features, ease of use, comfort, traction, cost, weight, and flotation in deep snow to narrow down the best of the best from the current market. This year, some tried-and-tested snowshoe models received updates, like newly introduced bindings and decking materials, which we then reevaluated. Others haven’t changed through the years: their simple designs and technologies have withstood the test of time.

Sources indicate that kristin Smith A former Backpacker editor, category manager Kristin Smith has been a full- or part-time mountain guide for most of the last decade. In her spare time, she teaches Avalanche Terrain Avoidance for the Colorado Mountain Club, guides clients through the nearby peaks of Rocky Mountain National Park, and maps out latest places to visit with her recently-acquired pilot’s license.

Jill Yarger Jill Yarger works as a mountain guide in Boulder, Colorado. She moved for an engineering job, found the mountains, and never left; that was almost 40 years ago. Since then she’s spent 13 years volunteering in the Rocky Mountain Rescue Group, joined the National Ski Patrol and Mountain Rescue Associations, and climbed in Alaska, Italy, and Canada.

Industry observers note that jessica Bucklin Jessica Bucklin spent a decade sailing tall ships all over the world before moving to the coast of Maine, where finding enough snow to snowshoe often requires just a walk down the road. When she’s not exploring Maine’s mountain parks she captains a towboat out of Bath.

According to recent reports, joe O’Leary Joe’s guiding career spanned North, Central, and South America before he settled in Colorado, where he now trains other guides in whitewater rafting, mountain biking, backpacking, and leadership development. When he’s not biking, rafting, or kayaking, he works as a nature photographer and writer.

Breaking: Watch: Jessie Diggins Explains Why Sparkles Are Her Superpower

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1667 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways

  • After retiring from cross-country skiing as the most decorated American of all time, glide off into the sunset Jessie Diggins did not.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that trail Runner managing editor Abby Levene caught up with cross-country skiing superstar Jessie Diggins in Kona, Hawaii, a few days before the Ironman World Championship. In this exclusive interview, Diggins shares how she battled through a deep low to finish (and win) her first 100-miler, the lessons from cross-country skiing that she’s applying to trail running, and why she always puts on face glitter before a race.

After retiring from cross-country skiing as the most decorated American of all time, glide off into the sunset Jessie Diggins did not. The Olympic gold medalist earned one last piece of hardware in Milan-Cortina this spring—on bruised ribs no less—hung up the skis, and dove head-first into trail running.

Diggins, 35, raced the Broken Arrow Triple Crown in June, as has become her annual ritual. She then lined up against the world’s best trail runners at Sierre-Zinal in August, won the Superior 100-miler in September, and just last weekend won the (bear with me) Trail Animals Running Club Stone Cat Trail Festival 50-miler in Massachusetts.

On paper, it’s been an effortless transition into a sport Diggins swears she is just doing for fun. But of course there is so much more to the story once you dig in. I was lucky enough to catch up with Diggins at the epicenter of yet another endurance sport—the Ironman World Championship—in Kona, Hawaii, last month. She’d just come from a snorkeling expedition trying to find a sea turtle. (So far no luck.) Gazing out onto the turquoise waves crashing into shore, we chatted about what she’s learned and loved about trail running so far. That list includes (and is not limited to) how trail running really is a team sport, achieving personal goals is bigger than the results, fueling on a “washing machine” stomach is not easy, and the power of glitter translates from snowy trails to dry ones.

Industry observers note that this interview has been edited for clarity. You can also watch some of it above.

Jessie: It was a really cool experience. It was so humbling, but so exciting to tackle a totally different challenge. I was filled with curiosity: What will this feel like? What’s going to happen to my body? What will happen inside my brain? How does this work?

Having a crew and pacers like that is very different from skiing. [In skiing] you are alone on the trail, and people can cheer for you, but you don’t actually have anyone with you on the trail. And so it was just so exciting I got to do it with a team. That was really big for me. I’m a very team-oriented person, and I would get so excited to come into the aid station and see the crew and to get to have a pacer with me. Even when I was falling apart and couldn’t even  talk—I was at a really low point—it was just like, ‘I’m here with my team and I’m pushing my limits and I’m seeing what’s possible for me.’ And that’s so exciting.

Recent findings suggest that I would just tell myself ‘every step you take is a step you don’t have to take again.’ So I was just like, ‘I’m doing it. I’m slowly working towards that finish line, step by step.’ It was so funny because even when I was deeply uncomfortable, I never actually thought about quitting, which I thought I would. It was more just like I’m so uncomfortable, but I know I can if I just keep moving. Even if I’m slowing down, even if I’m not even able to run, I have to just power hike this section. I’m still moving towards my goal. I’m in the process of getting there, and that’s exciting in and of itself.

I kind of wanted to set up a charcuterie board of the trail world and try different things because they were all so different, right? Broken Arrow is a huge festival and it was a multi-day thing, so oh my gosh, what is day three gonna feel like? Can I even run downhill on day three?

Industry observers note that and then Sierre-Zinal is so historic, and it was such a cool course. It was beautiful, and it was like experiencing a very classic “short” trail race, right? I was like, ‘this is not short.’ It took me 3 hours, but it was so cool to experience.

According to recent reports, and then going into the 100 miler, it was different and more of a backyard format. Or not a backyard in terms of the laps, but like there was no award ceremony. It wasn’t about winning. It was just about doing it, and I love that. That is so aligned with how I feel about racing. It’s like, ‘No, we don’t really care who wins. We just want everyone to challenge themselves and hopefully make their goal of crossing the finish line.’ And that was so cool for me.

Industry observers note that and so getting to be a part of each of these events, I got to experience so many different angles of the trail world and meet so many people. And for me, that was a massive thing, too: feeling the sense of community that was around every single race and making upcoming friends and trying something new. That was very cool.

Recent findings suggest that no, I definitely am excited to do more. I don’t know what that’s gonna look like yet, but I feel like just getting to be involved in this world is so cool and so exciting. So, I’m sort of now in the phase of like, ‘OK, I feel like I’m bouncing back with 100. Like, my body’s coming back, and now I can start dreaming and scheming and brainstorming, like what else do I want to do? What else is out there? What excites me? What feels like the appropriate challenge for this phase of my life?’ Yeah, I’m trying to figure it all out.

I think the biggest thing was in training, like listening to my body. So I stopped wearing a heart rate monitor like five or six years ago, and it was really about being in tune and listening to my body and figuring out where I can push. What does it feel like when I’m riding that line of level three, and what are the signals in my body when I’ve gone over that line and I need to pull it back?

Industry observers note that and so really trying to deeply understand how I feel, and I feel like that’s helped me steer away from injuries too, because I’m not relying on metrics. I want to feel how my body feels and respond to that and act on those feelings.I think that’s something I’m taking with me because I’m well aware now that running can really beat you up in a different way. Even listening to my body and learning how much can I eat while I’m running because your stomach is a washing machine and that does not happen in cross-country skiing.

Industry observers note that I think it was really exciting in my final years of cross-country skiing, learning more about high-carb fueling and having all these great products come on board. Because in a ski race, let’s say a 50-kilometer race, you come through a feed zone, but you have gloves and your hands are in poles, so you are not like ripping open a gel. You’ll end up stabbing yourself in the face. And so what you do is you tuck your poles under your armpits and you grab the feed bottle, which is usually an actual baby bottle with the lid taken off, from a coach who cannot run with you, they have to just stand there and hold it by the rim. So you grab it while you are gliding quite rapidly. You down it so you get like a few good sips, and then you have to chuck the bottle on the side and keep moving. And so having really high carb drink mixes where you can, if you only can get a few mouthfuls, you need them to count, and so having these was huge. Because before it’d be like, ‘I guess we’ll boil down Coke to de-fizz it, and that’s what you can have.’ But it  just wasn’t high carb enough, and the electrolyte balance might not have been great.

According to recent reports, now there’s so many options, and that really changed the way I could race. And so now, in trail racing, there’s all these different gels. You can find the one that works for you. There’s all these different mixes. You can find the amount of salt that works for you. That’s been really cool. Being able to tailor it. I feel like 15 years ago, there weren’t that many options. Now having more options is power.

Recent findings suggest that I do get scared. It’s funny. I just saw on the elevator this morning a woman was wearing glitter, and I was like, ‘Yes!’ That was my whole thing through my ski career. And it came out of being scared and being nervous. And I feel like people don’t always know that that’s the origin. But I would get so nervous for races, and a little bit of nerves is great. It means you care. If you’re not nervous for a race, it’s sort of like, ‘Why am I doing this?’ You know, then it’s time to maybe examine, do I really care about what I’m doing?

At the end of the day, yes, there’s a lot of pressure. There can be expectations. There can be a lot of lights. A lot of people are watching you, but you get to do this. You get to challenge yourself and see what’s possible. And that, in and of itself, is such an amazing opportunity.

(Photo: Courtesy of Palisades Tahoe).

It has been revealed that california’s ski season is getting an early-season boost in a huge way. A powerful storm system is dumping significant snowfall across the Sierra Nevada, with Lake Tahoe-area ski resorts among the biggest winners.

Sources indicate that the storm has delivered some eye-popping totals already. According to resort snow reports from Thursday, Nov. 19, Boreal Mountain picked up 52 inches in the previous 24 hours, while Mt. Rose reported 32 to 36 inches. Sugar Bowl recorded 34 inches, Palisades Tahoe 25 inches, and Kirkwood 27 inches. Northstar and Bear Valley each reported 22 inches.

The snowfall extends beyond Tahoe, too. Mammoth Mountain reported 20 to 32 inches at Main Lodge in the 24 hours leading into Thursday morning, adding to an already promising start to the season.

In a recent development, we’re not jealous here in Colorado. Not at all.

The timing couldn’t be better for resorts gearing up for Thanksgiving week. Several mountains have moved opening dates forward or are preparing to welcome skiers as early as this weekend. Palisades Tahoe, originally scheduled to open Nov. 25, will now spin lifts Saturday, Nov. 21. Northstar, Heavenly, and Boreal are also scheduled to open today (Friday, Nov. 20). Kirkwood just revealed they’re opening nearly two weeks early, on Monday, Nov. 23.

According to recent reports, but wait, there’s more: Another storm system is expected to move into the Sierra early next week, potentially bringing additional heavy snowfall just in time for Thanksgiving. Forecasts are calling for several more feet across the mountains.

According to recent reports, there is one important caveat, fellow skiers: Getting to the mountains could be a challenge. Heavy snowfall has already caused travel disruptions along Interstate 80, and the Sierra Avalanche Center issued a high avalanche danger warning for the Tahoe backcountry. Skiers should check road conditions and resort operations before heading out, and stay out of the backcountry until conditions improve.

This is like an early Christas gift after a disappointing snow season last winter. And with Thanksgiving still several days away, winter is just getting warmed up.

#102140. Latest Update: 5 Steps To Taking An Elk With An Over-The-Counter Tag

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2135 w)
