#102120. Stephanie Case Just Ran 100 Miles in Antarctica. She Doesn’t Even Like the Cold.

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1555 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Trailrunnermag ↗ Open Full Page

Stephanie Case Just Ran 100 Miles in Antarctica. She Doesn’t Even Like the Cold.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1555 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 2025, a photo of Stephanie Case breastfeeding her infant daughter, Pepper, at an aid station during a 100K ultra in Northern Wales went viral, and the human rights lawyer and ultrarunner became the face of postpartum badassery.
  • It has been revealed that now, she’s officially the first woman to run 100 miles in Antarctica.
  • It has been revealed that “The whole idea for this race came after I had my daughter and people were asking me if I was going to start to settle down,” Case, 44, shared with Trail Runner from her home in Chamonix, France.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2025, a photo of Stephanie Case breastfeeding her infant daughter, Pepper, at an aid station during a 100K ultra in Northern Wales went viral, and the human rights lawyer and ultrarunner became the face of postpartum badassery.

It has been revealed that now, she’s officially the first woman to run 100 miles in Antarctica. Case took on the November 8 challenge in part to prove that the things she did before becoming a mom weren’t behind her. If anything, she could come back and do them even better.

It has been revealed that “The whole idea for this race came after I had my daughter and people were asking me if I was going to start to settle down,” Case, 44, shared with Trail Runner from her home in Chamonix, France. “They were criticizing me after I came back for my first race postpartum, telling me that I was selfish to be taking that time to train. So I wanted to go out and really prove to myself and remind myself that I could keep doing big things.”.

Actually, big is an understatement. Of the eight runners who started the Antarctic Ice Ultra 100 miler on Union Glacier, Case was one of four finishers, and second overall. Her finishing time of 17 hours, 31 minutes and 39 seconds, a clip of 10:31 per mile, smashed the former overall course record by five hours. Only Yusheng Ni, a top ultrarunner from China with experience racing in Antarctica, ran faster in a fresh best-ever mark of 17:02:24.

Here’s the kicker: Case doesn’t even like running in the cold.

There’s cold, and then there’s Antarctica cold. The race started at 1 a.m. under a 24-hour sun, with temperatures as low as minus 35 degrees Fahrenheit—roughly 35 degrees colder than a typical kitchen freezer. And with fierce polar winds, no exposed skin is safe.

Recent findings suggest that “I’m someone who doesn’t like when the house goes below room temperature. My partner and I are constantly having a fight about where we set the thermostat,” Case shared. “So this was going to be a substantial challenge for me. I knew that I wasn’t going to love it. But I’m Canadian. There’s no bad weather, there’s just bad clothing, they say.”.

Recent findings suggest that finding the right gear was one of the biggest priorities in Case’s preparation. She reached out to other runners who had completed the Antarctic 100-miler in previous years to glean their insight. One offered an unexpected tip: Apply sunscreen inside of her nostrils, since the sun reflecting off the snow can burn there, too.

Recent findings suggest that she also worked with The North Face, one of her sponsors, to design a custom shoe specifically for the conditions. Breathability was key: She didn’t want moisture trapped inside the shoe, and the sole needed to remain flexible in extreme temperatures. There was also the matter of laces. Frozen laces—or having to tie them with mittens on—were not an option. The solution was a BOA closure system, which let her tighten the shoes by turning a dial. The design also included an integrated, insulated but breathable gaiter and removable spikes she could screw into the soles if conditions got icy.

According to recent reports, the setup worked better than she could have hoped. Case wore two pairs of socks—a thin liner underneath a wool pair—and didn’t change them once during the entire race.

“I just set it and left it,” she remarked. “And it was one of the things I was most stressed about, because with hands, you can put on more gloves. You can have hand warmers. But toe warmers don’t work when you’re running. They can’t fit in the shoe. And I knew if my toes were cold, I was just going to be screwed. And they were toasty the whole time.”.

As for the rest of her clothing, Case had to consider another challenge: her sweat rate.

Sources indicate that “I’m a heavy sweater. Even in just mild cold temperatures, I sweat a liter an hour, and in warm temperatures up to two liters,” she said. “So I knew that I would be at a pretty big disadvantage, because when you sweat, your gear gets wet and then you’re screwed.”.

Recent findings suggest that her strategy was to dress as lightly as possible through her core while keeping her hands, feet and face warm and protected. In the coldest stretches, she wore winter tights under wind pants, along with a thin base layer, a midlayer, and a shell on top. At some points, she stripped down to a thin base layer and shell.

In a recent development, “As long as I kept moving, I was fine,” she stated. “But I wouldn’t be able to kind of stop and walk if something went wrong.”.

In a recent development, she never quite felt warm, and some exposed skin on her face did get frostbitten. But she managed to find moments of equilibrium.

“I felt comfortable at times. And then other times I feel like I was just constantly on the edge,” she said. “I wasn’t freezing, but I was cold. But as long as my feet were OK and my hands were OK, then I was fine to keep moving.”.

The temperature wasn’t the only feature of Antarctica that concerned Case. She describes herself as a “mountain goat.” Living in Chamonix, she’s accustomed to steep trails and vert—not the flat, repetitive terrain of Antarctica’s 38-loop course.

In a recent development, working with her coach, Meghan Roche, she shifted her training toward flatter ground and faster running. The change paid off: during her workouts, Case set personal records at several distances, from the 10K through the marathon.

Recent findings suggest that “I had a love-hate relationship with it,” she stated of the training. “But the funny thing was that every time I had a training session, I was getting PRs, because I just don’t run on flat ground.”.

She also tested her gear in a cryotherapy chamber during a trip to Geneva, Switzerland, spending 20 minutes in temperatures that gradually warmed from minus 148°F to minus 22°F. The goal wasn’t so much to acclimate as to understand what the cold would feel like and test her logistics. The session made her rethink her fueling proposal: Pulling off gloves, unzipping a shell, and drinking from a flask in those conditions would be too cumbersome.

Sources indicate that instead, her camera operator doubled as her crew, handing her a SIS gel and flask every loop. While most competitors visited the aid tent every lap or two, Case aimed to go ten loops—roughly a marathon—between stops. She had to cut the first stretch short when her balaclava froze into a solid block of ice, but after that she managed three 10-loop stints.

The aid station offered some reprieve, with ramen noodles, mashed potatoes, shots of maple syrup, and Rice Krispies treats, but even small tasks there got complicated. Taking her gloves off for just 30 seconds to go to the bathroom could mean waiting 20 minutes for her hands to warm up again.

“There was not a single minute during this race when I kind of just relaxed and allowed myself to switch off,” she says. “In any other 100, I can usually just kind of push past [discomfort], but there, one tiny mistake could end the race for me.”.

Sources indicate that as Case recovers at home with collagen mask treatments to heal her frostbitten cheeks and nose, her next challenge is already on the calendar: becoming the first woman to complete the Montane Arctic Spine, a 500-kilometer race in February. This time, she’ll be on Nordic skis, pulling a sled and traveling solo, with checkpoints as far as 50 miles apart. She’ll need to melt her own snow, pitch her own tent, and carry out the journey without a crew.

She hopes Antarctica has prepared her for an even harder task.

“Sometimes the way to get through a really scary thing is to line up an even scarier thing afterwards,” she said.

It has been revealed that beyond that, Case is developing a project called “94 Degrees,” a film that will show her running the gamut of conditions from minus 40 degrees Celsius in the Arctic to 54 degrees Celsius at Badwater in California’s Death Valley, a 94-degree Celsius spread. (She’s qualified for Badwater but still needs to apply for an invitation, so that part isn’t yet confirmed.).

In a recent development, and in the meantime, she’ll continue her work for the U.N. while serving as the President of Free to Run, a non-profit organization that uses sport to empower women and girls in conflict-affected areas. And she’ll soak up all the cuddles she can with Pepper, now 2, while sharing stories of that one time she ran 100 miles in Antarctica. It’s a story that almost sounds like a fairy tale.

Sources indicate that “I actually brought one of her toys, a penguin rubber ducky, with me on the trip, just as a reminder of her,” Case noted. “And then this penguin came out on the course and actually ran alongside me for part of it. I’ve been showing her photos and videos … but still … it’s all kind of unbelievable.”.

Cut Off for 6 Years, Denali’s Only Road and Its Wildest Country Are Reopen for 2027

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1305 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the single road in Denali National Park winds through the heart of the park and ends in the remote historic mining town of Kantishna.
  • On the left!” I jolt forward from the front passenger seat to find where our driver has spotted a grizzly on the open tundra.
  • For the last six years, this mostly gravel mountain corridor—the only road through Denali National Park and Preserve—has been closed after mile 43 due to a landslide.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the single road in Denali National Park winds through the heart of the park and ends in the remote historic mining town of Kantishna. Hikers and cyclists are now able to cross the newly completed Pretty Rocks Bridge, and full public park bus service is set to resume in 2027. (Photo: Pursuit).

“Bear! On the left!” I jolt forward from the front passenger seat to find where our driver has spotted a grizzly on the open tundra. On a steep slope covered with birch trees, pops of autumn amber and rust scattered against green spruce trees, I can make out a moving boulder—then I spot its golden blonde fur. Olivia Juarez, general manager of Denali Backcountry Lodge, tells me it’s the signature coat of Denali grizzlies. Juarez is driving three of us, including her dog, on the entire 92-mile nearly unpaved stretch of the Denali Park Road, which feels precarious at times due to two-thirds of it being only one lane. But the speed limit is 35 mph, and we are the only ones on it.

For the last six years, this mostly gravel mountain corridor—the only road through Denali National Park and Preserve—has been closed after mile 43 due to a landslide. But in time for the 2027 summer season, access to the full 92 miles will reopen, allowing visitors to explore the depths of Denali’s backcountry once again.

According to recent reports, juarez slows the van to a stop, and we pass around binoculars. The grizzly is far in the distance, but it’s what surrounds it in every direction that catches my breath: striking volcanic cliffs in a kaleidoscope of earthy hues and gravelly, braided glacial streams stretching across an endless expanse of wild. It’s only us on the road, and this grizzly out yonder, for as far as we can see. And out there, somewhere hidden under a cloak of clouds, is Denali, or The Great One, as the peak’s traditional name translates from the Koyukon Athabascan language.

On September 2, 2026, the long-awaited Pretty Rocks Bridge in Denali National Park was completed, an architectural marvel that bypasses the still-active landslide. At 475 feet long and 24 feet wide, the steel single-span truss bridge is just wide enough for a park bus to drive through.

This $230 million federal project includes 23 underground thermosiphons—a passive cooling technology that pulls heat out of the earth to keep the permafrost frozen year-round. Pedestrians and cyclists are currently permitted to cross, with full bus and vehicle service scheduled to resume in 2027.

It has been revealed that I’ve spent the last four nights at Denali Backcountry Lodge, a remote all-inclusive outpost that sits at the end of the road. I flew in via a 45-mile helicopter ride, the only way guests can reach the property since the landslide. The lodge is the farthest place you can stay and still be in the park. We spent our days hiking through the spongy tundra, exploring the history of the Kantishna mining camp, and kayaking Wonder Lake with Denali in the background, a coveted sight since it was photographed by Ansel Adams on a rare cloudless day in 1947.

According to recent reports, since the road closure, no one other than guests staying at the three remote wilderness lodges has been able to visit these iconic areas of the park. While Denali Backcountry Lodge offers a chance to truly settle into the wild, all the excitement is found along the road. That is, nearly all our wildlife sightings (except for a grizzly sitting atop its moose kill spotted in the distance on one of our guided hikes) happened on a drive: a trio of caribou running, a moose moving through the willow marshes, a porcupine waddling across the road, a bear cub prancing out from the shrubs.

In a recent development, starting in 2027, visitors will finally be able to reach the end of the road again on a Denali park bus. Guests staying at Denali Backcountry Lodge will arrive and depart via a private bus next year, and their Creekside Cabins guests will take a private bus in and fly out on a single-engine bush plane. Day guests will be able to reach the end of the road and book a guided experience at Denali Backcountry Lodge.

More travelers returning to Denali’s backcountry means there’s more opportunity to transform them into stewards of this land. “Visiting a place like this is life-changing for people,” claims Alexa Donahe, vice president and general manager of Pursuit’s Alaska Collection, which includes Denali Backcountry Lodge. “Day traffic allows for more people who don’t have the time or resources to have an immersive backcountry experience like this and to experience the depths of the wilderness for a day.”.

According to recent reports, even with more visitors coming in by bus, it will still feel remote, notes Donahe. There will be strict park (and lodge) restrictions to preserve the landscape and wildlife. For comparison, more than 4 million people visit 2.2-million-acre Yellowstone yearly, with easy road access for private cars. Only 500,000 people visit Denali each year, but at 6 million acres, the park is the size of Vermont.

Sure, there are more people gathering at the park entrance, where you’ll find a visitor center and the famous Denali sled dogs, but once you reach the dirt road, it feels as remote as ever.

Recent findings suggest that only about 30 percent of visitors to Denali National Park and Preserve get a completely clear view of the peak. An even smaller subset—fewer than ten percent—experience a completely cloud-free, base-to-summit view. Visitors who stay multiple days (such as four days in Kantishna) see the mountain at much higher rates, around 85 percent. Because the massive 20,310-foot peak creates its own local weather system, heavy cloud cover frequently obscures the summit, especially during the summer tourism season.

Industry observers note that one morning at breakfast, a group of Natural Habitat guests wait out bad weather to depart. Their expedition leader Samantha Strauss shares with me her thoughts on the fully opened Denali. “For every person who comes out and sees this place, that’s one more person that cares about public lands. Especially right now, public lands are not promised to us,” she states. “Even if that means I have less square mileage allotted just to myself, even if that means I have to share this space with more people, it is a conservation win because it helps people create a connection to the landscape and have a stake in its future.”.

Industry observers note that I flew over Denali National Park in a helicopter and left on the Denali Park Road, just days after the Pretty Rocks Bridge bypassing the landslide was completed. Both ways gave me different perspectives on this vast expanse of raw wilderness.

While it was thrilling to soar over glaciers and peaks, it was seeing Denali from the ground, my eyes scanning the landscape for wildlife, moving through the changing early autumn hues, feeling the rush of brisk air as I rolled my window down to take a photo, that made me feel I was a part of it. The road is the center line of this wilderness, and it’s not only the best way to see Denali’s untamed backcountry and wildlife, but to feel its beating heart.

#102118. Industry News: What Does Trail Magic Look Like Around the World? These 5 Stories Show Us

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1243 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Backpacker ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: What Does Trail Magic Look Like Around the World? These 5 Stories Show Us

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1243 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The snacks at the hut made Matt's day, despite the mucky conditions (Photo: Matt Jordan).
  • According to recent reports, on the 2024 Highlander UAE, a multi-day 40-mile hike through the Hajar Mountains, I struggled far more than I had expected.
  • In a recent development, that’s when a local Emirati man came walking up the trail behind me.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The snacks at the hut made Matt's day, despite the mucky conditions (Photo: Matt Jordan).

According to recent reports, on the 2024 Highlander UAE, a multi-day 40-mile hike through the Hajar Mountains, I struggled far more than I had expected. The terrain was brutal, with steep descents over sharp, rocky granite tracks along the 6,345-foot Jebel Jais summit. My heavy pack weighed me down, and I could feel every stone beneath my boots. By day three, my two big toes hurt so much that on one challenging descent, I collapsed and couldn’t take another step.

In a recent development, that’s when a local Emirati man came walking up the trail behind me. He saw that I was struggling and stopped to pull out a roll of tape from his bag. Then, he peeled off my very stinky hiking socks without a second thought, taped up my toes, and bandaged my knees. He even carried my pack for several miles, guiding me down the remaining steep sections.

It has been revealed that this stranger had no reason to go out of his way to help me, and I know I could not have finished that day without him. Hikers call this kind of experience “trail magic.” The Appalachian Trail Conservancy defines the term as any instance of finding what you need most when you least expect it; experiencing something rare, extraordinary, or inspiring in nature, or encountering unexpected acts of generosity that restore one’s faith in humanity.

In a recent development, trail magic is often associated with Appalachian Trail history from the early 1980s. However, after my experience in the UAE, I started wondering what it looks like elsewhere. So, here are five stories from other hikers who have experienced trail magic in one form or another around the world.

In a recent development, matt Jordan, a hiking and backpacking guide with Intrepid Travel, was walking New Zealand’s 1,881-mile Te Araroa Trail southbound in 2023 when he hit the muddy Longwood Forest in Fiordland. After a miserable day of rain and bog, he pushed on toward Turnbull’s Hut, one of the last backcountry huts on that segment. He’d heard that sometimes, free supplies were stored there for hikers passing through. As he approached, he prayed it hadn’t already all been taken by the time he got there.

Industry observers note that “Thankfully it hadn’t,” he says. When he opened the store area, he found a cache of goodies.

In a recent development, “A local man who hikes in supplies, hauls out trash, and maintains the hut about twice a month leaves coolers stocked with beer, soda, and candy bars,” Jordan says. Excitedly, he grabbed a drink, then promptly slipped in the mud and fell on his backside. After days of awful weather conditions, though, that didn’t stop him from laughing out loud.

“For me, the gesture was about more than a cold drink. It was a reminder of the generosity of strangers and the sense of community that makes long-distance hikes unforgettable worldwide.”.

Meeta Singh Rao, a hiking guide in India, indicates some of her best trail magic came from shepherds who spend months in the high mountain pastures of the Indian Himalayas. In October 2022, she was leading a trek to Nawali Bugyal in Uttarakhand when the weather turned. Heavy rain began to fall, and strong winds blew. The mules carrying their gear were also lost, and camp was miles away.

Industry observers note that the group came across a shepherd with his flock. He heard where they were headed, and offered them shelter in his channi, a mountain hut made of stone, mud, and plastic sheets. “When rainwater leaked through the roof, he walked out into the downpour to rearrange the plastic so we stayed dry,” claims Rao.

When Rao offered to pay, the shepherd gently refused, saying they were his guests. “A couple with so little of their own opened their home to us, giving us a feeling of belonging in the mountains,” she adds.

Sources indicate that kaitlyn Bussell has walked four Caminos. But her second, the 62-mile Camino Inglés in September 2023 through Galicia, was particularly challenging. The rain was constant, few hostels and cafés were open in the fall, and she walked long stretches without seeing another pilgrim.

Recent findings suggest that on the second day, wet and ready for a break, she ducked into the first bar she found for a café con leche and to charge her phone. When she went to pay, the young woman behind the counter told her the coffee was free and handed her some water, prayer cards and a small Camino keepsake.

“It was a small thing, but it came at exactly the right moment,” Bussell recalls. “After days of rain, it lifted my spirits and made me realize that this pilgrimage is as much about the people you meet as it is the miles you walk.”.

Sources indicate that on Japan’s Shikoku 88 Temples Pilgrimage route, Lauren Roerick and her brother were leaving one of the temples when she spotted a sign offering matcha tea ceremonies for pilgrims. They initially walked away unsure whether they would be intruding but returned and decided to try it anyway.

“A Japanese man welcomed us inside where two women in kimonos were preparing and serving matcha under his instruction,” adds Roerick. “To make us feel welcome, he called a friend and had her on speakerphone, translating the whole ceremony from Japanese into English.” Lauren and her brother learned about the tradition, tried making tea themselves, and ate small Japanese sweets.

“It was proof that trail magic isn’t always a bottle of water or a helping hand,” says Roerick. “Sometimes a stranger opens his door, works around a language barrier, and shares a bit of culture with people passing through.”.

It has been revealed that on a windy hike to Matterhorn Base Camp, Libera Pagano, tour director with EF Adventures, noticed an older woman struggling. The altitude made her dizzy, her legs were shaking, and her friend had walked far ahead. “I offered to sit with the woman while she rested behind a large rock and we started chatting,” states Pagano.

Industry observers note that that’s when Pagano learned it was the woman’s 86th birthday, and the hike was a present she’d given herself. They stayed together, and when the woman felt ready, they walked slowly until they caught up with her companion. When the group met back at basecamp, the woman told Pagano that without her help, she would never have made it to the summit.

In a recent development, “I thought nothing of what I had done,” says Pagano. “But for that woman, it was the difference between giving up and fulfilling her birthday wish.”.

According to recent reports, I never learned the name of the man who bandaged my toes in the Hajar Mountains, and I probably never will. But I think about him whenever I struggle on a trail or see another hiker limping.

In a recent development, all these stories have one thing in common—human compassion. Sometimes that is stopping to help a stranger in need, sharing what little you have, or leaving a cache of supplies for a hiker you’ll probably never meet. These gestures don’t have to be grand or cost much, but they can make an enormous difference and are an easy thing to pay forward so everyone experiences a little magic outdoors.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Hand cracks are not the ideal terrain for the TX1, but they are just too fun to pass up. (Photo: Anthony Walsh).

There are three things that make an approach shoe “high value:” its price, versatility, and durability. At $159, La Sportiva’s all-fresh TX1 (replacing the cult-classic TX2) is decently affordable, and was versatile enough to take testers across a range of objectives, including fifth-class ridges in the Sierras and daily crag commutes, and be worn as a slip-on between limit boulder problems. I logged dozens of scrambling pitches in my TX1s and noted no signs of premature wear along the TPU-coated polyester upper or its Vibram MegaGrip outsole.

Industry observers note that the breathable upper and shallow dot lugs make the TX1 an excellent shoe for the fair-weather rock climber who dodges rainy forecasts and muddy approaches. Those little lugs provide just enough grip for your average walkoff, but really shine on technical, slabby approaches where surface contact is king. On the mile-long Eagle Lake Buttress Traverse (5.0), the TX1 smeared well across its opening slabs—but I wished for a taller rand while jamming hand-sized cracks.

Fit wise, all testers found the TX1 to be comfortable out of the box, thanks to a stock 4mm Ortholite Hybrid insole and a plush Air Mesh lining. (The TX1 fits a touch wider than the TX2, for those familiar.) One tester, who has a relatively narrow, low-volume foot, loved the fit of the TX1, saying its toebox felt roomy and allowed her toes “to spread and relax naturally.” My wider foot, meanwhile, had me eager to take the TX1 off after an hour-long approach. I wish this shoe came in a slightly wider last.

#102116. Tech Report: UTMB Moves to Wednesday in Major 2027 Schedule Shakeup

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1330 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Trailrunnermag ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: UTMB Moves to Wednesday in Major 2027 Schedule Shakeup

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1330 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the 2027 UTMB week-long festival events will take place on Sunday, August 22 to August 28.
  • Recent findings suggest that there are certain immutable facts in the world of trail running.
  • One of those things will change in 2027, as the world’s most famous trail running race series juggles its long-established order of events, Trail Runner learned from UTMB officials.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the 2027 UTMB week-long festival events will take place on Sunday, August 22 to August 28. The flagship Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB) will start on Wednesday, August 25, Trail Runner Chamonix correspondent Doug Mayer confirmed with UTMB officials. This article was written under embargo and has been updated with additional information.

Recent findings suggest that there are certain immutable facts in the world of trail running. Kilian and Courtney are the Greatest of All Time. A trailhead IPA will always be the best recovery drink. And UTMB week at the end of August in Chamonix, France, culminates with a 108-mile lap around Mont Blanc otherwise known as the eponymous UTMB.

One of those things will change in 2027, as the world’s most famous trail running race series juggles its long-established order of events, Trail Runner learned from UTMB officials.

For the past eight years, the alphabet stew of race acronyms comprising UTMB week started with the epic 300-kilometer PTL at the beginning of the week, followed by MCC (40K), TDS (148K), and YCC (a 5-15K youth event), before the three UTMB World Series Finals races: OCC (57K), CCC (108K) and finally UTMB (174K). A 15K event, ETC, was added in Courmayeur, Italy, in 2022.

There are three notable changes for next year’s event:.

According to recent reports, race start times are expected to stay largely the same for the UTMB World Series Final races. Start times for other races will be forthcoming shortly.

It has been revealed that two blazing hot meteors of the global sports world are colliding head on. The International Cycling Union (UCI) Cycling World Championships are taking place in France’s Haute Savoie region—which includes Chamonix. The dates? August 24 to September 5.

And one date looms particularly large: Sunday, August 29, when the UCI elite men’s road race is scheduled to take place in the towns of Sallanches and Domancy, just a handful of kilometers from Chamonix.

After the UCI announced the dates for the world championships, President of the French Cycling Federation Michel Callot suggested that UTMB shift its dates.

In a recent development, UTMB couldn’t move into September, as the Mont Blanc Tunnel that connects Chamonix with Courmayeur, Italy, is tentatively slated to be closed again for maintenance starting on Monday, August 30. The tunnel is critical to the infrastructure of the race series—in fact, it was the reopening of the tunnel in March, 2002, after a tragic fire that forced a nearly three-year closure, that allowed race organizers to host the first edition of UTMB a year later.

Earlier dates presented their own challenges, too. “We would have been right in the middle of the tourist season,” Isabelle Viseux-Poletti, director of UTMB Mont-Blanc, tells Trail Runner. “In terms of visitor numbers and the number of people using the trails, that simply wouldn’t have worked. Everyone around the table agreed on that point.”.

The discussions around the 2027 UTMB Mont-Blanc dates involved official representatives of the prefecture and of municipalities along the races’ courses, notably Chamonix, with its upcoming mayor, François-Xavier Laffin, and directors of the UCI Championships. In the end, they went with the most reasonable option: juggling the flow of the events to better accommodate the regional impacts, and shifting UTMB week a day earlier to avoid a literal collision of events on Sunday, August 29.

The 2027 schedule was developed in close coordination with the office of Chamonix Mayor François Xavier Laffin. Laffin, who himself raced UTMB in 2007, came into office this past spring promising to review UTMB’s relationship with the town, with an eye towards mitigating the growing impacts of the race on the local population and the valley’s fragile alpine ecosystem.

Those two sporting event meteors have been heading towards a collision for more than a year now.

It has been revealed that this will be the first time the UCI is holding a world championship that brings together all of its disciplines in the same place. That includes 20 events ranging from road cycling to mountain biking, para-cycling, and BMX. The overlap with UTMB in a region about the size of Rhode Island triggered a range of concerns about transportation, safety, and accommodations.

From the very beginning, the UCI worked jointly with UTMB. “We’ve been discussing this for quite a long time,” Viseux-Poletti claims. ”From the outset, we’ve been working collaboratively to find solutions.”.

According to recent reports, but coordinating two significant sporting events is about much more than just aligning the dates, and UTMB officials had to wait until the UCI could share details about its needs, too. “In particular, we needed to understand their requirements regarding road access and law enforcement,” Viseux-Poletti claims. Predictably, some of those decisions took months. And so, it was only in the last several months that coordinating decisions between the entities began in earnest.

Keith Byrne is one person who has watched UTMB race week play out for the last 11 years. An announcer for UTMB English broadcast, he’s taking the calendar shift in stride. “It’s pretty much going to be business as usual for us just with different days of the week,” he notes.

Recent findings suggest that overall, Byrne is hopeful about the changes: “Out of some disturbance and adversity, there’s an opportunity to move forward.” He does wonder if there will be fewer spectators out on the course during CCC and UTMB. “Wednesday and Thursday might not be the most productive days in the office,” he joked. “Because we’re going to make sure they have great live coverage to watch!”.

American Emily Schmitz placed third at UTMB this last year. A year-round Chamonix resident for the past four years, she’s not particularly concerned about lower numbers of spectators out on the course. “There were so many spectators this year. Even if there are fewer, there are still going to be a lot of people out there cheering for you,” she observed. “And, regardless, you’re really focused on your race when you’re out there.”.

According to recent reports, if there’s a race winner among these changes, Byrne thinks it’s going to be OCC. And that’s just fine with him. “OCC will have way more eyes on it, falling on a Saturday. That’s great news for OCC runners.” The race has had fierce competition in recent years, with this year’s race featuring a remarkable duel among the top two women, Lauren Gregory (U.S.) and Naomi Lang (U.K.), who finished three seconds apart. “It was the first time in UTMB week history that the women’s finish got more people watching than the men’s finish,” Byrne mentioned.

It has been revealed that for spectators, Byrne found the silver lining. “If you’re a trail running fan and a cycling fan, this year you’ll have two events for the price of one.”.

Could this schedule change-up, which further draws attention to the marquee events of the week, be a harbinger of things to come? UTMB officials are offering no clues.

It is clear, however, that juggling the schedule of UTMB’s many races opens a Pandora’s box of coordination headaches. There are three countries with whom to deal, plus regional authorities, nearly two dozen towns, and multiple public and private rescue services. Even for onlookers, it’s migraine-inducing.

UTMB officials declined to comment about whether this fresh schedule will remain the same in 2028. But they did say more changes are coming. Soon after the 2026 UTMB World Series Finals ended, UTMB officials and the Chamonix’s Mayor’s office began a series of meetings to address areas of concern raised by the mayor. Both parties have promised changes to address concerns. Viseux-Poletti expects the race series and the mayor’s office to jointly announce the news in about a month.

Industry observers note that doug Mayer is the author of The Race that Changed Running: The Inside Story of UTMB. He lives in Chamonix, France, and is the founder of the trail running tour company Run the Alps.

#102114. Gary Colliver Was a “Massive-Hearted” Climber Who Devoted Decades to Yosemite

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (484 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

Gary Colliver Was a “Massive-Hearted” Climber Who Devoted Decades to Yosemite

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (484 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gary Colliver on 'Lucky Streaks' (5.10+), a six-pitch trad climb on Fairview Dome in Yosemite, in 1980.
  • Gary Colliver passed away on August 30, 2026, in Denver, Colorado.
  • Throughout his life, Yosemite’s beauty was a current which drew him back, time and time again.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gary Colliver on 'Lucky Streaks' (5.10+), a six-pitch trad climb on Fairview Dome in Yosemite, in 1980. (Photo: Courtesy of Dave Sessions).

Gary Colliver passed away on August 30, 2026, in Denver, Colorado. He was 83. A longtime Yosemite Valley resident, he spent decades caring for the park as a ranger, medic, rescuer, and advocate.

Throughout his life, Yosemite’s beauty was a current which drew him back, time and time again. Colliver discovered climbing in college and soon moved to Camp 4. He met his future wife, Reva, in Tuolumne Meadows, married her in the Yosemite Valley Chapel in 1965, and built a decades-long career serving the park and its visitors.

In the early days of climbing in the Valley, Colliver was a quiet giant. With Richard McCracken and John Evans, he made the fourth ascent of the Nose (5.9 C2; 3,000ft) on El Capitan. He later returned to the route for the film El Capitan (1978), and in 1969, he climbed the Salathé Wall (5.9 C2; 3,500ft) with Chris Jones.

Later, his ambitions also took him beyond Yosemite. In 1964, he and Glen Denny made the first ascent of Jirishanca Norte (19,735ft) in Peru. In 1970, he joined Jones, Bob Cuthbert, and Gray Thompson for the first complete ascent of Mount Adamant’s north ridge in British Columbia. The following year, he participated in the International Himalayan Expedition to Mount Everest, where his team attempted a new route on Everest’s Southwest Face.

To Dave Sessions, Colliver’s second cousin, those accomplishments belonged to an exceptionally modest man. “He was one of the most modest people I ever met in my life. Incredibly soft-spoken,” Sessions said. “Never, never sought out attention or, you know, just very kind-hearted and modest and soft-spoken.”.

It has been revealed that colliver’s work in Yosemite included serving as a wilderness and climbing ranger, park medic, and volunteer firefighter. In 1983, he and two fellow rangers received a Department of the Interior Valor Award for rescuing a visitor from swift water.

His National Park Service colleague Mark Finscher worked alongside him on an early effort to develop a climbing management plan for the Valley, bringing together interest groups with opposing views on access, bolting, and responsible climbing.

Industry observers note that “There were some strong personalities in that group, and Gary did a good job of dealing with that,” Finscher said. Although that initial blueprint was never formally signed, Colliver continued working in park planning and compliance. Finscher remembered him as an ally in upholding wilderness protections. “He never took the easy way,” he said.

According to recent reports, as a teenager, Sessions had asked Colliver whether he had been scared climbing El Capitan. He answered simply, “No, it was just so beautiful.” But for Colliver, the joy of being in Yosemite extended beyond any particular massive wall. “If he was in Yosemite, he was happy,” Sessions remarked.

#102113. Make Uphills Easier With These Exercises for Explosive Strength

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1348 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Backpacker ↗ Open Full Page

Make Uphills Easier With These Exercises for Explosive Strength

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1348 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tackling steep slopes takes way more energy than walking or running at the same pace on flat ground: In fact, you burn roughly 44 percent more calories per hour walking up a 5 percent incline than on flat ground.
  • “On every uphill stride … the first thing that happens is a very, very sharp kind of eccentric stretching load on the leg as you step up, and then you need a much higher power spike to actually get the body moving,” states Alex Viada, head coach at Complete Human Performance, and author of The Ultimate Hybrid Athlete.
  • Explosive strength can be trained, though.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hills don’t just feel hard. Tackling steep slopes takes way more energy than walking or running at the same pace on flat ground: In fact, you burn roughly 44 percent more calories per hour walking up a 5 percent incline than on flat ground. If you’ve got that one hiking buddy who seems to power up the hills while you’re huffing and puffing, the reason isn’t just that they’re fit. It’s that they’ve built up power—specifically explosive strength, which is fitness jargon for their ability to rapidly muster the strength they’ve built. Explosive strength is the same stuff you use when you jump, bound, or push yourself up a steep step.

“On every uphill stride … the first thing that happens is a very, very sharp kind of eccentric stretching load on the leg as you step up, and then you need a much higher power spike to actually get the body moving,” states Alex Viada, head coach at Complete Human Performance, and author of The Ultimate Hybrid Athlete. “If you don’t have the ability to hit those little power spikes over and over and over again, that’s a much greater determinant of uphill performance.”.

Explosive strength can be trained, though. In a small 2011 study of women in their 60s and 70s published in the Journal of Aging and Physical Activity, one group was assigned to lift weights in a way that would build explosive strength. After 12 weeks, those women climbed stairs 17 percent faster than they did at the beginning of the study.

“Uphills are hard, and they’re hard for everyone,” says Mike Aidala, coach and owner of The Offense, a gym and mindset coaching business in Boulder, CO. He says that approaching your training with a goal of getting stronger, rather than faster, can help build uphill power.

Here’s a mental intent method from the study that can make every exercise build more explosive strength, and six specific exercises for building explosive, uphill strength from Viada, Aidala, and Rose Wetzel, a certified personal trainer and pro Spartan racer with multiple world championship podium finishes.

Explosive exercises are usually those where your body leaves the floor (like squat jumps or box jumps) or a weight leaves your hands (like medicine ball throws). But you can achieve the same benefit by performing the concentric phase—the “lift” phase—of any exercise with explosive intent. That’s how the elderly participants in the Journal of Aging and Physical Activity study built power. On each repetition of machine exercises, they did the eccentric—or “lowering”—portion of the lift at a controlled pace, and then they pushed the weight up in an explosive manner.

Lifting weights in this way gives a two-way boost to your uphill performance. Not only does it build power in the “push” portion of each lift, but lowering weights slowly and under control increases the strength of your tendons.

“When we train our tendons, we’re able to be more explosive,” states Wetzel. Stronger tendons, she says, “help with the body’s ability to spring off the ground, to explode off with all that strength.”.

According to recent reports, you can use this method with almost every strength exercise you do, says Viada. His recommendation: Start with a few sets of each exercise with explosive intent, and then move into your “regular” sets of the move. During the explosive sets, he says, don’t use as much weight as you will in the later, “normal” sets.

According to recent reports, for a starting weight, Viada suggests subtracting 25 percent from the maximum weight with which you could normally perform 10 reps. For example, if you regularly do 10 leg presses with 200 pounds, perform your explosive reps with 150 pounds.

In addition to using a lower weight, Viada also recommends doing fewer repetitions in each set. While you could probably do this weight for 15 or more repetitions, start with a handful, and make sure each one is done with maximum explosive intention.

“The only thing that matters is that they’re explosive and they’re fast,” he notes. “So when you go to the bottom of the movement, think about suddenly trying to push the bar or sled up through a wall. Pretend you’re trying to smash [the weight] up through the ceiling.”.

Do a few sets in this way for each move, then move to your normal, longer sets with your regular weights.

Our experts recommend these six moves to become more explosive and more stable as you trek or run uphill—they’re moves the coaches have used to train clients to climb 14ers, and that Wetzel herself has used to vault her way to multiple obstacle course race podiums.

According to recent reports, the first four exercises can be done anywhere, including as part of a run or hike warmup. For the last two, you’ll need some gym equipment.

These jumps let you practice exploding, but also train your knee not to wobble on each step. Not only will a stable knee help prevent injuries when you’re thrown off-kilter on the trail, but will prevent you from losing energy that could be used to propel you forward.

In a recent development, do one set of 10 jumps per leg three to four times per week. Over time, try to minimize wobbling, and then increase the distance of your jumps.

It has been revealed that similar to the previous exercise, these jumps incorporate side-to-side movement. Don’t rush through them, Aidala says. Land, get stable, take a beat, then repeat.

Do 10 jumps in each direction on each leg. Perform these three to four times per week.

These aren’t the plodding high knees you’re used to, Wetzel notes.

“When I do these drills, it’s for a very short amount of time, and I do them for power,” she notes. “I’m not doing high knees like someone might do for 30 seconds to get their heart rate up … it’s like six to eight seconds of hot potato, hot potato, hot potato, and then catch my breath for 30 seconds.”.

You can do these before every run or hike, or as a warmup before any workout.

It has been revealed that this move, Wetzel states, helps you to feel like you can spring off with each step up a hill. Unlike a longer jumping lunge, she does these mini lunges as promptly as possible, keeping the movement “fierce, short, and explosive.” Instead of dropping into a full lunge, bend your knees only slightly, with your feet moving front to back almost like you’re cross-country skiing while jumping slightly.

Do a few sets of 16 reps before every run, hike, or gym workout.

“Uphill running starts from the hips,” Viada claims. “And with Bulgarian split squat hops, when you start that explosiveness from the bottom, you’ll explosively engage those hips like nothing else.”.

Recent findings suggest that this takes one of the most dreaded moves in the gym and adds an explosive element, with the front foot leaving the ground on each repetition. Your foot doesn’t need to come way off the ground, though, Viada says. An inch or so is great. Since it’s already a tough move, he recommends using a light weight, or no weight at all.

Perform three to four sets of four to five hops per leg, focusing on explosiveness in each rep. Do these two to three times per week.

When lifting with explosive intent, coaches often recommend that you “explode out of the hole,” or the bottom of the move. With the Anderson squat, you start in the hole using a squat rack, pressing the bar off pins so you can focus even more on the powerful concentric portion of the lift.

According to recent reports, don’t set the stops on the rack too low, Viada notes. Aim so that when you get under the bar, your knees are bent 90 degrees, mimicking the angles you’ll need to hike uphill with power.

Perform three to four sets of four to five squats, focusing on explosiveness in each rep. Do these one to two times per week.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A person remains at large after poisoning at least 28 mature pines in three separate incidents over four years (Photo: Rachid Dahnoun/Getty Images).
  • Authorities in Nevada are looking for a person who has been poisoning trees on the shores of Lake Tahoe.
  • Now, the Washoe County Sheriff’s Office (WCSO) and other local organizations are offering a $147,000 bounty to catch the culprit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A person remains at large after poisoning at least 28 mature pines in three separate incidents over four years (Photo: Rachid Dahnoun/Getty Images).

Authorities in Nevada are looking for a person who has been poisoning trees on the shores of Lake Tahoe. Since 2022, at least 28 pines have been harmed or destroyed, totaling $300,000 in damages, authorities noted in a release.

Now, the Washoe County Sheriff’s Office (WCSO) and other local organizations are offering a $147,000 bounty to catch the culprit.

“We take these crimes very seriously and will utilize every available resource to identify and apprehend the person or persons responsible,” Sheriff Darin Balaam said in a statement. “The destruction of mature trees in the Tahoe Basin and the environmental damage caused by these deliberate acts are unacceptable.

In an email to Outside, WCSO spokesperson Rachel Piccinini mentioned the agency is continuing to investigate the crimes, which could result in felony charges.

“Our office has received numerous tips from the community, and we continue to encourage anyone with information that may assist in this investigation to contact our Detective Division,” Piccinini remarked.

Outside requested further information about whether the incidents pose a threat to people or pets recreating in the area. We will patch this article if we receive a response.

Industry observers note that the tree poisonings have occurred at Burnt Cedar Beach, a lakefront recreation complex in Incline Village, Nevada, along Lake Tahoe’s north shore. It’s also about a ten-minute drive from the community-owned Diamond Peak Ski Resort. Roughly 9,000 people live in Incline Village, but the area is a tourism hotspot in both winter and summer.

In a recent development, A person remains at large after poisoning at least 28 mature pines in three separate incidents over four years. Authorities say they believe the same person damaged all the trees. The suspect harmed the first six in 2022 and another six in 2024.

Sources indicate that most recently, on July 24, 2026, deputies responded to Burnt Cedar Beach after reports of a strong odor near the base of a large pine tree. The smell matched previous tree poisonings at the property. On August 2, deputies found another tree with a substance around the base; at the time, a trail camera captured a bright light near the area at 2 A.M.

At least 16 trees were damaged in 2026 as a result.

In some instances, someone poured the toxin directly over the tree’s base. In others, someone drilled holes near the roots and poured the substance in them.

Authorities say they have yet to identify the contaminant or determine why someone targeted the trees. They have collected soil samples and submitted them for testing. They hope to identify the substance used and determine whether the perpetrator used the same one in each incident.

WCSO asks anyone with information to call (775) 328-3001 and reference case number 26-4225.

#102111. How I Sent ‘The Prophet’ and ‘Free Rider’ on El Cap in 18.5 Hours

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2356 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

How I Sent ‘The Prophet’ and ‘Free Rider’ on El Cap in 18.5 Hours

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2356 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Left to right: Alex Honnold, Connor Herson, and Tommy Caldwell take a celebratory selfie at the top of 'The Prophet' on El Cap.
  • My alarm goes off, but I’m already wide awake; I never sleep well before an early start.
  • It has been revealed that established by Leo Houlding and Jason Pickles over a 10-year saga, The Prophet (5.13d/5.14a R; 1,800ft) has developed a reputation as one of El Cap’s scariest and most dangerous free routes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Left to right: Alex Honnold, Connor Herson, and Tommy Caldwell take a celebratory selfie at the top of 'The Prophet' on El Cap. (Photo: Courtesy of Alex Honnold).

My alarm goes off, but I’m already wide awake; I never sleep well before an early start. I’ve got half an hour to pull myself together before Alex gets here and we start hiking. As I choke down breakfast, I can’t help but wonder if I’m in over my head. Despite Alex and Tommy’s best reassurances, The Prophet scares me.

It has been revealed that established by Leo Houlding and Jason Pickles over a 10-year saga, The Prophet (5.13d/5.14a R; 1,800ft) has developed a reputation as one of El Cap’s scariest and most dangerous free routes. Indeed, it’s broken a few bones over the years, and to this day, Leo and Jason’s ground up attempt remains one of the boldest and most heroic chapters in El Cap’s history. Growing up, I always told myself that I’d never climb The Prophet. Maybe I’d rap into the A1 Beauty (the splitter crux pitch, rated 5.13d, though Leo, Sonnie Trotter, and Alex have all talked of upgrading it to 5.14a1) to try it, but the rest of the route was too dangerous for me—I don’t do dangerous stuff.

I wasn’t particularly surprised when Alex Honnold and Tommy Caldwell started trying The Prophet this season, but I watched their progress as a friend and spectator, not a potential suitor for the route. My own project on Leaning Tower was taking all my time this season.

Industry observers note that on November 11, while eating breakfast and preparing for a day on my project, I ran into Alex and congratulated him on his send. He was hiking up that afternoon to belay Tommy, who was four days into his send push and trying the A1 Beauty. Alex offered to jumar and belay me on a ground-up push the next day, promising that the route was safer with his beta. I joked that I’d take him up if I couldn’t find a partner the next day for my project.

I had a very promising session on my project, but that afternoon, I was still partnerless for the following day, so I called up Alex to ask if his offer was still valid. In between Tommy’s redpoint goes on the A1, Alex called me back to tell me what gear I’d need. We planned to start climbing around 4:00 a.m. the following morning.

Sources indicate that packing up that evening, I felt wholly unprepared. I’d been sport climbing all summer and hadn’t done more than about six pitches in a day since spring. The only valley granite I’d touched this season was my overhanging, physical project on Leaning Tower, which was almost certainly a different style from the slabby, polished, and technical El Cap granite ahead of me. I’d need to re-adapt efficiently and rapidly, working with a lower stamina threshold than I was used to.

Hiking up the following morning on November 12, Alex started breaking down the route for me. He told me how he and Tommy had cleaned all the pitches, how they ticked and recorded every gear placement. As I started leading the first few pitches, I realized just how helpful this was going to be: I took only the exact rack I’d need for each pitch, and I didn’t have to stress at all about beta or gear. I took Alex at his word about the relative safety of each section (a risky decision, I know…) and tried to turn my brain off to the fullest extent possible.

According to recent reports, I settled into a sort of flow state; with the darkness obscuring any large runouts and Alex reassuring me of each gear placement ahead of me, I climbed calmly and intentionally over the lower pitches of the route. I couldn’t fathom Leo and Jason coming up here to find loose rock, grass-filled cracks, and no obvious route. It was certainly a far cry from my own experience on the freshly cleaned and ticked route. I remained relatively calm even over pitches four through six, the first few 5.13 pitches.

In a recent development, as we climbed higher and dawn broke, we saw Tommy above us; he’d not quite sent the night before, but he’d decided to spend another night on the wall and watch my attempt in the morning. With Tommy’s encouragement, I climbed the Guillotine Pitch (pitch eight, 5.13b), then the Devil’s Reacharound (pitch nine, 5.13a). Before long, I joined him at his portaledge at the base of the A1 Beauty just as the morning sun hit. What a perfect splitter it looked like, too—everything I could ever want in a pitch, at the very top of El Cap.

Sources indicate that the A1 Beauty sees direct sun from first light until sunset, and it bakes. It was already quite warm, and I figured it would only get warmer as the day progressed. Without much waiting, I racked up and started what I thought would be a beta sussing mission. A few moves in, I realized this attempt could be more than just that; with Tommy hanging on a static rope above me, telling me exactly what to do, I found myself through the low crux (~V8), then through the next section. As I got higher and higher, I tried to push down the feeling that I might just pull it off on this first attempt and instead focus on each move, each foothold, each gear placement. It felt perfect. Before I knew it, I was at the next anchor, absolutely thrilled.

As excited as I was about the A1, suddenly the route became much more intense. I was only two pitches below the summit. Two pitches from flashing the entire route in a day. Two pitches from an El Cap flash. The following pitch was easy enough, but the exit pitch intimidated me: a 13b boulder problem right off the belay, involving an insecure standup on poor footholds.

Recent findings suggest that I climbed up to the boulder and back down to the belay a few times, feeling increasingly nervous. Eventually, I went for it: I placed the foot, took a deep breath, and stood. The foot held, and I excitedly reached for the next hold, which guards easier climbing to the top. I briefly lost focus, allowing a small voice to say, I’m doing it! It’s happening! The next thing I knew, my foot had slipped and I was hanging on the rope. My flash go was botched.

Recent findings suggest that at that moment, I lost all perspective of the incredible morning of climbing I’d had; I was devastated. Half an hour later, topping out The Prophet after successfully climbing the pitch, I felt the most hollow I’ve felt upon topping out El Cap. Alex and Tommy joined me on top. As they packed their haulbag and portaledge, I couldn’t help but regret my missed opportunity.

Within a few minutes, however, I regained some perspective. It had been an incredibly memorable morning of climbing, and I’d still freed The Prophet ground-up in about seven hours. Only that morning, doing this would have been a dream come true, and I smiled a bit. I checked the time: 11:30 a.m. “Wow! I can drive home and meet my family in time for dinner!” I laughed and joked to Tommy and Alex.

According to recent reports, alex turned and gave me a wry smile. “You know, you could do a Double right now. Compared to The Prophet, Free Rider will probably feel pretty easy.”.

Tommy pitched in: “Yeah, I’d jug Free Rider this afternoon if you want!”.

According to recent reports, I stopped sorting my gear and stared. Great. I’m getting peer pressured by my heroes.

Recent findings suggest that among the rules I live by is that if Alex or Tommy offers something, I don’t turn them down. Especially a support mission on El Cap. As tired and emotionally drained as I was, I reminded myself just how much I’ve wanted to do the El Cap Double my entire life. I remembered topping out the free Nose-in-a-day last year, when I called every climber in the Valley to see if I could find a partner for a Double that day, to no avail. This sort of opportunity doesn’t come around particularly often. Even as I waffled about whether to go for it, the decision had been made. In a few hours’ time, I knew I’d be starting up Freeblast.

Recent findings suggest that the climbing on Free Rider is significantly easier than on The Prophet, and I’d done most of the pitches when I freed the Salathé in 2022. I knew there would be little suspense about whether I’d be physically capable of sending it. However, I also knew I wasn’t in major walling shape, and besides, this would be far and away the most pitches I’ve climbed in a day. I remember watching the video of Tommy freeing the El Cap double back in 2005, where he nearly lost it at the Enduro Corner. I wondered if I was in for a similar bout.

Sources indicate that the first few pitches on Free Rider went remarkably smoothly. Alex, still keen on supporting me, had jugged our day pack up the Heart Lines, which made Freeblast an absolute breeze. My feet were hurting, but I could feel the ibuprofen I’d pounded at the base starting to kick in. I settled into a flow, and pitch after pitch flew past. I felt remarkably fresh. With Tommy’s encouragement and psych, I was optimistic.

Around the Monster Offwidth (pitch 20 of 30 on Free Rider), darkness fell. I could feel the fatigue building; our pace slowed, but we kept moving. I was making a conscious effort to stay positive and cheerful, to act like I had endless energy in the hopes that I could fake that energy into existence.

Sources indicate that when we reached the crux, I opted for the Teflon Corner instead of the Boulder Problem. I’d never tried the Boulder before, and I didn’t want my first attempt to be 40-odd pitches into the day. The Teflon went down on my first try, and before long, we were at the Enduro Corner. Tommy suggested that I skip the hanging belay at the end of the Enduro Corner and link it into the Round Table Traverse. I rolled my eyes, thinking that I’d be lucky to scrape my way up the Corner on its own, but to my surprise, I felt remarkably fresh. I reached the hanging belay and kept climbing, thankful to have cleared that last hurdle.

According to recent reports, at 10:45 p.m., a little more than eight hours after starting Free Rider and 18.5 hours after starting up The Prophet, Tommy and I topped out to strong, cold winds. We didn’t stick around long to celebrate; already shivering, we promptly packed and started running to stay warm on the hike down. As we got lower and warmed up, however, we slowed down and soaked in the unforgettable day we’d just had: around 45 pitches of climbing for a free El Cap Double!

Alex and Tommy both have families. They both had good reason to rush home ahead of the incoming storm instead of supporting some kid who wanted to try their project. And to be honest, I wouldn’t have blamed them if they didn’t want me to mooch off their hard work prepping The Prophet. There’s absolutely no way I could have done The Prophet ground up and in a day without the labor Tommy and Alex spent to find the route, clean loose rock, and find all the gear beta. After four days on the wall and away from his family, I would have completely understood if Tommy wanted to get home to his kids rather than go up El Cap a second time that day—especially with Tioga Pass imminently closing, which meant supporting me on Free Rider would lengthen his drive home by about an hour.

Nevertheless, their support that day exemplifies the exact values I love to see in climbing. This is the sport I want climbing to be: one where the giants, the biggest legends of the game, are generous enough to go out of their way to help younger up-and-comers. A sport where the younger generation is not seen as a fresh wave of competition but is instead embraced and mentored.

Not flashing The Prophet is certainly going to sting for a while. I still replay that moment on the exit pitch daily, and I’m sure I’ll always feel some regret about it. Still, the more I reflect on that day, the more Alex and Tommy’s support stands out to me. Every outing leaves us with a lesson or slightly shifted worldview. In 10 or 20 years, I’m confident that looking back on the El Cap Double will remind me that there is a world larger than my own climbing; that, like Tommy and Alex, I can make another climber’s entire season by simply offering them a few hours of my time and a bit of encouragement. As I grow and find my place in the climbing world, I can only hope to be as influential a mentor to future generations.

1It’s hard to guess after only one attempt, but I wouldn’t argue with 5.14a for that pitch! I also could see upper-end 5.13d, though.

#102110. Industry News: A Basset Hound Showed Up Alone at a Hiking Area—and Kicked Off a Lifesaving Rescue

Industry News: A Basset Hound Showed Up Alone at a Hiking Area—and Kicked Off a Lifesaving Rescue

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (742 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • (Photo: NYS Department of Environmental Conservation).
  • Rescuers saved a 69-year-old hiker in Newly introduced York’s Adirondack Mountains on November 13 thanks to a swift search effort—and a Basset Hound named Becky.
  • The day prior, Becky showed up at the base of Whiteface Mountain without her owner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: NYS Department of Environmental Conservation).

Rescuers saved a 69-year-old hiker in Newly introduced York’s Adirondack Mountains on November 13 thanks to a swift search effort—and a Basset Hound named Becky.

The day prior, Becky showed up at the base of Whiteface Mountain without her owner. Staff immediately recognized the dog. They knew her owner suffered from dementia, and the fact that he wasn’t with Becky concerned them. They contacted 911 to report the owner missing.

New York State police officers responded and located the hiker’s car at a nearby trailhead. According to Syracuse.com, several officers searched the trails in the immediate area and a branch of the Ausable River. However, they found nothing. Four forest rangers joined the effort, deploying a drone and bloodhound to the area.

But time wasn’t on their side. Night fell without any sign of the lost hiker, and organizers called off the search with plans to resume it in the morning. According to the Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC), temperatures on the night of Thursday, November 12, dropped to between 25 and 30 degrees around Whiteface Mountain.

In a recent development, when the sun rose, the search continued with even more resources and rescuers. Fourteen rangers and state police aviation began combing Whiteface Mountain. Using cell phone data, police pinpointed the hiker’s phone; however, when searchers located it, they discovered the phone abandoned along with the hiker’s backpack.

Finally, around 10 a.m., the searchers got lucky. A hunter in the area heard someone scream in the woods. A ranger responded to sweep the area and located the missing hiker in an open meadow.

Sources indicate that “This gentleman didn’t have shoes on when we found him in the morning, or mittens or gloves,” Charlie Foutch, a ranger who had been part of the search, told Syracuse.com. “Sometimes when you keep moving in that situation, you generate enough heat to do OK, and he was still alive.”.

Foutch noted that’s largely also thanks to Becky.

“It definitely would have been much harder to find him [without her]. He may not have survived the rest of the day, and probably not another night,” Foutch said. “The dog definitely contributed to him being saved so quickly.”.

The hiker’s hands and feet were severely frostbitten and required immediate medical attention. A helicopter airlifted him to a nearby hospital.

People with Alzheimer’s or other types of dementia are common subjects of wilderness searches. In an interview with the Fisher Center for Alzheimer’s Research Foundation, Kimberly Kelly, an international rescue specialist, mentioned there are around 125,000 SAR operations involving missing Alzheimer’s subjects every year—and that number is on the rise.

“In most categories, SAR missions are going down, or declining, for a variety of reasons,” Kelly says. “However, SAR missions for the missing at-risk, wandering Alzheimer’s patients are increasing dramatically, and that is expected to continue to increase exponentially over the coming years.”.

Wes Cooper is a volunteer field leader with Seattle Mountain Rescue (SMR). He told Backpacker that roughly a third of SMR’s search operations involve individuals with dementia or Alzheimers. Most occur in urban settings, but he states SMR has responded to this type of rescue in the wilderness as well.

“Say it’s the middle of the night and we need to try to find somebody quickly, or if it’s turning into a multi-day mission with a larger SAR planning strategy, we will not only deploy ground teams to canvas neighborhoods, the backcountry trails, or even off-trail, but we’ll throw technology at the search, too.”.

He says e-bikes not only expand their reach, but also increase response times and deployment speed. Drones help them scan larger areas from above. And they even use algorithms that predict how far someone might have wandered, based on how long they’ve been missing.

Urgency is particularly notable in these cases, Cooper says. Research shows that subjects with Alzheimer’s whom rescuers are unable to find within 24 hours have a 46 percent mortality rate. In areas like the Adirondacks, when terrain and weather are factored in, that number can be much higher.

Recent findings suggest that that’s why Cooper indicates, “Don’t hesitate to call 911 and get the agencies going,” as Whiteface Mountain staff did in the case of Becky’s owner. It’s better to get help fast, even if you find the lost person close to home, rather than trying to look for them yourself and letting valuable time slip away.

#102109. The Forest Service Just Released Bigfoot Records Dating Back to the 1940s. Here’s What They Say.

The Forest Service Just Released Bigfoot Records Dating Back to the 1940s. Here’s What They Say.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (894 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that wilderness explorer C.
  • According to recent reports, in the 1940s, a man named Leo Kinney described in an informal written account a disturbing encounter along Petty Creek, a tributary of the Clark Fork River west of Missoula, Montana.
  • “On arriving where the elk was supposed to be lying, we found the entrails only, and in the snow coming to and leading away from the area was a large set of tracks,” Kinney wrote in his 1980 retelling.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that wilderness explorer C. Thomas Biscardi, who spent nearly a decade searching for Bigfoot, claimed he photographed the elusive creature during an expedition in Northern California (Photo: Bettmann/Getty Images).

According to recent reports, in the 1940s, a man named Leo Kinney described in an informal written account a disturbing encounter along Petty Creek, a tributary of the Clark Fork River west of Missoula, Montana. At the time, he and three other hunters went into the woods to pack out a six-point bull elk they had shot down.

“On arriving where the elk was supposed to be lying, we found the entrails only, and in the snow coming to and leading away from the area was a large set of tracks,” Kinney wrote in his 1980 retelling.

At first, the men guessed a large bear had eaten the elk—but the tracks appeared in sets of two, and bears don’t tend to walk on their hind legs.

“Whatever it was had picked up the elk whole and clear off the ground,” Kinney continued.

The men followed the tracks for about a half-mile and, according to Kinney’s account, came across a felled log measuring three feet in diameter. They could see where the elk’s horns had been dragged across the snow and over the timber.

Recent findings suggest that “At this point we held a conference and decided that we were not particularly anxious to catch up to whatever it was,” Kinney wrote. “Though we didn’t confess it at this time, in later conversations we found out that we all had a very uneasy feeling and could feel chills running up and down our backs.”.

Recent findings suggest that the following year, another person, W.W. Schmitz, was hunting in a nearby area called Bills Creek when he found the same type of tracks, smelled a similarly strong odor, and also heard grunting noises.

In a recent development, kinney’s story is one of three historical files the U.S. Forest Service (USFS) released on October 15, describing Bigfoot encounters in Washington, Oregon, and Montana. In a world rife with sasquatch hunters and Bigfoot believers, the newly unveiled reports are shedding light on a long-held conspiracy theory. The public can access the files through the USFS website.

About 70 miles away in Plains, Montana, locals described an equally bizarre Bigfoot encounter in a January 15, 2003, article published by the Clark Fork Valley Press. According to the story, around January 3, hundreds of large, human-like footprints appeared in fresh snow outside Jim Rohweder’s sawmill shop. His neighbor, Bob Mesing, reportedly measured the prints at 16.5 inches long and 8.5 inches wide, with visible toes, an arch, and a stride that spanned about five feet.

Mesing and Dean Peterson, a former Kalispell policeman, followed the tracks about 100 yards into the woods, where the trail eventually faded.

“I don’t know if I believe in the Bigfoot theory, but the tracks were right there,” Mesing reportedly said. “What else could it be?”.

According to the Clark Fork Valley Press, the men did not contact authorities but had planned to give a sample to wildlife officials.

Mesing said he believed the visitor walked up to the shop and turned back, startled by a motion-sensor light. Peterson reportedly added that his dog barked around 3:40 A.M. that day, but he saw nothing.

Rohweder’s wife, Gladys, claimed to have seen a hairy, two-legged creature when the couple first moved to the area.

A June 16, 1982, account published by the U.S. Department of Agriculture took place in Umatilla National Forest, which hugs the southern border of Washington State and northern Oregon. In it, wildlife biologist Rodney Johnson reports that the agency asked him to investigate three sets of Bigfoot tracks and record the details of his trips.

The tracks were recorded in three locations of the Mill Creek Watershed, a 36.5-mile tributary of the Walla Walla River about 262 miles from Portland.

Sources indicate that site A contained six identifiable tracks going down a muddy trail for about 25 feet. Similar tracks were also seen at a second location near a bog, Site B, this time 18 prints spanning about 40 feet.

Johnson took photos and plaster casts of both sites, but skipped the third, citing terrain challenges.

But was it actually Bigfoot? Likely not.

“It is my opinion that the tracks observed at Site ‘A’ and Site ‘B’ along Low Creek were made by something other than a 300-pound-plus two-footed being,” Johnson wrote.

It has been revealed that when a two-legged being walks, its stride changes with gradient—shorter uphill and longer downhill. According to Johnson, the distance between the tracks remained a consistent four feet and did not change with the slope. The tracks also had a clear beginning and end, rather than following an existing trail. Furthermore, Johnson added that the imprints did not resemble an authentic print—for example, a human footprint reveals a distinct big toe pad and typically exhibits heel slippage on a steep gradient.

What’s more, at certain points, it appeared that pine needles had been intentionally brushed aside before the track was made.

It has been revealed that “It was obvious that the litter had been displaced sideways from the track area in an unnatural manner,” Johnson wrote. “If the tracks were faked, someone went to a great deal of trouble and detail.”.
