  • She loves that through Moms.com, she can put her chronic overthinking of every parenting decision to good use by saving readers time and hopefully a headache or two.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Katie Leigh Matthews is a contributing writer for Moms.com. As the mom of a sweet and sensitive 9-year-old boy and a wild and free 5-year-old girl, she brings her ever-evolving experience of parenting to everything she writes.

She’s been writing forever, and professionally for three years. With a degree in communications and a fascination for all things mental health, she seeks to uncover and share what genuinely helps us be more of who we are capable of being, especially with our kids. Towards that end, she writes often on introversion and the trait of high sensitivity to highlight their strengths and promote more self-compassion among all who share them. She regularly collaborates with experts in these fields to create content that informs, encourages, and empowers.

She loves that through Moms.com, she can put her chronic overthinking of every parenting decision to good use by saving readers time and hopefully a headache or two.

Katie lives in Birmingham, Alabama, with her husband and two kids. On any given day she’s probably either rewatching her favorite shows for the 100th time or dipping her toes in any creek she can find.

You’ve booked your tickets. You’ve planned your itinerary. You’ve figured out the My Disney Experience App (you think.) You’re as ready as you can be for your family’s first trip to Disney World. Then it dawns on you: What do you need to pack? Shopping for essentials for your first family trip to Disney World is an art – it’s about knowing your family and what you all need to thrive on one of the most exciting, most magical, and yes, sometimes stressful family vacations.

A little online searching will quickly convince you you'll need to buy extra luggage just to pack park essentials, but don’t stress. As an easily-overwhelmed mom who recently braved Disney World for the first time, I've got some hard-won advice to help guide your vacation prep and inform your packing list. Plus, I've scoured the internet for top picks of the most-used sanity-saving products to make the happiest place on earth live up to its name for you and your family.

For many parents, taking the kids to Disney World at least once during their childhood is a bucket list goal. When that dream is finally realized, there is a mix of idyllic anticipation and anxious uncertainty. It’s not surprising that many parents find planning for a trip to Disney World to be a stressful experience.

It has been revealed that when it comes to Disney World, there are two types of parents: those who have fond memories of their own childhood Disney vacation, and those who hope to give their own kids the trip they didn’t get to experience growing up. Whichever type you are, the goal is the same: To give your kids a core-memory-making family vacation they’ll cherish forever. Of course, a love of Disney also evokes childhood nostalgia that is so fun to share with your own children. The legacy of classic and modern Disney characters, movies, and parks is a special thing to pass on to the next generation and something that carries a lot of weight for many.

Sources indicate that along with all the hopes and expectations wrapped up in a family trip to Disney World, the cost of the vacation only adds to the pressure to make it the best trip ever. For budget travelers, the average weeklong Disney World vacation for a family of four can cost $6,000 or more, according to NerdWallet, so ensuring you get your money’s worth is a huge factor. Not only that, but with so much to see, do, and experience in the parks, a vacation to Disney World is a complex trip to strategy. Some families even turn to Disney vacation planners and travel agents to help with the sheer volume of logistical planning involved.

According to recent reports, as tempting as it may be, you don’t need to add-to-cart every single item you see on ‘Must Have Disney Essentials’ lists. Before you start shopping, it pays to think through what will help your family enjoy your trip the most. The best travel products for families will vary, so evaluate these factors before you start shopping:.

According to recent reports, of course, start with the makeup of your family. How old will your kids be on the trip, and what needs and preferences correspond with their ages? Strollers are a significant decision for many, and there are lots of pros and cons to consider: Will it help or hurt to have a stroller for airports? Is it worth it to lug a stroller to the parks? Would renting Disney World strollers be a better option? The answer will be different for every family, so don’t listen to advice that insists on a right answer. Our youngest was six on our trip and I seriously considered taking or renting a stroller. She ended up walking the parks like a champ and I was glad we didn’t have to deal with a stroller! Had she been a year younger, though, I am sure a stroller would have been our saving grace.

Industry observers note that what are your kids most looking forward to in the parks? How will they handle long lines? Will you need to anticipate an afternoon nap each day? Should you stock up on a few fun toys ahead of time so your kiddos aren’t pining for the theme park loot, or do you just need to upgrade your child’s luggage? A Disney World vacation will look very different depending on the ages of your kids, so narrow your list of essentials based on them.

It has been revealed that A surefire way to preemptively ruin your first trip to Disney World is to forget your own needs in the process. For parents, Disney World is fun, sure, but there’s also a lot of planning, incessant crowds, unrelenting heat, not to mention the never-ending soundboard of the kids' needs and wants. Take a moment and think about what essentials you need to make the most of the trip, and perhaps even a few indulgent spa day gifts to help melt stress away at the end of a non-stop Disney World day.

A travel-size umbrella that offers heavy-duty weather protection.

Weather is a massive factor in whether Disney World lives up to being “the happiest place on earth.” You likely know to expect warmer temperatures year-round, and extreme heat in the summer. But surprise rain showers are also a common occurrence in Orlando. Luckily, the Repel Compact Umbrella can help on both fronts. Not only will you be happy you have it if you get caught in a shower, but it will also filter UV rays when the sun is beating down. In fact, Repel even offers a UPF 50+ UV protection version of the umbrella to block out 99% of UV rays.

The umbrella's double-vented canopy is designed to withstand winds up to 85 MPH, so you won’t have to worry about it inverting. It is a heavy-duty umbrella packed into a compact travel size, opens and collapses with a push of a button, and is definitely worth tossing in your park bag. Reviewers say it performs as advertised – one even said the umbrella “loves wind” – with just a few saying the only issue they’ve had is closing it. (And yes, Disney World does allow umbrellas!).

This microfiber towel will save the day in all sorts of ways when you’re out and about, and packs into its own travel bag.

According to recent reports, when you’re at the parks from sun up to sun down, unexpected needs are bound to arise, and the Rainleaf Microfiber Towel will be a lifesaver for many of them. Kid drop Dole Whip down their shirt? Want to dry off a wet seat? Need to add more sun shade to the stroller? Chances are you’ll be reaching for this towel all day long. Not only is it compact and made for travel, but it also absorbs five times its own weight and dries incredibly fast. If it’s super hot, drench the towel in cold water to help you cool off, then drape it over your backpack or stroller as you walk around to let it air dry.

Running from $9 to $20 a piece, depending on the size, it’s worth giving each family member their own, or grabbing a few to designate for certain purposes – one for clean up, one for shade and sweat, and one as a picnic blanket for parades or just a quick rest.

This compact travel charger keeps your devices topped up all day long.

It has been revealed that between taking a million pictures and using the Disney app to do everything from making meal orders and reservations to finding the next ride (or nearest restroom!), you’ll be using your phone a lot in the parks. The Anker Portable Charger ensures your devices stay charged up all day long. It has a universal USB-C cable and delivers 10,000mAh (milliamp hours), delivering the equivalent of two full smartphone charges. At 30W charging speed, you can expect it to fully charge a phone in about an hour – which is how long you’ll be lining for some rides anyway.

The charger is just a tad bigger than a credit card, and weighs about as much as a phone. It can charge three devices at once (you just need extra charging cables) and the cable connector stores in the battery pack for safekeeping between uses. Coming in under $30, it’s well worth the peace of mind so you don’t miss a single picture-perfect moment, even as the last firework illuminates the night sky.

One tip I got from a Disney World cast member is to take screenshots of the QR codes, order confirmations, lightning lane arrival windows, and anything else you may need for reference from the My Disney Experience App so you aren’t constantly having to access the app, which can drain your phone battery.

Take a rest whenever you need to with this super practical compact folding stool.

The Boreeman Folding Stool is as close as it gets to realizing the idea of pants that turn into a chair, but arguably way more practical. If your back just isn’t what it used to be, or you’ve got a kiddo who you know will complain about standing in line, this folding stool will single-handedly save your Disney World trip. The collapsible seat locks into place at various heights up to 17.72 inches. It packs down into a disc that is 9.84 inches by 2.36 inches with a carrying strap for added convenience. Use it in ride lines, waiting for parades or indicates, or just whenever you need to take a load off. It also comes in handy to help little ones with bathroom needs.

In a recent development, the stool is highly rated with 4.4 stars from over 8,000 reviewers, but some say it’s not super comfortable, while others warn theirs broke while sitting on it. Still, other reviewers say they still use theirs often over a year later. It comes in tons of fun colors and can slide into bags, backpacks, or stroller compartments. It’s also light enough at 2.5 pounds for many kids to carry it through a ride line themselves.

Make any moment magical with these Disney-themed bubble wands.

The struggle to not buy every cute thing you see in Disney World is real, and the Little Kids Disney Light and Sound Musical Bubble Wand is here to help. Light-up bubble wands are all the rage in the parks, and they come with a hefty price tag. If you’re looking to save money where you can on your trip, surprise your little one with a pre-bought bubble wand for a fraction of the cost of the park varieties, which cost upwards of $35.

These wands are themed with all their favorite characters, including Mickey Mouse, Tiana, Elsa, Moana, and more. They light up, play music, and come with extra bubbles so your kiddo can join in the bubble wand fun all day long. Some reviewers were not satisfied with the durability and quality of the wand, while others say it was perfect for their Disney Parks trip.

Outsmart unpredictable weather with this family pack of reusable ponchos.

According to recent reports, my family didn’t end up needing the Lingito Rain Ponchos Family Pack for rain, but we were so glad we used them on Tiana’s Bayou Adventure! We got in one of the first virtual queue time slots of the morning, and without the ponchos, we would have been utterly soaked for the rest of the day. This family pack gets the job done at keeping your family (and your backpacks) dry, whether the water is weather or ride-related. The adult ponchos have drawstrings, and while I understand they might pose a hazard for kids, I wish the kid ponchos could tighten for a better fit. My kids held theirs closed just under their chins when we dropped down the log flume.

According to recent reports, they come compactly packed in small disposable bags, and you’ll be hard-pressed to fold them back in after you open them. The Amazon listing describes these ponchos as both reusable and disposable, which is accurate. While they can be dried out and used again on a trip, they might be too much trouble to save for your next adventure (however, one reviewer reports their family has used their set again and again). Still, at $10 for a pack of four (two adult and two kid-sized ponchos), they are well worth throwing in your bag every day in case you get caught in one of those notorious surprise Orlando rain showers – or just so you stay dry on wet rides.

This wearable fan rests around your neck for hands-free cooling wherever you go.

If you're worried about the relentless Orlando heat more than any other part of your Disney trip, do yourself a favor and pack the FrSara Portable Neck Fan. It’s encased blade vents blow air all the way around the back of the neck and out the ends to keep you noticeably cooler without having to worry about hazards like tangling hair. With a noise level of 25 dB – the equivalent of the ambient noise of a ‘silent’ PC – you can even keep it running indoors through those winding ride lines without being a nuisance to yourself or others …though it’s worth noting that some reviewers find it too loud.

In a recent development, the fan's working time ranges from four to 16 hours, and its USB-C charging port means you can recharge on the go with a portable device charger. With three speeds and 360-degree surround airflow, it might not quite make you forget you’re in Orlando, but it can certainly take the edge off the heat.

This lightweight travel stroller folds down easily and has four recline positions with tons of storage.

To pack a stroller or not to pack a stroller, that is the question for families making the pilgrimage to Disney World. If you decide to bring your own, the Summer Infant 3Dlite Stroller is our pick for Disney World for a few reasons. First, the stroller complies with Disney World’s list of prohibited items regarding stroller size, and reviewers do confirm that they used this stroller in Disney World. Second, the price is right at under $100, though it’s worth noting that single-stroller rentals at Disney World go for $15 per day, and $13 per day for multi-day rentals.

It has been revealed that the stroller is lightweight, has four recline positions for napping on the go, a pop out weather canopy, and tons of extra storage, including a cup holder, close-top bag, and large storage compartment underneath the seat. Reiewers agree that this is a great, budget-friendly stroller for travel, and is highly rated at 4.6 stars with over 7,000 reviews. Plus, it has a weight capacity of 50 pounds, which is on the upper end for most travel strollers. So if you have an older kid who might not be able to last the entire day on foot, this stroller can be a lifesaver.

Industry observers note that take it from me, even anxious, stressed-out parents can make the most of their family’s first trip to Disney World. Resolve to manage your stress level by taking good care of yourself, setting yourself up for success by planning based on what will make it magical for your family, and packing essentials that will help everyone enjoy the trip.

Sources indicate that the key is managing expectations, especially your own. Knowing that a vacation with kids is still parenting, just in a different location – and understanding that parenting in Disney World isn’t always a walk in the park – can help you make this trip every bit as magical for your kiddos as you hoped, though it likely won’t feel like it to you. So make sure you stop and take in their sweet faces when they meet their favorite characters, when they go on the ride they were so excited for, and as they watch as fireworks illuminate the night. You’ll experience the magic, guaranteed!

When can a kid ride in the front seat?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that katie Leigh Matthews is a contributing writer for Moms.com. As the mom of a sweet and sensitive 9-year-old boy and a wild and free 5-year-old girl, she brings her ever-evolving experience of parenting to everything she writes.

Sources indicate that she’s been writing forever, and professionally for three years. According to recent reports, has your big kid started asking – or downright begging – to graduate to the front seat of the car finally? Most kids start pining for the coveted spot long before they are big enough to safely sit up front.

According to recent reports, of course,safetyis your number one concern, butas their endless pleas wear you down, you might be wondering:when can I let them sit up front? Is it really that massive of a deal to keep them in the back? We’ve been there. For help, we reached out to childhood safety experts to understand why the AAP recommends waiting until at least the age of 13 before letting your child ride in the front seat.

It has been revealed that while the AAP guidelines are clear, local and federal laws (or, rather, lack thereof) muddy the waters. Lia Tuso, a Child Passenger Safety Technician (CPST) based in Buffalo, Latest York, tells Moms.com, “Unfortunately, when it comes to child passenger safety, the laws are the bare minimum.” There are no federal laws in the U.S. prohibiting children from riding in the front seat, but there are a handful of state laws. Delaware, for example, requires children to be at least 12 years old and 65 inches tall to sit in the front seat, while California mandates that children must be eight years old and over 57 inches tall. And it’s not just the U.S. – other peer nations’ laws are surprisingly lax around the topic. Most state laws in Australia, for example, require children to be at least seven years old to ride shotgun.

Industry observers note that tuso does not mince words about why younger children in the front seat of a car is so dangerous, saying, “The frontal airbags are designed to protect adult male bodies, not pre-pubescent children. The frontal airbags deploy at about 200 mph and they are designed to make contact with the average-sized male adult's bones. They simply aren't designed to protect children who don't have the same bone strength as an adult.”.

Industry observers note that corri Miller-Hobbs, a safety expert with the Children's Hospital of Richmond at VCU, agrees. She also oversees the Virginia chapter Safe Kids Worldwide and tells Moms.com, “[Keeping children under 13 in the back seat] places the child in a seating position that is further away from a frontal crash, the most common type of crash.”.

Tuso points out that research performed by the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia highlights that children who are exposed to frontal airbags are twice as likely to suffer injury than children riding in the back seat. “The injuries that are most frequently seen from children riding in the front seat are head injuries such as traumatic brain injury and superficial head trauma, thoracic/chest injuries, abdominal injuries, pelvic injuries, and orthopedic injuries such as long bone fractures,” Dr. Alexis Javier, a Pediatrician with Memorial Hermann Health System in Houston, Texas, tells Moms.com. Importantly, Miller-Hobbs adds, “Injuries vary and can depend on how close the child is sitting to the frontal airbag and whether they were correctly restrained with a child restraint or safety belt.”.

Tuso recommends seeking guidance from Child Passenger Safety Technician for every car seat transition, saying that too often, “parents will schedule a car seat installation check with a CPST for their newborn, but don't finish the journey to the front seat.”.

Industry observers note that “Oftentimes we see kids sitting upfront, who should still not only be in the back seat, but also in a booster!” Tuso says, “Most children will need a booster until ten to 12 years old. So parents should first ask, has the child maxed out the height/weight limits on their current booster seat?”.

In addition to being physically developed enough to be safe in the front seat, Tuso shares important guidelines to ensure the correct fit for an adult seatbelt on a child, called the Five-Step Test.

In a recent development, “Even if your child passes the seat belt fit test in one seating position in one vehicle, that doesn’t mean they will pass the test in all vehicles and seating positions… so be sure to perform the seat belt fit test in any vehicle and any seating position your child may utilize,” Miller-Hobbs claims. She also advises moving the passenger seat as far back from the airbag as possible for your child.

“Be sure to consider your child’s developmental level and personality when explaining the rationale,” Miller-Hobbs states, “Avoid using scary details about injuries versus talking about making healthy and safe choices, as with other aspects of their life.” She offers a few ideas to help make the backseat more appealing, such as:.

Tuso adds that watching crash test videos together on YouTube can be an effective way to demonstrate the necessity for strict rules around riding up front. “There is a lot of peer pressure around this age, especially with school drop-offs, but reminding your child of the importance of riding safely will set them up for success... even when they're driving on their own!” she notes.

“We understand caregivers and children are excited and proud when new milestones are achieved,” Miller-Hobbs adds, “However, moving out of a car seat or belt positioning booster seat into a seat belt system should not be a milestone that is rushed.” Tuso agrees, saying, “The safest place for children under 13 is the back seat. While growing up is inevitable, injuries are preventable... there's no rush to the front seat.”.

The Silent Health Problem Vets Say Most Cat Owners Never See Coming

📅 14 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1315 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Catster

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, catster is reader-supported.
  • Dental disease is one of the most common health problems seen by vets, yet it's also one of the easiest to overlook.
  • Recent findings suggest that by the time obvious signs appear, the problem may already have been developing for months or even longer, and suddenly a minor matter is a major disaster.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Dental disease is one of the most common health problems seen by vets, yet it's also one of the easiest to overlook. Cats are particularly good at hiding discomfort, so a cat with painful teeth or inflamed gums may carry on behaving normally for a surprisingly long time.

Recent findings suggest that by the time obvious signs appear, the problem may already have been developing for months or even longer, and suddenly a minor matter is a major disaster. The good news is that dental disease is largely preventable, and keeping a cat's teeth healthy doesn't necessarily mean relying on a toothbrush alone.

Plaque is where the problem begins. It forms when bacteria mix with saliva and food particles on the surface of the teeth. If plaque isn't removed, it can harden into tartar â aka calculus â within days.

In a recent development, tartar leads to inflammation of the gums, a condition known as gingivitis. This can progress to periodontitis, an infection involving the tooth root, weakening the attachment between the gum and the tooth, and eroding enamel. Eventually, the tooth starts breaking down from the inside.

It has been revealed that these conditions can all be painful. A cat with advanced dental disease may drool, paw at its mouth, drop food while eating, or stop eating altogether. Bad breath, bloody saliva, teeth chattering, and even sneezing can also be warning signs.

Unfortunately, cats don't always make their discomfort obvious, which is why prevention is so notable.

Regular toothbrushing remains the most effective way to prevent dental disease in cats. Daily brushing removes plaque before it has the chance to harden into tartar and tackles one of the main causes of dental problems.

It has been revealed that A toothbrush or finger brush designed for cats should be used with toothpaste specifically formulated for felines. Human toothpaste contains ingredients that can be harmful if swallowed.

In a recent development, it's much easier to establish the habit when a cat is young, making it an enjoyable, even fun part of their routine. Older cats can learn too, although a slow approach with plenty of positive reinforcement gives the best chance of success.

Even brushing every few days is better than not brushing at all, although daily brushing provides the greatest benefit.

For cats that arenât tolerating a brush, dental wipes can be a good option.

For cats that won't tolerate brushing, dental diets and treats can provide another option. Dental dry foods contain ingredients and have a texture that are designed to help reduce plaque formation. The limitation is that not every cat actually chews its food. Some cats swallow their food with very little chewing, which reduces the potential benefit.

When choosing dental products, the Veterinary Oral Health Council seal is a useful indicator of effectiveness. Products carrying the VOHC seal have been independently tested and shown to reduce plaque or tartar.

Recent findings suggest that prescription dental diets are also available through veterinarians. They typically use oversized kibble designed to encourage more contact with the teeth during chewing and may be worth considering for cats with a history of dental problems.

Sources indicate that dental treats and chews have a similar action to dental diets, but are often made from more palatable ingredients to encourage cats to chew them. As a result, they can be quite high in calories, so make sure you include them in your catâs daily allowance.

More recently, powders containing brown algae or seaweed have been showing promising results in the fight against tartar formation, but some cats arenât keen on the taste.

Oral rinses offer another preventative option for cats that resist brushing and aren't suitable for dietary changes. They can be applied using gauze or a soft cloth and work by chemically reducing plaque and tartar before they build up.

The VOHC seal can again help when choosing between products. A veterinarian can also recommend an appropriate rinse for an individual cat.

Industry observers note that water additives are one of the easiest dental care options because they are simply added to a cat's drinking water. They work by helping inhibit plaque formation.

According to recent reports, there are some vital limitations, however. A cat that doesn't drink enough water may not receive much benefit, while some additives can change the smell or taste of the water enough that a cat avoids drinking it.

A VOHC-approved water additive can be a useful addition to a broader dental care routine, but it is unlikely to be enough on its own.

It has been revealed that plaque prevention gels are often used after a professional dental cleaning. They can help protect newly cleaned teeth and extend the time before another cleaning is needed.

Sources indicate that veterinarians commonly recommend these gels as a follow-up to professional dental treatment rather than as a standalone daily solution. Any instructions about feeding and drinking after application should be followed carefully.

Even cats receiving regular dental care at home may eventually need a professional cleaning. This is performed under general anesthesia, allowing the veterinarian to clean below the gum line, examine each tooth closely, take dental X-rays when necessary, and identify teeth that need to be removed.

The need for anesthesia can understandably concern some owners, but untreated dental disease can lead to chronic pain, infection, and systemic illness.

Senior cats and cats with a history of dental problems may also need their teeth assessed more frequently than during a standard annual examination. Finding problems early generally means treatment can be simpler and less invasive.

There has been a rise in the number of businesses offering dentals without anesthesia, at a price much lower than a dental procedure with your vet. While the idea of a cheaper dental cleaning without the worry of your cat going under anesthetic is appealing, the most significant periodontal disease happens below the gumline. Cats in particular are susceptible to a painful condition known as feline oral resorptive lesions (FORLs), in which the tooth slowly dissolves. FORLs can develop in completely clean teeth. They often form in the roots and need to be diagnosed using dental x-ray.

A catâs teeth may look clean after an anesthetic-free dental, but there could be painful problems going on beneath the surface.

Sources indicate that dental disease isn't inevitable, but preventing it requires more than waiting for obvious symptoms to appear. Cats can hide dental pain remarkably well, meaning a seemingly healthy mouth may already have problems developing beneath the surface.

Regular brushing is the most effective option, but dental diets, treats, rinses, water additives, and professional cleaning can all play a role. The right combination will depend on the individual cat and how well they tolerate each approach.

Keeping on top of dental care can help prevent painful problems from becoming something a cat has to quietly live with for years.

#102053. The Origin of "Dad" And Why Some Men Prefer to Be Called "Father"

📅 30 May 2025 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (985 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fatherly ↗ Open Full Page

The Origin of "Dad" And Why Some Men Prefer to Be Called "Father"

📅 30 May 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (985 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The nicknames we use for parents go in and out of fashion, age to age and era to era.
  • But why have we ditched ‘father’ for dad?
  • “It’s from ‘dada,’” claims Professor John H.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The nicknames we use for parents go in and out of fashion, age to age and era to era. At one time, men preferred “Sire.” Other times, “Father” was preferable. What we do know is that the most agreed-upon way to refer to dad these days is by calling him, well, ‘dad.’.

But why have we ditched ‘father’ for dad? The short answer is that things have gotten a little less formal. But the reason we’ve moved away from formality is that we’ve embraced what’s more linguistically natural for children and parents. ‘Father’ comes from the Proto-Indo-European “pəter” and Old English ‘fæder,’ meaning “he who begets a child,” reflecting the baby-talk sound “pa” as well as a phonetic shift from ‘p’ to ‘f’ in Middle English.

However, ‘dad’ did not evolve from ‘father.’.

“It’s from ‘dada,’” claims Professor John H. McWhorter, a professor at Columbia University, “a natural sound from children’s mouths as a second stab at consonants after they try the most natural ‘mama.’ Next is often either ‘dada, ‘tata,’ ‘baba’ or … ‘papa.’ Upon which, ‘father’ starts in Proto-Indo-European as “puh-TAIR,” and the ‘puh’ part is this same thing: what started as ‘pa’ in ‘papa.’ The words for Mommy and Daddy are the closest thing to linguistic universals because they are about mouth anatomy in infants rather than thought.”.

There are also another key reason why this is reinforced over time. Emie Tittnich, a specialist at the University of Pittsburgh, speaking to Live Science, noted that parents generally refrain from using pronouns like ‘I’ or ‘you’ to avoid confusing their kids with abstract concepts early on. “‘Parents will use [‘mommy’ and ‘daddy’] to help their children learn the role names and also to indicate the relationship, ‘mommy and me,'” says Tittnich. “It usually takes the child awhile to understand that the same person can be called two different names.”.

The agreed-upon naturality of these linguistic principles mean that as American society has become more colloquial and secular over time, we move (at least in this instance) away from a term that’s reflective of a status quo based in rigid concepts of class and religion—one of the meanings of ‘fæder’ in Old English is ‘supreme being,’ according to the Online Etymology Dictionary. As a result, we’re generally caught off guard when we hear a child refer to a parent as ‘father.’.

However, this is not the case unanimously. We spoke with six dads who prefer — or simply stuck with — ‘father’ instead of ‘dad.’ Some do it as an homage to their own fathers; others do it to sound more authoritative. Others do it because it’s what their kids like. All have their reasons and, maybe, deep inside, some are just big fans of Proto-Indo-European language. Here’s what they say.

I sometimes worry that it sounds a little austere out loud, but it’s just what my father always asked us to call him, and it felt like it was important to me that we carry that on. No one in my family has had a problem with it. I think you can still be a ‘dad’ and be called ‘father,’ if that makes sense. It’s basically semantic, in that way, but it’s also more than semantics. — John, Baltimore, MD.

It’s less of a request or a demand or anything, but when we were teaching my oldest what everything is called, we always just remarked ‘this is your mother’ and ‘this is your father,’ and he liked to say that, too. So we’ve kept it. I’d be lying if I said I didn’t think it was just adorably proper to have our little man coming up to us and saying, “father, mother, may I use the bathroom,” or what have you. But as with everything, I don’t mind anything that seems to feel natural for my kids and makes them happy. — Eric, Austin, Texas.

According to recent reports, my son didn’t start until he was older. I think he thought it sounded more respectful, or just more professional. We’ve always been a more traditional family, in how we carry ourselves, I guess you would say. So perhaps this was his way of taking that in stride, or contributing to that. My wife teases me about it sometimes. I should clarify, it’s generally him introducing me to other people that way. ‘This is my father, have you met my father?’ etc. — Patrick, Twin Cities, MN.

In the past two years, my older daughter, age 21, began calling me ‘father’ and as strange as I found it, I didn’t mine it at all. Now, my four-year-old calls me “father” and I guess I now have a upcoming title. As long as I am not being called ‘Henry,’ I am okay with it. — Henry, Boston, MA.

Sources indicate that I have eight children—three boys and five girls. I’ve always asked that they call me ‘father’ not to be domineering but because the house could get a little chaotic, as you can imagine, and my wife and I felt that it was a label that was more authoritative and kept things from being too chaotic. ‘Please don’t touch your father’s golf clubs’ just has a better ring to it, I guess. — Elliott, Charlotte, NC.

In a recent development, I love that my children call me ‘father,’ because of the sense of responsibility it instills in me. Your ‘dad’ or ‘daddy’ is there to lend you the car, your ‘father’ is there to raise you, and protect you and make sure that you have the tool you need to succeed in life. When my kids call me ‘father,’ it reignites that sense of purpose for me every day, and reminds me it’s up to me to make their world a great place to grow up in. — Sam, Alachua Country, FL.

This article was originally published on May 17, 2019.

Industry observers note that throughout October, we are throwing our support behind the mission to turn Feral Cat Day into Feral Cat Awareness Month, an opportunity to raise awareness about community cats (also called feral or stray), promote Trap-Neuter-Return, and recognize the millions of caring people who dedicate their time and energy to improving the lives of the cats & kittens most in need of support. With around 60-100 million stray cats in the US, we know it takes more than just one day to make a meaningful difference in a problem this overwhelming, and one group that understands this more than most is The Cat Network in Miami, Florida.

According to recent reports, founded in 1995, The Cat Network is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization supported by more than 2,500 volunteers and donors, helping community cats, stray, abandoned, and homeless cats throughout South Florida while supporting the people who care for them. Through education, low-cost spay/neuter services, adoption assistance, and advocacy, the organization works to humanely reduce cat overpopulation and improve the lives of cats and the communities they live in.

The Cat Network is dedicated to humanely reducing cat overpopulation in South Florida through five core pillars: education, sterilization, adoption, advocacy, and humane public policy. Our story begins more than 30 years agoâ¦.

Sources indicate that in July 1995, the City Manager of Miami Beach contracted with a commercial trapper, Humane Animal Removal, to trap and euthanize the cityâs feral cats, with a bounty of $35.00 for each cat trapped and killed. When this became public, a local and national outcry ensued, and the media had a field day. The Cat Network, still in its infancy, helped organize local opposition to the trap-kill plan. Susan Fleming, president of The Cat Network and a Miami Beach resident, was instrumental in negotiating with the City to institute TNR instead. With help from Animal Controlâs mobile animal clinic and SoBe spay/neuter certificates, we convinced the City to implement the more humane approach of TNR.

The following year, we began our spay/neuter certificate program with participating veterinary clinics, the first of which was Galloway Animal Clinic. Since 1995, we've helped sterilize more than 122,000 cats and assisted in the adoption of more than 24,000 cats.

Industry observers note that what makes us unique is our comprehensive approach. Rather than simply responding to the symptoms of overpopulation, we focus on preventing future litters while helping cats in need. Our programs include the Miami Meow Mobile, low-cost spay/neuter vouchers, adoption referrals through an extensive foster network, public education, and advocacy for Trap-Neuter-Return (TNR) as the most humane and effective way to manage community cat populations.

According to recent reports, one of our biggest challenges is simply the sheer number of cats needing help. Because South Florida has warm weather year-round, kitten season never truly ends. This creates an ongoing demand for spay and neuter services, foster homes, adoptions, and community education. Every day we receive calls from residents who have discovered kittens, injured cats, or growing community cat colonies.

There really isn't an "off season" for cat rescue here, so our volunteers and veterinary programs stay busy throughout the entire year. Preventing unwanted litters through early sterilization is one of the most effective ways to reduce this constant cycle.

Industry observers note that funding is another ongoing challenge. Keeping our veterinary programs affordable requires significant community support, and the costs of medical supplies, equipment, and operations continue to rise.

People can make an enormous difference by:.

Donating to support our programs.

Becoming a volunteer or foster caregiver.

Spaying and neutering their own pets.

Helping community cats through TNR.

Sharing our educational resources and adoptable cats on social media.

Becoming a member of The Cat Network.

Every donation, volunteer hour, and shared post helps save lives.

Recent findings suggest that over the past 30 years, The Cat Network has become one of South Florida's leading organizations dedicated to reducing cat overpopulation. Sterilizing more than 122,000 cats and helping over 24,000 cats find homes are milestones that represent countless lives saved.

Recent findings suggest that we're especially proud of the Miami Meow Mobile, which has dramatically increased access to affordable veterinary care, and our long-standing network of volunteers and foster caregivers who make our adoption program possible. Together, these programs have helped thousands of residents become part of the solution while improving animal welfare throughout South Florida.

According to recent reports, the Miami Meow Mobile is a fully equipped veterinary clinic designed specifically for cats. Originally envisioned in 2001 and released in 2005, it was created to make affordable veterinary care accessible to more people throughout the community.

Sources indicate that today, the Meow Mobile provides low-cost spay and neuter surgeries, vaccinations, testing, microchipping, parasite treatments, and basic wellness services. Originally designed as a traveling clinic, it presently operates from a fixed location in Kendall, allowing us to serve a large number of cats efficiently and safely.

The Meow Mobile remains one of our signature programs because every surgery performed helps prevent future litters and reduces shelter overcrowding throughout South Florida.

In a recent development, our Spay/Neuter Certificate Program partners with participating veterinarians throughout South Florida. Residents can purchase discounted certificates that cover sterilization surgery, a rabies vaccination, and ear tipping for community cats.

This partnership expands access to affordable veterinary care beyond our own clinic. If someone discovers a stray or community cat in their neighborhood, the voucher program provides an affordable pathway to have that cat sterilized before additional litters are born.

By working together with local veterinary clinics, we're able to reach far more cats than we could alone and give residents practical tools to help solve the community cat problem.

Working with cats means no two days are ever alike. Volunteers have rescued kittens from engine compartments, construction sites, shopping centers, and backyard sheds. Every rescue brings its own surprisesâand often a few scratches and plenty of memorable stories.

The resilience of these cats never stops amazing us. Watching frightened community kittens transform into affectionate family pets is one of the most rewarding experiences we witness over and over again.

Every cat that is sterilized prevents countless future kittens from being born into homelessness. Every adoption changes two livesâthe cat's and the family's.

Knowing that thousands of volunteers, donors, veterinarians, and community members are working together toward the same goal makes every success even more meaningful.

As we celebrate over 30 years of service, our goal remains the same: continuing to expand access to affordable spay and neuter serviceswhile working toward a future where no healthy or treatable cat is euthanized simply because there are too many homeless animals.

We continue to strengthen our community partnerships, grow volunteer involvement, support foster caregivers, and educate the public about responsible pet ownership and Trap-Neuter-Return practices.

Anyone interested in getting involved can learn more by visiting TheCatNetwork.org. There they can become a member, volunteer, foster cats, adopt, donate, or schedule services through the Miami Meow Mobile.

📅 30 May 2025 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (445 w)

How Fatherhood Changes Men's Brains And Bodies Forever

📅 30 May 2025 | ⏱️ 2 min read (445 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Men experience neurobiological and physiological changes to prime them for fatherhood — not unlike how women’s bodies prepare them for motherhood.
  • Recent findings suggest that we know how women’s bodies adapt to motherhood.
  • In 2014, a team of scientists at Emory University recruited 88 heterosexual, biological, married fathers of children between the ages of 1 and 2, for an unprecedented experiment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Men experience neurobiological and physiological changes to prime them for fatherhood — not unlike how women’s bodies prepare them for motherhood.

Recent findings suggest that we know how women’s bodies adapt to motherhood. Hormonal shifts, neurological flips, and, of course, the obvious post-partum biological changes. But only recently have scientists begun to focus on how men’s bodies adapt to fatherhood. We now know that fathers experience changes in their hormone levels (especially testosterone and oxytocin); their brains respond differently to parent-related stimuli, and even their socioeconomic status tends to change once children arrive.

Here’s the data behind these conclusions:.

In 2014, a team of scientists at Emory University recruited 88 heterosexual, biological, married fathers of children between the ages of 1 and 2, for an unprecedented experiment. They tested their hormone levels (among other metrics) and compared these results to a group of 50 non-fathers. One of the most striking results is depicted below. Compared to non-fathers, dads had lower levels of testosterone, a male hormone linked to aggression, and higher levels of oxytocin, a hormone thought to play a role in maternal (and now, perhaps, paternal) attachment. The findings suggest that fathers, not just mothers, experience hormonal changes to help them adapt to their fresh roles as highly attached and less aggressive caregivers.

Recent findings suggest that after running the hormone analysis, the researchers at Emory took the experiment one step further. They hooked each man up to an fMRI—which measures activation of different brain regions—and show him images of children and adults making happy, sad, and neutral faces. In the middle frontal gyrus, a brain region responsible for face emotion processing, fathers’ brain activities spiked for children’s faces significantly more than for adult faces. As depicted below, non-father brains made no such distinction. The results suggest that fathers’ brains change, too, helping them augment empathy towards children.

Sources indicate that beyond the biological implications of fatherhood, studies have shown that men with children experience psychological and social changes, too. But, unlike women who take pay cuts when they give birth, the financial impact of fatherhood on men is quite positive. The data below comes from City University of Upcoming York research, which found that fathers in the city have made more money, on average, than non-fathers since at least 1990. It is unclear whether the sudden burden of diapers and saving for college drives men to earn more, or whether it’s simply wealthier men who choose to start families. But one thing is clear from the preponderance of research: fatherhood changes men. Financially, hormonally, and neurologically.

According to recent reports, this article was originally published on Jan. 25, 2019.

#102045. What They Don’t Tell You About Paternity Leave

📅 09 Jun 2025 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1249 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fatherly ↗ Open Full Page

What They Don’t Tell You About Paternity Leave

📅 09 Jun 2025 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1249 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Paternity leave is a time to take in the necessary seismic shift in the way you think about time management, work, and life.
  • The first month that you have a child is life-changing in ways that are hard to describe.
  • In a recent development, don’t become a statistic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Paternity leave is a time to take in the necessary seismic shift in the way you think about time management, work, and life.

The first month that you have a child is life-changing in ways that are hard to describe. While there is plenty of scientific research to back up the idea that fathers get their brains rewired by having a child, the biggest change that occurs is that your concept of time is forever altered. And that’s why, at the start of your child’s life, you need to take some time off. Taking paternity leave is one of the most important things a dad can do, not just for their partner and their child, but for themselves. This may seem obvious on paper, but the vast majority of men who have access to reasonable paternity leave benefits end up not taking advantage of it.

In a recent development, don’t become a statistic. Your time will become more precious to you than ever before once you’re a parent. And paternity leave is the only buffer you have to get yourself and your family adjusted to the upcoming normal.

Here’s how dads need to advocate for paternity leave, and what to do with your time once it happens.

Regardless of the job you're in or the pay structure, the conversation with your boss about leave shouldn’t be a question of permission, it should be a conversation about how much time you’re taking off. There may be some legal questions about what your state is technically obligated to offer you, so certainly do your homework first. But, even in the absence of a clear paternity leave policy, you shouldn’t be begging for time, but rather, approaching the conversation as a negotiation for exactly how much time is reasonable for you, versus what makes sense for your job.

If your job already has a paternity leave policy, the amount of time you should take should be the maximum amount offered. “But I don’t need all that time?” you say. Well, you probably do.

You’re going to end up needing other parenting time off, and you’re going to have to negotiate a upcoming relationship with work. This is one of the many things that paternity leave does. From pretty much now until the end of time you will have someone else’s schedule on your mind. This will impact your work schedule — not for better or worse, it just will — and paternity leave is your transition to this new juggling of schedules. In another sense, you’re setting a precedent with your job. Do you want it to be one that is sustainable? If so, take paternity leave.

Industry observers note that no matter how you think of your career, having a kid is, without question, a pivot point for it. Before now, work-life balance was more of a theory; a calculus about how many drinks you could have at happy hour versus how hungover you’d be the next day. Having a child makes all of those prior considerations seem quaint. And so, the best way to think about paternity leave is that it’s the transition from one kind of career to the next.

In your previous life, you managed your time and money, perhaps, with a shoulder shrug and a “good enough” mentality. But being a parent isn’t like that. Everything you do, from hitting a deadline to taking out the trash, matters a little bit more. Good enough isn’t really good anymore. Yes, you’re going to make mistakes. That’s what parenting is all about. But it’s also nothing like a job. You’re not clocking in and out. If you think you’re suddenly going to have time off from being a parent, you won’t.

Sources indicate that this is what makes time management so crucial — and why you need to take paternity leave to get your latest schedule in order. Because you’re not at work, you are able to live in this period of transition. It’s weird. It’s hard. But without paternity leave, you’d barely be able to process it.

According to recent reports, unless you are the primary caregiver who is nursing with the child, the vast majority of the time you’ll have a job that will suddenly be more key than you’ve ever realized — cleaning up. When it comes to bottles, breast pump parts, latest baby clothes, and blankets, keeping everything clean in those early months is essential. If your wife was the person who did laundry before, or kept an eye on your dirty dishes, those days are over.

Here’s a hot tip: Do you still have your apron from when you waited tables? Don’t have an apron? Get an apron. Preferably one with pockets. It's great for storing bottles, burp clothes, diapers, and pretty much everything else to keep your household sane.

When you add it all up, parents lose about six years of sleep when they have a child. This will not magically get resolved when your child turns six, by the way. But the strange sleep patterns that you have during those first few weeks are truly hellish. The only way to deal with this is to accept it as soon as possible. Again, this is one of the reasons why paternity leave is so key. Both you and your partner are going to have to come up with an ad hoc sleep schedule in order to literally not lose your minds.

The sooner you understand that feeding and caring for a newborn is like working a double shift that never ends, the better. If you slept on a few chairs pushed together in the delivery room when your kid was born, the first month or two aren’t too different from that. It does get better, but the sooner you get over how horrible it is, the better.

It has been revealed that chances are, your partner will be even more exhausted than you are. And so, amid all the cleaning, helping, and wrestling in your mind with your raging id, you have to remember how special this time is. Yes, take a ton of pictures. No, you’ll never regret taking a million pictures when your child is a newborn. If anything, these photos will become even more incredible to you as the years pass. You’re lucky to live in a time when you have a movie studio in your pocket. Take advantage of it. Pay for the extra phone data. Get those digital photos printed up into albums right away. It’s all worth it.

According to recent reports, but when you’re not being the support parent, when you’re not contemplating how the rest of your life is forever different, the best thing you can do is hold your child as much as possible. You’ve probably heard of the “football” grip by now, the thing where you can fit your kid into the crook of your arm. This is one of the coolest things ever, and it may seem like it will never end, but you won’t believe how fast this time goes.

Newborn babies sleep all the time. Yes, statistically, they’re going to do a significant chunk of that sleeping with mom. But you’re on paternity leave for one big reason, a reason that is more important than all the other reasons: You need to put that kind on your chest, and in your arms, and make sure this little person knows that they are safe with you, forever.

#102042. The 25 Most Crucial Fatherhood Moments In the Past 25 Years

📅 12 Jun 2025 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3282 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fatherly ↗ Open Full Page

The 25 Most Crucial Fatherhood Moments In the Past 25 Years

📅 12 Jun 2025 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3282 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The 21st century has been the century of dads.
  • Regardless of the chaos we’ve experience in the last twenty-five years, it’s been a decent time to be a father.
  • According to recent reports, sure, you might have spent more time with the family on the farm in the 18th century, but that was primarily as a manager for your child laborers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The 21st century has been the century of dads. Never before has the idea of being a father become part of the national conversation, and never before have dads faced an onslaught of shifting mores and expectations.

Regardless of the chaos we’ve experience in the last twenty-five years, it’s been a decent time to be a father. Scratch that — it’s probably the best point in human history to be a dad.

According to recent reports, sure, you might have spent more time with the family on the farm in the 18th century, but that was primarily as a manager for your child laborers. If you were parenting during the industrial revolution, let’s just say the whole child labor thing got a lot worse — and off your watch. And what of the booming ’40 and ’50s, those supposed halcyon days that are so often held on high? Don’t let false nostalgia fool you — the infant mortality rate alone tells a different story: It has dropped 85% since the Baby Boom.

According to recent reports, it’s truly never been easier to raise a healthy and maybe even happy kid — and the past 25 years bear the fruits of this fact. From public policy shifts to pop culture moments, to an evolving conversation about the nature of masculinity, the past twenty-five years have been full of great moments for fatherhood.Here are twenty-five of our favorite moments so far this century, all of which highlight how the culture of being a dad has grown, changed, and been celebrated.

Industry observers note that if you’re not a dad, it’s easy to assume that Jerry Seinfeld stopped being relevant in the 1990s. But, one of the wonderful things about the 21st-century Seinfeld, is seeing this venerable comedian turn into a Dad Comic. In his 2020 special 23 Hours to Kill, Seinfeld brilliantly compares parenting to keeping a baby alligator in your house.

“You put it in your tub…and you feel the little…bitey…teeth. And then time passes, and you think — You know, I think we have to get this thing the hell out of here!”.

While it’s fair to say that the legacy of Bill Cosby has been tarnished, it is significant that the very first animated series to ever air on Nick at Nite is a now-defunct show called Fatherhood.

In a recent development, to be clear, Cosby wasn’t really in the show, and though it was based on one of his books called Fatherhood, this show was very much its own thing. It’s sort of hard to imagine an animated show called Fatherhood in 2025, but that doesn’t mean there shouldn’t be.

For what it’s worth, Cosby isn’t the only person who has a book titled Fatherhood. The editors of Fatherly published one, too, back in 2021. And ours is almost as funny as the Nick at Nite cartoon.

Recent findings suggest that we’re gonna have two mentions of the Star Trek franchise on this list, so get ready for that. But, honestly, in terms of fascinating pop culture moments around fatherhood, the J.J. Abrams-directed 2009 Star Trek reboot has to be discussed. First of all, the trailers for this movie really used this tagline: “This is not your father’s Star Trek.”.

The funny thing was, with that sh*t-eating grin, Chris Pine’s James T. Kirk was very much representative of an old-school take on Star Trek, a ton of action, punching, and one-liners. The movie was also literally about fathers and sons, and how people forge their own paths outside of the legacy they’re expected to carry. Plus, can you believe that a pre-Thor Chris Hemsworth played Chris Pine’s dad?

In a recent development, today, George Lucas has four kids in total, but during the era of the Star Wars prequels, from 1999 to 2005, he had three: Amanda, Katie, and Jett. And all of them were in Star Wars. But, because Lucas is classy and didn’t want to make this into a major nepotism thing, those kids are all in fairly under-the-radar, secret roles.

In a recent development, katie was even credited as “Jenna Green” for a background role in The Phantom Menace. Meanwhile, Jett plays a young padawan named “Zett Jukassa,” seen briefly in Revenge of the Sith. Finally, Amanda had a small background role in Revenge of the Sith, alongside her father.

Is being a father the way you see yourself? If you were a dad in the 20th century, the answer would be very different than it is today. According to a Pew Research Center survey published in 2023, 85 percent of fathers with kids under 18 claim that being a parent is either the most or one of the most “crucial aspects of who they are as a person.”.

Recent findings suggest that this is huge. Identifying as a father first is simply something that wasn’t in vogue a few decades back. In the 1980s, comedies like Mr. Mom seemed edgy because of a challenge to gender norms. Now, those gender norms are utterly different.

Though the late Gene Hackman’s portrayal of patriarch Royal Tennenbaum gets a lot of the attention in The Royal Tenenbaums, this modern classic has another great dad role model. Yes, Ben Stiller is the man who gave us Zoolander, and currently, the mind behind Severance. But, in Wes Anderson’s modern classic, he also gave us a tender and hilarious portrayal of fatherhood.

It has been revealed that chas Tenenbaum is a widow, and as such, strives to be the ultimate parent, concerned with safety, and essentially begins the movie as a laughable helicopter parent. But by the end of the movie, Chas makes peace with his own dad, his demons, and learns to lighten up a bit. We could all have a bit of this character’s desire for organization for our kids. And we could all learn to change, too.

Industry observers note that people can disagree on various concerns around youth sports, but one thing all dads know is true is simple: You’ve got to support your kids. And so, NBA legend Dwyane Wade’s support of his daughter, Zaya Wade, is an exceptional example of what it looks like when dads step up.

Sources indicate that on February 25, 2023, at the 54th NAACP Image Awards, Wade made it clear that standing with Zaya, who is trans, was his duty as a father. “Zaya, as your father, all I’ve wanted to do was get it right,” he said. “I admire how you’ve handled the ignorance in our world ... that you face every day. To say that your village is proud of you is an understatement. Thank you for showing me that there’s more than just one way to communicate effectively.”.

It has been revealed that the fact that Eminem sings a track rather than raps would be a significant cultural moment. But, Eminem’s “Hailie’s Song” in 2002 was a bigger deal than perhaps we’ve admitted. Prior to “Hailie’s Song” the image of Eminem was a little less sympathetic, but the utterly honest sentiment of the song for his daughter changed all that.

It’s a song about a parent trying to explain the conflicting emotions inside all of us. Whether or not Eminem is a great dad or not isn’t the point. This song was a big deal.

Go to a party and talk to a dad about what they’re reading. At least half the time, if you mention Lee Child’s Jack Reacher books, you’re going to get a substantial smile. Boomer dads love Reacher. GenX dads love Reacher. Millennial dads love Reacher. Right now, the Amazon Prime Video version of Reacher is one of the biggest shows on the planet, which makes sense since the fan base has been ready for this show since 1997.

It has been revealed that but what’s significant about Reacher as a TV series is that it’s a vast improvement over the forgettable Tom Cruise movies Jack Reacher (2012) and Jack Reacher: Never Go Back (2016). Crusie was totally miscast as Reacher in those films, and as such, those flicks nearly ruined an excellent action franchise. Reacher is popular because he’s a vargant Sherlock Holmes fused with an American James Bond. Alan Ritchson’s take on the character has done what Cruise couldn’t do: Bring Reacher to the people.

In a recent development, although Matthew McConaughey’s father passed away in 1992, he’s more recently come forward about how that death impacted him and his worldview. “Through the mourning and the pain, it’s the biggest moment of becoming a man.”McConaughey explained in a 2025 conversation with Interview. “There’s a certain safety net that I’ve always had behind me that’s gone.”.

In a recent development, for many of us, McConaughey is like a Texan version of Yoda; he seems like he contains endless wisdom, and his approach toward life, love, and family is endlessly inspirational. And so, for him to be so clearly vulnerable about losing a parent is incredible. Losing a parent rewires your brain, regardless of age.

There had never really been midnight releases for books until the year 2000. And this meant that the beginning of the century was kicked off with moms and dads driving their little witches and wizards to bookstores to get the latest Harry Potter books.

While the first three books were very successful, the release of Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire in the year 2000 created an utterly new phenomenon. Many kids were driven to these midnight events by their parents, and a ton of those kids are parents now themselves.

We have a complicated relationship with Hogwarts and the Wizarding World these days, but for parents and kids, the Harry Potter midnight madness was a uniquely 21st-century event.

As soon as Mark Zuckerberg made Facebook available to the general public, the era of the chat room officially died, and the world of Facebook groups was born. Today, Facebook skews a bit older than some of the other social media platforms, and that’s probably because 19 years ago, contemporary dads were all still in their twenties.

We got on Facebook back then, we created friend groups around different interests (Soccer, Video Games, Seinfeld memes), and now, we’re still there. Facebook groups didn’t start as Dad Groups, but that’s what time does to you.

LeVar Burton and Mica Burton, father and daughter, playing, father and daughter.

Industry observers note that if there’s anyone who really should have the title of America’s TV Dad, it’s LeVar Burton. Not only did he raise generations of readers on Reading Rainbow, thanks to his role as Geordi La Forge in Star Trek: The Next Generation, but he also inspired countless people to tackle the STEM fields in newly introduced and innovative ways.

In 2023, Burton brought all of this metafictionally full circle. In the critically acclaimed Season 3 of Star Trek: Picard, Burton co-starred with his real-life daughter, Mica Burton, who played his onscreen daughter, Alandra La Forge. When those episodes aired, Fatherly talked to Burton about how Geordi was portrayed as a sweetly overprotective parent. Burton’s response was perfect: “I don’t know a dad who’s not overprotective. All dads are overprotective. I mean, we live in a culture and in a society where that is our primary responsibility, to protect, defend, and provide for. That’s why we’re here.”.

Today, it is well understood that The National is the most “dad rock” bands presently in existence on the planet. But this wasn’t always the case. There’s no way the band thought of themselves this way back in the early aughts, but something changed after the release of their 2010 masterpiece High Violet.

Without really meaning to, The National transitioned from being a really good band to the most notable rock band for a certain kind of 30-something and 40-something man. High Violet is the beginning of the version of The National we have now, and fifteen years later, we still owe money to the money, to the money that we owe.

When Robert Downey Jr. uttered the words “I am Iron Man” in 2008, it changed the game for male cinematic heroes. And so, it’s still hard to grasp that just eleven years later, in Avengers: Endgame, the heroic Tony Stark would die. But the most compelling thing about the journey of fatherhood across the saga of Iron Man wasn’t him defeating Thanos. Instead, it was Tony’s relationship with his daughter, Morgan Stark (Lexi Rabe).

As all dads know, sometimes kids come up with hilarious phrases to express their affection, and Lexi’s “I love you 3000” remains perfect because it’s so real.

Sources indicate that one of the toughest afflictions that parents have to suffer in the modern age is the existence of a militia of mutant canines hellbent on providing alternative forms of law enforcement, healthcare, and basic public safety. We don’t know if the Paw Patrol is funded at all by taxpayer money, and we don’t want to know. (In the 2021 movie, we’re meant to think raw capitalism funds the Paw Patrol.).

It has been revealed that in any case, Paw Patrol is a whole thing, and so, the moment in which Dax Shepard both embraced and mocked Paw Patrol in an ad for Paw Patrol was a perfect catharsis. Paw Patrol kind of sucks, but it also knows that it sucks.

Paid paternity leave is more robust in the 2020s than it's ever been before. In fact, laws around giving employees paid paternity leave have only been strengthened in the past few years, not weakened. If you are a new dad and you’re wondering about taking time off in those early months, you shouldn’t really wonder. There’s a whole world of benefits for dads out there that simply weren’t as prevalent in the previous century.

No excuses, check out our guide to paid time off right here.

Daniel Craig’s 2021 swan song as James Bond wasn’t necessarily the best-loved 007 movie of all time, but it did deliver one of the best dad moments of the century. For decades, James Bond was a symbol beloved by dads, but a character who existed in a childless space.

Sources indicate that no Time To Die flipped the script on all of that, by revealing that 007 has a five-year-old daughter, Mathilde Swann (Lisa-Dorah Sonnet), whom Madeleine Swann (Léa Seydoux) has kept a secret. By the end of the movie, Bond has to die to make sure Madeleine and Mathilde can live. It would have been nice for Bond to live and be a family man, but as a symbol, the idea that 007 ends his life for his family was a powerful moment.

Recent findings suggest that regardless of how you feel about Bluey, the fact of the matter is that in terms of cartoon dads, the character of Bandit (voiced by David McCormack) has eclipsed all other cartoon dads. Not as overtly progressive as Daniel Tiger’s dad, but also not as horrible and useless as, say, Homer Simpson, the character of Bandit straddles the line between realism and aspiration with impressive nuance.

We may not all want to be Bandit at all times, but there is some version of various dads in him. Like it or not, this is the one that all future cartoon dads will be compared to.

It has been revealed that when Professor Robert Kelly had a work call interrupted while on global news, a meme was born. He didn’t mean to become “BBC Dad,” but the hilarious moments in which his Kelly’s children waltzed into his work-from-home office touched a nerve with the parenting population of the world.

Sources indicate that ironically, just a few years later, after the lockdowns of 2020, many of us became BBC Dad, and in truth, many of us still are. The nice thing about BBC Dad, was that we could all agree that it was normal for your kids to exist right alongside your professional life. Things are messy, and you’re doing a lot of jobs at the same time. For many of us, it seems like our working hours never end, and that’s because, in truth, as a father, you’re never off the clock.

In a recent development, prior to the 21st century, nobody needed to explain why J.R.R. Tolkien’s books were wonderful. And yet, in 2001, with the debut of Peter Jackson’s major screen adaptation The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring, an entirely latest pop culture vocabulary was codified. Fathers benefited from this because they either shared the films and the stories with their kids for the first time or were kids themselves when these films hit theaters. (Using Hobbit math, we’re counting being a teenager or being in your early 20s as a “kid” here.).

Recent findings suggest that for those who haven’t read Tolkien out loud to their kid, you’re missing out. And, it’s possible, without the popularity of The Lord of the Rings movies, several generations of parents wouldn’t have had the renewed permission to do so.

Of all 21st-century presidents, regardless of party or ideology, Barack Obama is easily the best symbol of a father figure who is as aspirational as he is relatable. As the dad of Sasha and Malia, Obama was present and also honest about his shortcomings.

In 2021, Fatherly spoke to President Obama about how to find time to slow down and see your child grow up. He mentioned coaching Sasha’s basketball team, “even in the midst of the presidency.” He talked about the sheer “joy” of those moments, and regretted that he hadn’t “planned to have more of that” and a little “less of meetings in the situation room.”.

The reason this is so powerful is that Obama, like so many dads, admits when it gets it wrong. Having regrets and feeling like you wanted to be more present is part of the journey of fatherhood, and as a leader and example for other dads, Obama gets it.

Recent findings suggest that whether you think about Bob Odenkirk as one part of Mr. Show, or maybe Saul from Breaking Bad and Better Call Saul, the truth is, the man is a national treasure. Brilliantly, he also showed parents everywhere how to be better at their most important job.

In 2023, along with his daughter Erin (who provided the illustrations), Odenkirk released a collection of children’s poetry called Zilot. Here’s the thing: These poems were ones that Odenkirk wrote with his kids when they were much smaller. “I want to tell everyone, any parent who's thinking of trying this, and I hope you are, that I really did let the kids write the poems,” Odenkirk told Fatherly when the book was released. The result was not only a great book (seriously, quirky kids will love it) but also an important lesson to parents everywhere: Make things with your kids.

In a recent development, during the age of the Baby Boomers, it was still possible to think of dads as distant, uninvolved people. Martin Amis described this phenomenon as being a “parent emeritus.” You’ve got the title. You’re hanging around. But what do you actually do?

This attitude has shifted substantially in the 21st century. As of 2022, according to The Institute for Family Studies, college-educated fathers with children under age 18 at home now spend an average of 10 hours, 12 minutes a week on child care. Overall, the trend indicates that dads are 33 percent more involved with caregiving than they were in the previous century. Basically, the latest generations of dads are nothing like the dads we grew up with. Which, hopefully, means the future will be even better.
